Part 1 

General organization of CNS 

Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) 

1. Choose the INCORRECT matching: 
a. Diencephalon - 37 ventricle. 
b. Midbrain - cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius. 
c. Cerebral hemisphere - lateral ventricle. 
d. Hind brain - 4™ ventricle. 
e. Mesencephalon - 2"d ventricle. 

2. Choose the CORRECT statement: 
a. In spinal cord, white matter is H-shaped. 
b. In brain stem, white matter surrounds grey matter. 
c. Cerebral hemispheres contain deep nuclei formed of grey matter. 
d. In cerebellum, white matter forms the outer cortex. 
e. In spinal cord, grey matter surrounds white matter. 

3-7. For each term in the left column, choose the appropriate description 
in the right column: 
3. Ganglion. a. A collection of cell bodies within CNS. 
4. Tract. b. A Bundle of nerve fibers outside CNS. 
5. Nucleus. c. A collection of ascending fibers within 

brain stem. 
6. Lemniscus. d. A collection of cell bodies outside CNS. 
7. Nerve. e. A bundle of nerve fibers within CNS. 

8. The nucleus is: 
a. A group of cell bodies within peripheral nervous system. 
b. A group of cell bodies within central nervous system. 
c. A group of nerve fibers within peripheral nervous system. 
d. A group of nerve fibers within central nervous system. 
e. A collection of nerve fibers in brain stem. 

9. Choose the CORRECT matching: 
a. Ganglion - a group of cell bodies within CNS. 
b. Pathway - a chain of successive tracts having different functions. 
c. Lemniscus - a collection of descending fibers within the brain stem. 
d. Afferent - an output going away from a certain structure. 
e. Tract - a bundle of nerve fibers within CNS. 

1



10. A chain of successive tracts in CNS having the function is called: 
a. Fasciculus b. Pathway 
c. Lemniscus d. Commissure 
e. Decussation 

11. A bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS having the same beginning, 
termination and function is called: 
a. Pathway b. Tract 
¢. Lemniscus d. Commissure 
e. Decussation 

Answers of MCQs 

Remarks 

Mesencephalon = midbrain. Its cavity is cerebral aqueduct. 
Cerebral hemispheres contain deep nuclei formed of grey M. 
(a) is wrong because in spinal cord, grey matter is H-shaped. 
(b) is wrong because in brain stem, grey matter form deep nuclei. 
(d) is wrong because in cerebellum, grey matter forms outer cortex. 
(e) is wrong because in spinal cord, white matter surrounds grey 

matter. 

Ganglion = A collection of cell bodies outside CNS. 

Tract = A bundle of nerve fibers within CNS. 

Nucleus = A collection of cell bodies within CNS. 

Lemniscus = A collection of ascending fibers within brainstem. 

Nerve = A Bundle of nerve fibers outside CNS. 

The nucleus is a group of cell bodies within PNS. 
The tract = a bundle of nerve fibers within CNS. 
(a) is wrong because Ganglion = group of cell bodies within PNS. 
(b) is wrong because Pathway = a chain of successive tracts having 
same functions. 
(c) is wrong because Lemniscus = a collection of ascending fibers 
within the brain stem. 
(d) is wrong because Afferent - an input going towards a certain 
structure. 

10 Pathway = a chain of successive tracts in CNS having same functions. 
11 Tract = A bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS having the same 

beginning, termination and function.

Essay Questions 

1. Describe venous drainage of face & its applied anatomy. 
2. Give an account on branches of facial artery in face. Describe the 
anastomosis in which it shares. 
3. Enumerate the arteries of the scalp. Mention the origin of each artery. 
4. Enumerate nerves of scalp in front of auricle. 
5. Enumerate nerves of scalp behind of auricle. 
6. Describe branches of Ophthalmic nerve that share in nerve supply of face. 
7. Describe branches of Maxillary nerve that share in nerve supply of face. 
8. Describe branches of Mandibular nerve that share in nerve supply of face. 
9. Describe branches of facial nerve in neck & its terminal branches. 
10. Describe parts of orbicularis oculi muscle. 

Cases 

* Case 1: A patient with an abscess in the upper lip was advised not to 
squeeze it for fear of spread of pus to a venous sinus inside skull. 
a. What is the name of sinus at risk? 
b. Describe 2 alternate pathways for passage of infection to the sinus. 
c. What other areas that have similar risk? 

* Case 2: A D years old child fell off his bicycle & his head hit the 
pavement. A 2 cm long wound in his scalp was seen. Soon, he was 
sitting in a pool of blood. 
a. Why does the scalp bleed profusely? 
b. Name the arteries that supply the scalp. 
c. Which is the dangerous layer of the scalp? Why is it dangerous? 

* Case 3: A 12-years old boy fell from a bicycle & wounded his scalp. At 
the hospital, the doctor sutured the wound to limit its gaping & to 
stop the bleeding. Later, the boy returned to the hospital with black 

14



eye. The doctor prescribed an antibiotic to avoid dangerous 

complications. 
a. Why scalp bleeding cannot be stopped except by suturing? 
b. Gaping of scalp wound indicates involvement of which layer of scalp? 

c. Explain the development of black eye. 
d. What dangerous complication did the doctor expect? 

Answers of Cases 

* Answers of Case 1: 

a. Cavernous sinus. 

b. First pathway: Facial vein - ophthalmic vein -> cavernous sinus. 
Second pathway: Facial vein - deep facial vein = pterygoid plexus of veins 

emissary veins -> cavernous sinus. 

c. Medial angle of eye, nose & cheecks. 

* Answers of Case 2: 

a. Because the scalp has a rich blood supply & the fibrous tissue in the 
connective tissue layer prevents the local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels 
in this layer. 

b. * Three arteries in front of auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital & 
Superficial temporal arteries. 

* Two arteries behind the auricle: posterior auricular & occipital arteries. 

c. Loose areolar tissue layer because it contains the emissary veins that are 
valveless & can take infection to the inside of the skull. 

* Answers of Case 3: 

a. Because the scalp has a rich blood supply & the fibrous tissue in the 

connective tissue layer prevents the local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels 
in this layer. 
b. Gaping of scalp wound indicates involvement of aponeurosis of occipito- 
frontalis muscle. 
c. If the wound causes subaponeurotic hematoma -> the blood gravitates the 
the eyelids deep to the frontal bellies of the occipito-frontalis muscle which are 
attached to the skin of eyebrows & so hematoma extends deep to it & reaches 
eyelids causing black eye. 

d. Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Cases 

Casel: A 55-year old lady developed right-sided hemiplegia together with 
affection of lower + of 7™ cranial nerve & 12™ cranial nerve due to 
cerebrovascular accident. 

a. Where is the site of the lesion? 
b. Explain the effect on 7th & 12™ cranial nerves only. 
c. Describe the function of affected area. 

Answers of Cases 

Answer of Case 1: 
a. UMNL in part of area 4 of left hemisphere. 
b. Lower %* of 7 cranial nerve nucleus & 12™ cranial nerve nucleus receive 

cortico-nuclear tract from opposite side only, while the rest of the 
cranial nerve nuclei receive bilateral cortico-nuclear tract, so they are 
not affected when the lesion is on one side. 

c. Area 4 controls voluntary movements of opposite side of body. Body is 
represented upside down & according to the skill of the movement.

Answers of MCQs 

Crus cerebri is a part of midbrain. 
Abducent N. is attached to lower border of pons above pyramid. 
Trochlear nerve is attached to back of brain stem. 

Anterior perforated substance lies outside interpeduncular fossa. 
Vestibulo-cochlear nerve is attached to cerebello-pontine angle. 
The 4™ ventricle has lateral recesses. The other recesses belong 
to the 37 ventricle. 
Medial eminence in floor of fourth ventricle is formed by fibers of 
facial nerve arching & overlies the nucleus of Abducent nerve. 
Superior angle of fourth ventricle leads to cerebral acquiduct. 
Trigeminal nerve is a pontine cranial nerve that is not attached to 
lower border of pons. It is attached to the middle of the ventral 
surface of the pons. 

10 Brain stem does not include cerebellum. However, it includes 
medulla oblongata, pons, midbrain & cerebral acquiduct which is 
enclosed within the midbrain. 

11 Rootlets of hypoglossal nerve lie between pyramid and olive.

furrow between pons and medulla

15 Facial colliculus overlies Abducent nucleus. 
16 The facial colliculus is formed by Abducent nucleus and facial 

nerve fibers arching around it.

cerebral peduncles.

Cases 

Casel. A 60 year old female complained of a sudden disturbance in gait, 
intension tremors, ptosis of right eyelid, decreased sweating on right 
side of face, decreased pain sensation on right side of face, a 
difficulty in swallowing. Pain sensation was decreased on left side of 
the body. A diagnosis of lateral medullary syndrome was made. 
a. What causes this syndrome? 
b. Analyze each of the patient's symptoms? 

Case 2. An old man starts to develop headache and by MRI proved to have 
tumour at the cerebellopontine angle. 
a. What is the 15" cranial nerve to be effected by that tumor? 
b. Enumerate the symptoms resulting from compression of that nerve? 

Case 3. A male patient was brought to the hospital with sudden onset of 
vertigo & nystagmus. The doctor discovered that the patient had 
dysphagia, Dysartheria & hoarseness of voice. On examination, the 
laryngeal & palatine muscles on the left side were paralyzed & there 
was loss of pain & temperature sensation on the left side of the face 

76



& on the right side of the body. A vascular lesion in the brain stem 
was diagnosed. 
a. Identify the case. 

Which artery is occluded? In which side (right or left)? 
Which nucleus affection that caused laryngeal & palatine paralysis? 
Explain loss of pain & temperature from left side of face. 
Explain loss of pain & temperature from right side of body. 

Answers of Cases 

* Answers of Case 1: 

a. Occlusion of right posterior inferior cerebellar artery. 
b. Analysis of symptoms: 

i. Disturbance of gait & intension tremors > due to lesion of 
spinocerebellar tract & ICP. 
ii. Ptosis of right eyelid + decreased sweating - due to ipsilateral 

Horner's syndrome -> due to lesion of descending sympathetic fibers. 
iii. Decreased pain sensation of right side of face - due to lesion of 
spinal N & tract of V. 
iv. Difficulty in swallowing = due to lesion of nucleus ambiguus > 
paralysis of muscles of palate, pharynx & larynx. 
v. Decreased pain sensation in left side of body = due to lesion of spinal 
lemniscus - contralateral loss of pain & temperature from body. 

* Answers of Case 2: 

a. Cranial nerves affected: Facial & vestibule-cochlear nerves. 

b. Compression of facial nerve -> facial paralysis & compression of vestibule- 
cochlear nerve > deafness & vertigo. 

* Answers of Case 3: 

a. Lateral medullary syndrome. 
b. Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery. 
¢. Nucleus ambiguus. 
d. Due to affection of ipsilateral spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve. 
e. Due to affection of left spinal lemniscus which carries pain & temperature 

from opposite side of body.

Cases 

Case 1: A patient presented with a red swollen and painful right eye. The 
movements of the right eye were painful and the pupil of the eye was 

86

or 



fixed and dilated. CT scan showed thrombosis of cavernous sinus. 
a. Define the venous sinus & its function. 
b. Describe the site & the contents of the cavernous sinus. 

c. Define the dangerous area of face. Explain Why this drea is dangerous. 
d. Name the veins that terminate in cavernous sinus. 

Case 2: A 20 year old student was playing baseball when the ball hit him on 
the side of the head. He immediately fell to the ground unconscious. 
After 30 seconds he felt well & decided to sit & watch the match. 
An hour later, he felt so sleepy & then he became unconscious again. 
He was taken to the hospital & a skull X-ray showed a fracture in 
the region of the pterion. 
a. Define the pterion. 
b. Why are fractures in this region extremely dangerous? 

Answers of Cases 

* Answers of Case 1: 

a. Venous sinuses are dilated venous channels situated between dural layers. Its 
functions include: i. Venous drainage of brain, skull & meninges. 

ii. Equalization of venous pressure outside & inside skull. 
iii. Drainage of CSF. 

b. Site: in middle cranial fossa on each side of body of sphenoid. Its contents 
are internal carotid artery & abducent nerve. 
¢c. The dangerous area is the triangular area of face that extends between 
medial angles of eyes & lateral angles of mouth. It includes upper lip, nose & 
medial angles of eyes. It is dangerous because infection of this area can reach 

the cavernous sinus causing its thrombosis. 
d. Refer to tributaries & communications of cavernous sinus in text book. 

* Answers of Case 2: 

a. It is the center of H-shaped sutures between 4 bones: frontal, parietal, 

temporal & greater wing of sphenoid. 
b. Because deep to it lies anterior branch of middle meningeal artery that may 
be cut causing extradural hemorrhage that may press on motor area of the 

cerebral hemisphere.

Cases 

Case 1. A patient opened his mouth widely while yawning, after which he 
could not close his mouth. 
a. Name the joint affected & its type. 
b. List the ligaments of the joint. Which one of them is important 

functionally? 
c. Mention the nerve supply of the joint. 

Case 2. During surgical removal of a tumor in the infratemporal fossa, an 
intense hemorrhage occurred. The surgeon clamped the main source 
of the arterial supply to the area. 
a. Which artery dis the surgeon clamp to stop the hemorrhage? 
b. Name the main nerve located in the fossa & its branches. 
c. After the operation, the patient complained of loss of taste sensation 

from anterior 2/3 of tongue. What is your explanation for this case. 
Name the nucleus that receives the taste sensation. 

Answers of Cases 

* Answers of Case 1: 
a. Temporo-mandibular joint - synovial condylar. 
b. Lateral temporo-mandibular ligament (most important functionally), 

stylomandibular ligament & sphenomandibular ligament. 
c. Auriculo-temporal & masseteric nerves. 

* Answers of Case 2: 
a. Maxillary artery. 
b. Mandibular nerve. 
c. Injury of lingual nerve (which contains fibers of chorda tympani) - solitary 

nucleus.

Cases 

Casel: A patient when asked to protrude his tongue outside the mouth 
cavity the doctor observed that the tip of tongue is directed to the 
left side. Facial muscles & rest of body muscles were normal. 
a. Name the injured nerve. 
b. Mention the side of the lesion. 
¢. Mention how this nerve exits the skull. 

Case 2: A passenger sitting beside an open window suddenly developed 
spasmodic pain in his neck accompanied by turning of his face to the 
right side. 
a. Name the affected muscle and its side. 
b. Mention its nerve supply. 
¢. Name the fascia enclosing this muscle. 

Case 3: A 50 year old male started to complain from difficulty in swallowing 
few weeks ago. He had a computerized tomography scan (CT scan) on 
the neck done; it revealed the presence of a swelling (most likely 
cancer) near the jugular foramen. 
a. In this patient, which nerves could be involved & led to dysphagia? 
b. Which venous sinuses are endangered by the cancer? 

Case 4. A 54 years old man presented with a tumor in the posterior cranial 
fossa. The neurologist wanted to check the integrity of the 9™, 10™ 
and 11™ cranial nerves. 
a. How can you test for integrity of vagus nerve? 
b. Enumerate sensory branches of glossopharyngeal nerve. 
c. Name the muscle(s) supplied by accessory nerve. 

127



Answers of Cases 

* Case 1: a. Hypoglossal nerve. b. Left side. 
¢c. Through hypoglossal foramen. 

* Case 2: a. left sternomastoid. b. Spinal accessory nerve. 
c. Investing cervical deep fascia. 

* Case 3: a. Cranial accessory nerve which supplies the muscles of the 
pharynx (responsible for swallowing). b. Inferior petrosal sinus. 

* Case 4: 

a. Test the integrity of the vagus nerve by examining the palatal arches 
on both sides. In case of paralysis > there is no arching & the 
uvula is deviated to the normal side. 

b. Sensory branches of glossopharyngeal nerve = tympanic, carotid, 

tonsillar & lingual. 
c. Muscles supplied by accessory nerve: 

i. spinal accessory > sternomastoid & trapezius. 
ii. cranial accessory - muscles of palate, pharynx & larynx.

Cases 

Case 1: An old man starts to develop headache and by MRI proved to have 
tumors of the medial geniculate body. 
a. Where is the medial geniculate body located? 
b. Where do its efferent fibers project to? 

* Answers of Case 1: 
a. Located below the posterior end of the thalamus. 
b. Its efferents form the auditory radiation which projects directly to the 
auditory area of cerebral cortex.

3. Describe blood supply of internal capsule. 
4. Enumerate the parts of corpus callosum & their connections. 
5. Enumerate cortical structures, subcortical structures & connecting pathways 
of limbic system. 
6. Enumerate the subarachnoid cisterns. 
7. Enumerate functions of CSF. 
8. Describe formation, circulation & absorption of CSF. 
9. Enumerate branches of internal carotid artery. 
10. Enumerate branches of vertebral artery within cranial cavity. 
11. Enumerate branches of basilar artery. 
12. Give an account on the circle of Willis (site, formation & branches). 

13. Describe central branches of circle of Willis. 
14. Enumerate branches of anterior cerebral artery. 
15. Enumerate branches of middle cerebral artery. 
16. Enumerate branches of posterior cerebral artery. 
17. Give an account on the site, blood supply & effect of lesion of the following 
cortical areas: auditory area, visual area & anterior part of paracentral lobule. 

Cases 

Case 1. An old man suddenly developed right-sided hemiplegia & hemi- 
anaaesthesia, more pronounced in the lower limb than the upper 
limb. His speech was normal. 
a. Which cerebral hemisphere was harmed? 
b. Which cerebral artery was most-likely occluded? 
c. Explain the reason for your conclusion. 
d. From where does this artery arise? 

Case 2. A 50-year-old hypertensive woman suddenly developed loss of 
sensation & weakness in her right hand. 
a. Occlusion of which cerebral artery can cause this? Explain. 
b. From where does this artery arise from? 
c. What are the deep structures that are supplied by the central 
branches of this artery? 

156



Case 3. An old man had a right-sided hemiplegia sparing the distal part of 
the lower limb following a stroke. Neurological examination & 
investigation diagnosed an intracerebral hemorrhage that interrupted 
the blood supply to the frontal & parietal lobes. 
a. Which cerebral artery was involved? 
b. List the functional areas of the parietal lobe. 
c. Would you expect the speech to be affected in this right-sided 

patient? Explein the reason of your answer. 

Case 4. An old man suddenly developed a right-sided hemiplegia with 
aphasia. He could move his foot weakly but was unable to close his 
fist at all on the affected side. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) 
proved the occurrence of cerebral embolism. 
a. Which cerebral artery was likely-occluded? Explain. 
b. Locate the speech areas that you know & mention their functions. 

Case 5. A mother brought her two-month old baby to the doctor 
complaining that her child had a large head. MRI confirmed 
hydrocephalus with enlarged lateral ventricles. 
a. Where do you expect the site of obstruction to the flow of the CSF 

exists? 
b. Describe the formation & flow of CSF. 
c. Describe the flow of the blood from the superior sagittal sinus to the 

outside of the skull. 

Answers of Cases 

* Answer of Case 1: 

a. Right hemisphere. 
b. Anterior cerebral artery. 
c. Since the speech is normal, so the lesion is not in the dominant hemisphere 
(which is the left hemisphere, if the patient is right-sided). Since the affection 
of the lower limb is more, this indicates the affection of the paracentral lobule 

(which lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere & is supplied by the 
anterior cerebral artery). 
d. Arises from internal carotid artery. 

157



* Answers of Case 2: 

a. Left middle cerebral artery due to the affection of the lower part of the 
precentral gyrus (which is supplied by the middle cerebral artery). Affection of 
the right limb indicates a lesion in the left hemisphere. 

b. Arises from internal carotid artery. 
c. Central branches of this artery supplies posterior parts of caudate & 

lentiform nuclei + upper 3 of anterior & posterior limbs of internal capsule. 

* Answers of Case 3: 

a. Middle cerebral artery. 

b. Functional areas of parietal lobe: 
i. First somatosensory area (SI) — in postcentral gyrus & post. part of 

paracentral lobule. 
ii. Second somatosensory area (SII) — in sup. lip of post. ramus of lat. sulcus 
behind central sulcus. 
iii. Taste (gustatory) area (area 43) — in sup. lip of post. ramus of lat. sulcus. 
Iv. Area of stereognosis — in superior parietal lobule. 
v. Wernicke's sensory area for speech — in supramarginal & angular gyri. 
c. Yes, there is affection of speech. Since the hemiplegia is on the right side — 
therefore, the lesion is in the left cerebral hemisphere which is the dominant 
hemisphere that contains Broca's motor area for speech. 

* Answers of Case 4: 

a. Left middle cerebral artery which supplies the lower part of the precentral 

gyrus (that controls voluntary movements of opposite upper limb). 

b. Speech Centers: 
a. Broca’s motor area of speech: It lies in the inferior frontal gyrus of 

dominant hemisphere (in pars triangularis & pars opercularis). It is the 

motor speech center. 

b. Wernicke's sensory speech area: It lies in the inferior parietal lobule 

(in supramarginal & angular gyri) & in the posterior part of superior & 

middle temporal gyri. Its function is understanding auditory & visual 
information. 

c. Supplementary motor area (in frontal lobe): superior speech center. 

158 



* Answers of Case 5: 

a. Interventricular foramen of Monroo. 
b. CSF is formed by choroid plexus of lateral ventricle - interventricular 

foramen of Monroo > 3" ventricle - cerebral acquiduct of Sylvius -> 4" 
ventricle -> subarachnoid space (through median foramen of Magendi & lateral 

foramina of Luschka) = circulate around the brain - to be absorbed by 

arachnoid villi & granulations to superior sagittal sinus. 
c. Superior sagittal sinus = right transverse sinus -> right sigmoid sinus -> right 
internal jugular vein OR superior sagittal sinus -» confluence of sinuses -> right 
& left transverse sinuses - right & left sigmoid sinuses -> right & left internal 
jugular veins, 

159

Anatomy Wrap Up

**Question 1**  
A 25 year old woman suffers from a traumatic scalp avulsion due to a revolving machinery at her workplace. All the following are considered boundaries for the scalp EXCEPT:  
A. Superior nuchal line  
B. Zygomatic arch  
C. Zygomatic bone  
D. Supraorbital arch  
E. External occipital protuberance  

**Correct Answer: C. Zygomatic bone**  
*Explanation: The scalp boundaries include the superior nuchal line, zygomatic arch, supraorbital arch, and external occipital protuberance, but not the zygomatic bone.*

---

**Question 2**  
A 30-year-old patient comes to the emergency room with a laceration on the scalp following a head injury. The wound appears to be bleeding profusely. Which layer of the scalp is primarily responsible for this bleeding?  
A. Skin  
B. Subcutaneous tissue (Superficial Fascia)  
C. Galea Aponeurotica (Epicranial Aponeurosis)  
D. Loose Connective Tissue  
E. Pericranium (Periosteum)  

**Correct Answer: B. Subcutaneous tissue (Superficial Fascia)**  
*Explanation: The subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of the scalp is highly vascular and contains many blood vessels, leading to profuse bleeding when injured.*

---

**Question 3**  
A 30-year-old patient presents with a painful, swollen area on their scalp. Upon examination, you notice a localized, raised, and red lesion in the frontal region. The patient reports tenderness when they comb or brush their hair. Which layer of the scalp is most likely affected in this case?  
A. Skin  
B. Subcutaneous tissue  
C. Galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis)  
D. Loose connective tissue (areolar tissue)  
E. Periosteum  

**Correct Answer: B. Subcutaneous tissue**  
*Explanation: The subcutaneous layer contains nerves and vessels; inflammation here causes pain and tenderness (e.g., folliculitis).*

---

**Question 4**  
A 25-year-old patient sustains a head injury during a bicycle accident. On examination, there is a palpable swelling on the scalp that appears to be filled with blood. The hematoma is located between the periosteum and the galea aponeurotica. Which specific type of scalp hematoma is this most likely indicative of?  
A. Epidural hematoma  
B. Subdural hematoma  
C. Subperiosteal hematoma  
D. Subcutaneous hematoma  
E. Subgaleal hematoma  

**Correct Answer: E. Subgaleal hematoma**  
*Explanation: A subgaleal hematoma occurs between the galea aponeurotica and the periosteum (pericranium).*

---

**Question 5**  
A patient undergoes a surgical procedure on their scalp, and during the operation, there is profuse bleeding from an artery in the scalp. The bleeding is located near the superior nuchal line. Which artery is most likely the source of this bleeding?  
A. Occipital artery  
B. Supraorbital artery  
C. Middle temporal artery  
D. Superficial temporal artery  
E. Posterior auricular artery  

**Correct Answer: A. Occipital artery**  
*Explanation: The occipital artery runs near the superior nuchal line and supplies the posterior scalp.*

---

**Question 6**  
A 50-year-old man presents with a deep laceration to the side of the scalp in front of the ear, following a bicycle accident. Profuse bleeding is noted from the wound. Which artery is most likely the source of this bleeding?  
A. Facial artery  
B. Occipital artery  
C. Middle meningeal artery  
D. Superficial temporal artery  
E. Vertebral artery  

**Correct Answer: D. Superficial temporal artery**  
*Explanation: The superficial temporal artery runs in front of the ear and is a major artery of the lateral scalp.*

**Question 7**  
A patient presents with a complaint of persistent numbness and tingling on the posterior aspect of their scalp, especially on the left side behind the ear. They report no other neurological symptoms. Which nerve is likely responsible for this sensation?  
A. Posterior division of great auricular  
B. Lesser occipital  
C. Greater occipital  
D. Third occipital  
E. Posterior auricular branch of facial  

**Correct Answer: B. Lesser occipital**  
*Explanation: The lesser occipital nerve supplies sensation to the scalp behind the ear.*

**Question 8**  
A 45-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of numbness and tingling on the right side of his head. On physical examination, the patient has decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick on the right side of his forehead, scalp, and approaching the ear. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured in this patient?  
A. Auriculotemporal nerve  
B. Greater occipital nerve  
C. Lesser occipital nerve  
D. Supraorbital nerve  
E. Zygomaticotemporal nerve  

**Correct Answer: D. Supraorbital nerve**  
*Explanation: The supraorbital nerve supplies the forehead and anterior scalp.*

**Question 9**  
A 55-year-old male patient presents with a complaint of right eyebrow is drooping. On physical examination, the patient has weakness of the right frontalis muscle. Which nerve is most likely damaged in this patient?  
(A) Auriculotemporal nerve  
(B) Supratrochlear nerve  
(C) Greater occipital nerve  
(D) Lesser occipital nerve  
(E) Facial nerve  

**Correct Answer: (E) Facial nerve**  
*Explanation: The temporal branch of the facial nerve innervates the frontalis muscle.*

**Question 10**  
A 65-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of inability to close her right eye. The patient noticed this problem a few days ago and it has been getting worse gradually. She also reports that her right eyelid droops and that she has difficulty smiling on the right side of her face. She has no other medical problems and is not taking any medications. Which of the following muscles is most likely affecting the chief complaint in this patient?  
(A) Orbicularis oculi  
(B) Levator palpebrae superioris  
(C) Zygomaticus major  
(D) Buccinator  
(E) Mentalis  

**Correct Answer: (A) Orbicularis oculi**  
*Explanation: The orbicularis oculi is responsible for eye closure; its weakness causes inability to close the eye.*

**Question 11**

A. Orbital

(A) Orbicularis oris

**Question 13**  
A 20-year-old man presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of burning sensation in his forehead for 3 days duration, that lately is developing vesicles. A. Mandibular  
B. Trigeminal  
C. Facial  
D. Ophthalmic  
E. Maxillary  

**Correct Answer: D. Ophthalmic**  
*Explanation: Herpes zoster (shingles) of the forehead involves the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve.*

**Question 14**

A. Temporal  
B. Zygomatic  
C. Mandibular

**Question 15**  
A 28-year-old patient is involved in a car accident and sustains a traumatic injury to their spinal cord. As a result, they lose motor function below the waist and have no sensation in their lower limbs. Based on the location of the injury, which region of the spinal cord is most likely affected?  
A) Cervical  
B) Thoracic  
C) Lumbar  
D) Sacral  
E) Coccygeal  

**Correct Answer: C) Lumbar**  
*Explanation: The lumbar region supplies motor and sensory function to the lower limbs.*

**Question 16**  
Which part of the spinal cord is responsible for transmitting motor signals to the muscles that control fine movements of the fingers and hands?  
A) Cervical region  
B) Thoracic region  
C) Lumbar region  
D) Sacral region  
E) Coccygeal region  

**Correct Answer: A) Cervical region**  
*Explanation: The cervical enlargement (C5-T1) gives rise to nerves that control fine hand movements.*

**Question 17**  
During a normal child delivery, the attending physician noticed a swelling at the back of a newly born infant, giving a suspicious look for a birth defect. An urgent MRI was requested to assess the structure of the spinal cord. Where should u expect the spinal cord to end in this infant  
- L1  
- L2  
- L3  
- L4  
- L5  

**Correct Answer: L3**  
*Explanation: The file states the conus medullaris may terminate as low as L3 vertebra, especially in infants.*

**Question 18**  
A 50-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of right-sided hemiparesis. She reports that she woke up this morning and was unable to move her right arm or leg. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?  
A. Post central gyrus  
B. Angular gyrus  
C. Precentral gyrus  
D. The opercular and triangular parts of the inferior frontal gyrus  
E. Superior lip of posterior ramus of lateral sulcus  

**Correct Answer: C. Precentral gyrus**  
*Explanation: The precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) controls voluntary movement; a lesion here causes contralateral hemiparesis.*

**Question 19**  
A 65-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty speaking. He reports that he has been having trouble saying the right words and forming sentences for the past few months. Which of the following functional areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?  
(A) Broca's area  
(B) Wernicke's area  
(C) Primary somatosensory cortex  
(D) Primary motor cortex  
(E) Visual cortex  

**Correct Answer: (A) Broca's area**  
*Explanation: Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) is responsible for speech production; damage causes expressive aphasia.*

**Question 20**  
A 45-year-old patient presents with sudden difficulty in comprehending spoken language. They can speak fluently, but their speech lacks meaningful content. Which area of the brain is most likely affected in this case?  
A) Primary motor cortex  
B) Primary somatosensory cortex  
C) Broca's area  
D) Wernicke's area  
E) Visual cortex  

**Correct Answer: D) Wernicke's area**  
*Explanation: Wernicke's area is responsible for language comprehension; damage causes fluent but meaningless speech (receptive aphasia).*

**Question 21**  
A 45-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty walking. He reports that he has been having trouble balancing and coordinating his movements for the past few months. He also has difficulty judging distances and reaching for objects. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?  
(A) Cerebellum  
(B) Frontal lobe  
(C) Parietal lobe  
(D) Temporal lobe  
(E) Occipital lobe  

**Correct Answer: (A) Cerebellum**

He reports that he has been having trouble staying focused on tasks and remembering things for the past few months. He also has difficulty controlling his impulses and making decisions. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?  
(A) Frontal lobe  
(B) Parietal lobe  
(C) Temporal lobe  
(D) Occipital lobe

**Correct Answer: (A) Frontal lobe**

**Question 23**  
A 5-day-old child has been treated in the intensive care unit since birth. A sample of cerebral spinal fluid is required. Where would be the safest place to perform a lumbar puncture?  
1. Between C7 and T1 vertebrae  
2. Between T12 and L1 vertebrae  
3. Between L1 and L2 vertebrae  
4. Between L3 and L4 vertebrae  
5. Between L4 and L5 vertebrae  

**Correct Answer: 5. Between L4 and L5 vertebrae**  
*Explanation: In infants, the spinal cord ends at L3; L4-L5 is below the conus medullaris, avoiding cord injury.*

**Question 24**  
A patient presents with difficulty in walking, a loss of proprioception (awareness of body position), and a positive Romberg sign (swaying or falling when asked to stand with eyes closed). Imaging reveals a lesion in the spinal cord. Which neural tract is most likely affected in this case?  
1. Corticospinal tract  
2. Spinocerebellar tract  
3. Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway  
4. Spinothalamic tract  
5. Anterolateral system  

**Correct Answer: 3. Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway**  
*Explanation: Loss of proprioception and positive Romberg sign indicate dorsal column damage.*

---

**Question 25**  
A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty walking, muscle weakness, and a loss of proprioception (awareness of body position). Imaging reveals a lesion in the spinal cord. Which major ascending tract in the spinal cord is most likely affected, leading to these symptoms?  
1. Corticospinal tract  
2. Spinothalamic tract  
3. Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway  
4. Spinocerebellar tract  
5. Anterolateral system  

**Correct Answer: 3. Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway**  
*Explanation: Proprioception is carried by the dorsal columns.*

**Question 26**  
A patient complains of unsteadiness during that is profound during darkness. Examination shows a marked diminution of position sense, vibration sense, and stereognosis of all extremities. He is unable to stand without wavering for more than a few seconds when his eyes are closed. There are no other abnormal findings. The lesion most likely involves the:  
1. Lateral columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally  
2. Inferior cerebellar peduncles, bilaterally  
3. Dorsal columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally  
4. Spinothalamic tracts, bilaterally  
5. Corticospinal tracts  

**Correct Answer: 3. Dorsal columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally**  
*Explanation: Loss of position and vibration sense with sensory ataxia (Romberg sign) indicates bilateral dorsal column disease.*

**Question 27**  
The spinal tract involved with the control of trunk muscles is:  
1. anterior corticospinal  
2. anterior spinocerebellar  
3. spino-olivary  
4. lateral corticospinal  
5. vestibulospinal  

**Correct Answer: 1. anterior corticospinal**  
*Explanation: The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed) controls axial/trunk muscles.*

---

**Question 28**  
Acute-stage upper motor neuron lesions result in:  
1. hypertonia  
2. extensor toe response  
3. clonus  
4. flaccid paralysis  
5. spastic paresis  

**Correct Answer: 4. flaccid paralysis**  
*Explanation: In the acute stage of UMN lesion, spinal shock causes flaccid paralysis; hypertonia and spasticity appear later.*

---

**Question 29**  
A 32-year-old male patient presents with a loss of lower extremity motor control on the left side. He exhibits a Babinski sign and has increased deep tendon reflexes in the left lower extremity. He has no loss of sensation. The structure lesioned in the spinal cord is the:  
1. left lateral corticospinal tract  
2. right lateral corticospinal tract  
3. left sciatic nerve  
4. right sciatic nerve  
5. right fasciculus gracilis  

**Correct Answer: 1. left lateral corticospinal tract**  
*Explanation: UMN signs (Babinski, hyperreflexia) on the left side indicate damage to the left lateral corticospinal tract.*

---

**Question 30**  
A 44-year-old female patient has a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle in the midbrain. She would present with a loss of:  
1. fine touch and pain sensation from the entire left side of the body  
2. fine touch and pain sensation from the entire right side of the body  
3. skeletal motor control to the entire right side of the body  
4. skeletal motor control to both sides of the body  
5. skeletal motor control to the entire left side of the body  

**Correct Answer: 5. skeletal motor control to the entire left side of the body**  
*Explanation: The corticospinal tract decussates in the medulla; a lesion above the decussation (cerebral peduncle) causes contralateral motor loss.*

---

**Question 31**  
A 26-year-old man presents with spinal cord injury. Neurological examination reveals motor weakness of his left lower limb and loss of pinprick sensation on the right side of his body from the C8 dermatome downward. Which of the following might be an associated finding in this patient?  
1. Plantar flexion of right great toe on plantar stimulation  
2. Plantar flexion of left great toe on plantar stimulation  
3. Dorsiflexion of right great toe on plantar stimulation  
4. Dorsiflexion of left great toe on plantar stimulation  

**Correct Answer: 4. Dorsiflexion of left great toe on plantar stimulation**  
*Explanation: Motor weakness on left (UMN) leads to extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) on the left.*

---

**Question 32**  
Which of the following might be the location of lesion in this patient? (referring to Question 31)  
1. Right C6 cord  
2. Right C8 cord  
3. Left C6 cord  
4. Left C8 cord  

**Correct Answer: 1. Right C6 cord**  
*Explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome: right cord lesion causes left motor loss and right pain/temp loss. Level C6 explains upper limb involvement.*

---

**Question 33**  
A patient with a traumatic lesion of the left half of the spinal cord at the level of the eighth cervical segment might present the following sign(s) and symptom(s):  
1. Loss of pain and temperature sensations on the left side below the level of the lesion  
2. Loss of position sense of the right leg  
3. Right hemiplegia  
4. Left positive Babinski sign  
5. Right-sided lower motor paralysis in the segment of the lesion and muscular atrophy  

**Correct Answer: 4. Left positive Babinski sign**  
*Explanation: Left cord lesion causes left UMN signs (Babinski) below the lesion.*

---

**Question 34**  
24-year-old man was brought to the ER following a driving accident. Neurological testing revealed paraplegia and loss of all sensory modalities in bilateral lower limbs. Sensation for the upper limbs and the trunk was intact. Which of the following might be the nature and location of the lesion in this patient?  
1. Complete section of spinal cord at C8 level  
2. Hemi section of spinal cord at C8 level  
3. Complete section of spinal cord at T8 level  
4. Hemi section of spinal cord at T8 level  
5. Central cord syndrome  

**Correct Answer: 3. Complete section of spinal cord at T8 level**  
*Explanation: Paraplegia with loss of all sensation in lower limbs but intact upper limbs indicates complete transection at T8 (thoracic level).*

---

**Question 35**  
A 42-year-old man presents with an inability to feel extremes of temperature in both lower limbs. He also had a spastic type of paralysis affecting his right lower limb muscles. If this is consequent to a vascular injury, which of the following might be an additional feature in this patient?  
1. Loss of vibration sensation from right lower limb  
2. Loss of fine touch sensation from right lower limb  
3. Flexor plantar response from left lower limb  
4. Extensor plantar response from left lower limb  
5. Loss of vibration sensation from left lower limb  
6. Loss of fine touch sensation from left lower limb  

**Correct Answer: 1. Loss of vibration sensation from right lower limb**  
*Explanation: Combined findings suggest a lesion affecting both anterior and posterior spinal cord territories; loss of vibration on the same side as spastic paralysis is typical.*

**Question 36**  
A 42-year-old right-handed male arrives to the emergency department and is intoxicated. At the time of presentation, he is unable to move his hands and arms. The following day, once he is sober, a more thorough neurological examination reveals a complete flaccid paralysis of the upper limbs and severely diminished-to-absent reflex activity. What is the most likely area of spinal damage?  
*(Note: This question originally referenced an image area, but the text description is sufficient. Keeping as a purely text-based question.)*  
1. Area A  
2. Area B  
3. Area C  
4. Area D  
5. Area E  

**Correct Answer: 3. Area C**  
*Explanation: Flaccid paralysis of upper limbs with areflexia suggests lower motor neuron damage at the cervical enlargement (area C).*

Below are all questions from the two additional files, merged into a single numbered list (1–43). Each question includes all answer choices, the correct answer, and a very brief explanation based on the file content or standard knowledge. Questions that depend on images are not present in these files.

---

**1)** Fatal dermatitis is a serious adverse effect of which of the following drugs?  
A. Levetiracetam  
B. Topiramate  
C. Lamotrigine  
D. Thiopental  

**Correct Answer: C. Lamotrigine**  
*Explanation: Lamotrigine can cause severe skin reactions such as Stevens‑Johnson syndrome.*

---

**2)** Which of the following does not have an antidote?  
A. Clonazepam  
B. Thiopental  
C. Alprazolam  
D. Midazolam  

**Correct Answer: B. Thiopental**  
*Explanation: Thiopental is a barbiturate with no specific antidote; benzodiazepines have flumazenil.*

---

**3)** Which of the following drugs is preferred in case of penicillin allergy in a patient with Streptococcus Pneumoniae?  
A. Cefixime  
B. Rifampicin  
C. Gentamicin  
D. Vancomycin  

**Correct Answer: D. Vancomycin**  
*Explanation: Vancomycin is a common alternative for serious pneumococcal infections in penicillin‑allergic patients.*

---

**4)** The following drug(s) can be used in treatment of myoclonic epilepsy:  
A. Levetiracetam  
B. Valproate  
C. Topiramate  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: D. All of the above**  
*Explanation: Levetiracetam, valproate, and topiramate are all effective for myoclonic seizures.*

---

**5)** Buspirone is effective in case of:  
A. Panic attack  
B. Anxiety  
C. Insomnia  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: B. Anxiety**  
*Explanation: Buspirone is indicated for generalized anxiety disorder, not for panic attacks or insomnia.*

---

**6)** Which of the following is the best choice for patients with dementia due to substantia nigra lesion (Parkinson’s disease)?  
A. Rivastigmine  
B. Memantine  
C. Donepezil  
D. Galantamine  

**Correct Answer: A. Rivastigmine**  
*Explanation: Rivastigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor approved for Parkinson’s disease dementia.*

---

**7)** The following anti‑epileptic drug acts by binding to SV2A to modify glutamate release:  
A. Valproate  
B. Levetiracetam  
C. Lamotrigine  
D. Gabapentin  

**Correct Answer: B. Levetiracetam**  
*Explanation: Levetiracetam binds to synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating neurotransmitter release.*

---

**8)** Fampridine drug in treatment of Alzheimer’s disease:  
A. Blocks Na⁺ channel  
B. Causes hyperpolarization  
C. Blocks K⁺ channel  
D. Decreases neuronal depolarization  

**Correct Answer: C. Blocks K⁺ channel**  
*Explanation: Fampridine (4‑aminopyridine) is a potassium channel blocker.*

---

**9)** Patient intolerant to SSRIs due to their correlation with sexual disturbances can instead take:  
A. Venlafaxine  
B. Imipramine  
C. Amitriptyline  
D. Mirtazapine  

**Correct Answer: D. Mirtazapine**  
*Explanation: Mirtazapine has fewer sexual side effects compared to SSRIs.*

---

**10)** Moclobemide is preferred to phenelzine because:  
A. It inhibits MAO‑A and MAO‑B enzymes  
B. It is a selective MAO‑A inhibitor only  
C. It can be safely used in combination with SSRIs  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: B. It is a selective MAO‑A inhibitor only**  
*Explanation: Moclobemide is a reversible MAO‑A inhibitor, safer and with fewer dietary restrictions than non‑selective phenelzine.*

---

**11)** Gingival hygiene and care is highly recommended when taking which of the following drugs?  
A. Phenytoin  
B. Valproate  
C. Carbamazepine  
D. Topiramate  

**Correct Answer: A. Phenytoin**  
*Explanation: Phenytoin is known to cause gingival hyperplasia.*

---

**12)** The following drug is characterized by ultra‑short duration of action:  
A. Clonazepam  
B. Lorazepam  
C. Midazolam  
D. Alprazolam  

**Correct Answer: C. Midazolam**  
*Explanation: Midazolam has a very short half‑life due to rapid redistribution.*

---

**13)** Abuse and expanding closed gas spaces are adverse effects of which of the following anesthetics?  
A. Ketamine  
B. Nitrous oxide  
C. Propofol  
D. Halothane  

**Correct Answer: B. Nitrous oxide**  
*Explanation: Nitrous oxide can diffuse into closed air spaces and has abuse potential.*

---

**14)** Flumazenil can be used as an antidote with which of the following drugs?  
A. Zolpidem  
B. Thiopental  
C. Secobarbital  
D. Riluzole  

**Correct Answer: A. Zolpidem**  
*Explanation: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist and also reverses the effects of z‑drugs like zolpidem.*

---

**15)** All of the following drugs have slower onset when taken intra‑muscular except:  
A. Alprazolam  
B. Midazolam  
C. Diazepam  
D. Lorazepam  

**Correct Answer: B. Midazolam**  
*Explanation: Midazolam has rapid onset after IM injection due to high water solubility.*

---

**16)** Lidocaine is preferred to bupivacaine in local anesthesia due to:  
A. Higher pKa  
B. Longer duration  
C. Higher potency  
D. More rapid onset  

**Correct Answer: D. More rapid onset**  
*Explanation: Lidocaine has a lower pKa and faster onset than bupivacaine.*

---

**17)** All of the following anesthetic drugs can cause respiratory irritation except:  
A. Halothane  
B. Sevoflurane  
C. Isoflurane  
D. Desflurane  

**Correct Answer: A. Halothane**  
*Explanation: Halothane is non‑irritating to the respiratory tract; desflurane is the most irritant.*

---

**18)** Chloramphenicol is the last antibiotic of choice to be used due to:  
A. Anaphylactic shock  
B. Agranulocytosis  
C. Ototoxicity  
D. Pseudo cholelithiasis  

**Correct Answer: B. Agranulocytosis**  
*Explanation: Chloramphenicol can cause dose‑dependent bone marrow suppression and aplastic anemia.*

---

**19)** Dexamethasone is injected IV in meningitis for:  
A. 2‑4 days every 12 hours  
B. 2‑4 days every 6 hours  
C. 10‑14 days every 6 hours  
D. 10‑14 days every 12 hours  

**Correct Answer: B. 2‑4 days every 6 hours**  
*Explanation: The standard regimen is 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 2‑4 days.*

---

**20)** Which of the following statement is Wrong about using corticosteroids in meningitis?  
A. Taken for 2‑4 days every 6 hours  
B. Dexamethasone is used not cortisone  
C. Should be started immediately after empiric antibiotic  
D. May decrease penetration of vancomycin to BBB  

**Correct Answer: C. Should be started immediately after empiric antibiotic**  
*Explanation: Corticosteroids should be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics, not after.*

---

**21)** Which of the following is 1st choice as empiric antibiotic in meningitis suspected to be due to streptococcal Agalactiae in a 55‑year‑old patient?  
A. Ampicillin + ceftriaxone  
B. Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone  
C. Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone + Ampicillin  
D. Vancomycin + Cefepime  

**Correct Answer: C. Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone + Ampicillin**  
*Explanation: Ampicillin is added to cover Group B streptococcus and Listeria in elderly patients.*

---

**22)** Which of the following is Wrong about meningitis due to streptococcal Pneumoniae?  
A. Duration of treatment up to 21 days  
B. Ceftriaxone is chosen in ampicillin MIC >1 µg/ml  
C. Addition of vancomycin to ceftriaxone if MIC of both Ampicillin & ceftriaxone is high  
D. Rifampicin is added to Vancomycin during using dexamethasone because it increases metabolism of vancomycin  

**Correct Answer: D. Rifampicin is added to Vancomycin during using dexamethasone because it increases metabolism of vancomycin**  
*Explanation: Rifampicin is added for synergistic effect, not because it increases vancomycin metabolism (vancomycin is not metabolized by liver).*

---

**23)** Chemoprophylaxis is not recommended in meningitis due to:  
A. Neisseria meningitidis  
B. Streptococcus Pneumoniae  
C. Haemophilus Influenzae  
D. Listeria monocytogenes  

**Correct Answer: B. Streptococcus Pneumoniae**  
*Explanation: Prophylaxis is indicated for meningococcal and Hib, but not for pneumococcal meningitis.*

---

**24)** Choose from the following pair of antibiotics not crossing BBB even if inflamed:  
A. Aminoglycosides and β‑lactam  
B. Chloramphenicol and Aminoglycosides  
C. Rifampicin and Monobactam  
D. Amphotericin and Aminoglycosides  

**Correct Answer: D. Amphotericin and Aminoglycosides**  
*Explanation: Both amphotericin B and aminoglycosides have poor CNS penetration even with inflamed meninges.*

---

**25)** Principles of antimicrobial therapy for meningitis:  
A. Antibiotics should be lipophilic‑ionized in physiological pH  
B. Steroids should be administered after starting empiric antibiotics  
C. Lumbar puncture should be done before choosing empiric antibiotics  
D. Once organism is identified, treatment should be continued for 7 to 21 days  

**Correct Answer: D. Once organism is identified, treatment should be continued for 7 to 21 days**  
*Explanation: The duration depends on the organism, typically 7‑21 days.*

---

**26)** Prophylaxis of close contact by rifampicin for 2 days is used in case of:  
A. Haemophilus influenzae meningitis  
B. Streptococcus agalactiae meningitis  
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis  
D. None of the above  

**Correct Answer: D. None of the above**  
*Explanation: Rifampicin for 2 days is used for Neisseria meningitidis, which is not listed.*

---

**27)** Prophylaxis of close contact by rifampicin for 4 days is used in case of:  
A. Haemophilus influenzae meningitis  
B. Streptococcus agalactiae meningitis  
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis  
D. Neisseria meningitidis meningitis  

**Correct Answer: A. Haemophilus influenzae meningitis**  
*Explanation: Hib prophylaxis requires rifampicin for 4 days.*

---

**28)** Intrapartum Group B streptococcus prophylaxis requirements:  
A. GBS carrier mother  
B. History of delivery of infant with GBS  
C. History of GBS bacteriuria at any time during pregnancy  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: D. All of the above**  
*Explanation: All listed indications are correct for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis.*

---

**29)** Pseudocholelithiasis is associated with:  
A. Aminoglycosides  
B. Penicillin  
C. Chloramphenicol  
D. Ceftriaxone  

**Correct Answer: D. Ceftriaxone**  
*Explanation: Ceftriaxone can cause biliary sludge, mimicking gallstones.*

---

**30)** Prolonged QT interval is associated with:  
A. Moxifloxacin  
B. Chloramphenicol  
C. Ceftriaxone  
D. None of the above  

**Correct Answer: A. Moxifloxacin**  
*Explanation: Fluoroquinolones like moxifloxacin are known to prolong the QT interval.*

---

**31)** Grey baby syndrome is associated with:  
A. Ceftriaxone  
B. Moxifloxacin  
C. Penicillin  
D. Chloramphenicol  

**Correct Answer: D. Chloramphenicol**  
*Explanation: Chloramphenicol causes gray baby syndrome in neonates due to inadequate glucuronidation.*

---

**32)** Dexamethasone is injected intravenous for:  
A. 2‑4 days every 12 or 24 hours  
B. 10‑14 days every 6 hours  
C. 2‑4 days every 6 hours  
D. 10‑14 days every 12 or 24 hours  

**Correct Answer: C. 2‑4 days every 6 hours**  
*Explanation: Same as question 19 – dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h for 2‑4 days.*

---

**33)** TB meningitis:  
A. Duration will take 9‑12 months  
B. Ethambutol may be used  
C. Corticosteroid may be required in stage 2 or 3  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: D. All of the above**  
*Explanation: All statements are correct for tuberculous meningitis.*

---

**34)** Riluzole mode of action (choose incorrect sentence):  
A. Block Na⁺ channel  
B. Block GABA release  

**Correct Answer: B. Block GABA release**  
*Explanation: Riluzole blocks sodium channels and inhibits glutamate release, not GABA.*

---

**35)** Riluzole is prescribed in Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to:  
A. Decrease onset of dementia  
B. Decrease confusion and headache  
C. Decrease need for ventilator  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: C. Decrease need for ventilator**  
*Explanation: Riluzole slows disease progression and delays the need for mechanical ventilation.*

---

**36)** Which of the following is incorrect regarding Natalizumab?  
A. Taken IV infusion monthly  
B. Decrease BBB invasion by T‑lymphocyte  
C. Indicated in mild controlled Multiple sclerosis  
D. Monoclonal antibody  

**Correct Answer: C. Indicated in mild controlled Multiple sclerosis**  
*Explanation: Natalizumab is used for aggressive or relapsing forms of MS, not mild controlled disease.*

---

**37)** Which of the following is correct regarding Fingolimod?  
A. Decrease BBB invasion by T‑lymphocyte  
B. Prevent T lymphocyte migration from Lymph node  
C. Used with caution in cardiac patient  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: D. All of the above**  
*Explanation: All statements are correct; fingolimod traps lymphocytes in lymph nodes, reducing CNS entry, and causes bradycardia.*

---

**38)** Which of the following is correct about Fingolimod?  
A. Associated with 1st dose tachycardia  
B. 1st parenteral & oral Diseases modified drug  
C. Used with caution in Diabetic patient  
D. Increases T‑lymphocyte penetration to BBB  

**Correct Answer: B. 1st parenteral & oral Diseases modified drug**  
*Explanation: Fingolimod was the first oral disease‑modifying drug for MS (though not parenteral).*

---

**39)** Interferon (choose incorrect sentence):  
A. 1st line therapy for patient with MS  
B. Injected IV  
C. Prevent demyelination process  
D. Associated with increased hepatic enzymes  

**Correct Answer: B. Injected IV**  
*Explanation: Interferon beta is given subcutaneously or intramuscularly, not intravenously.*

---

**40)** Macular edema is mainly occurred with:  
A. Natalizumab  
B. Fingolimod  
C. Interferon  
D. Riluzole  

**Correct Answer: B. Fingolimod**  
*Explanation: Fingolimod is known to cause macular edema.*

---

**41)** Depression is mainly associated with:  
A. Methylprednisolone  

**Correct Answer: A. Methylprednisolone**  
*Explanation: Corticosteroids like methylprednisolone can cause depression and mood changes.*

---

**42)** Increased risk of infection is mainly associated with:  
A. Prednisone  
B. Fingolimod  
C. Interferon  
D. A + B  
E. None of the above  

**Correct Answer: D. A + B**  
*Explanation: Both prednisone (immunosuppression) and fingolimod (lymphocyte sequestration) increase infection risk.*

---

**43)** To improve walking speed in patient with Multiple sclerosis; you should prescribe:  
A. Fingolimod  
B. Fampidine  
C. Prednisone  
D. None  

**Correct Answer: B. Fampidine**  
*Explanation: Fampridine (4‑aminopyridine) is used to improve walking speed in MS.*

Medial Longitudinal Bundle 
• an association bundle extending from brainstem till cervical segments of spinal cord. 
• In brain stem:  anterior to the central gray matter close to median raphe   
• In spinal cord: in anterior column of cervical segments. 
 
Structure 
o In brain stem:  formed of ascending & descending fibers. 
o In spinal cord: formed of  descending fibers only (crossed & uncrossed) 
Fibers originate from multiple nuclei in brain stem. 
Afferents 
o In brain stem:   
                1.Interstitial nucleus of Cajal. 
                2.Superior colliculus (tectal nucleus) 
                3.Inferior colliculus. 
                4.Vestibular nuclei (medial & superior) 
o In spinal cord  
                1.Pontine reticulospinal tract 
                2.Tectospinal tract 
                3.Vestibulospinal tract 
Efferents 
1. Ascending fibers:  
vestibulooccular fibers mainly  
[to the motor nuclei of 3rd, 4th and 6th cranial nerves]. 
2. Ascending fibers from 6th nucleus [supply lateral rectus]  
to the 3rd nucleus [supply medial rectus] of the opposite side 
3. Descending fibers:   
• Tectobulbar fibers: to nuclei of E.O.M. 
• Tectospinal fibers. 
• Vestiblospinal fibers. 
• Fibers from tracts in anterior column. 
Function 
o Control conjugate eye movement [vestibule-ocular] 
o Control reflex eye & head movement to visual, auditory, labyrinthine & sensory stimuli.

Phenytoin  
Carbamazepine 
 
 
Good combinations with L-dopa 
• carbidopa: as it decreases its dose by 75% by inhibiting peripheral decarboxylase which 
metabolizes L-dopa (without it 99% of L-dopa is converted to dopamine peripherally 
which can't cross the BBB and increase peripheral side effects of L-dopa). 
• Entacapone : COMT Inhibitor → ↓L-Dopa peripheral metabolism → ↑its bioavailability & 
prolongs its action →↓ fluctuations. 
• Selegiline: MAO-B Inhibitor → delay the breakdown of nigrostriatal DA → prolongs L
Dopa action →↓ fluctuations. 
• COMT and MAOI inhibitors: to manage end of dose akinesia & ↓”off” time. 
• Domeperidone : as it decrease  L-dopa induced nausea &vomiting. 
Bad combinations with L-dopa: 
• Anti-muscarinic drugs: as they decrease GIT motility → decrease absorption of L-dopa 
• Pyridoxine ( vit. B6 ): as it increase L-dopa peripheral degradation →↓ its effect.

• Therapeutic uses:

as it potentiates GABA in limbic system (diazepam , alprazolam). 
2. Insomnia (triazolam), sleep walking , night terrors as it potentiates GABA in RF 
(Diazepam).

Question 7: Benzodiazepines: mechanism of action and therapeutic uses and choices 
(1998-99-2000) (sep2004-2006) (may2007-2013) and mechanism of action of Diazepam 
(sep2012)? 
 
(Sep/June 20XX) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
47 
 
 
 Increase stage of N REM  
 decrease nightmares  
 decrease REM  
 decrease night terrors  
 decrease stage 3,4 of NREM sleep  
3. conscious sedation, preanesthesia, balanced anesthesia as it acts on brain stem 
causing amnesia and sedation (midazolam, lorazepam, diazepam) 
4. Status epilepticus (lorazepam, midazolam, diazepam). 
5. Muscle spasticity in Trauma and cerebral palsy (diazepam) 
6. alcohol withdrawal 
Diazepam: 
• prototype Binds to BZD receptor and increase frequency of opening cl channels and 
hyperpolarization.  
 
 
 
General guidelines: 
1. Proper diagnosis. 
2. Monotherapy. 
3. Start with minimal dose and gradual increase or add another drug if no effect is noted. 
4. Long duration of treatment.  
5. Gradual withdrawal over 6 months. 
6. Folic acid supplement to decrease teratogenicity in pregnant females. 
7. Periodic monitoring of serum level of drugs. 
8. Use of phenytoin, phenobarbital & clonazepam is limited due to their adverse effects. 
Mechanism of action: 
1. Na channel blocker e.g.: valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin. 
2. T-type calcium channel blocker e.g.: Ethoxuamide , valproate . 
3. Increase GABA e.g.: valproate. 
4. GABA modulators e.g.: BZD, phenobarbital. 
5. NMDA Glutamate receptor antagonists e.g.: valproate. 
6. Blockade of presynaptic voltage gated Ca channels e.g.: lamotrigine

Question 38 :A five-year-old child fell off his bicycle and his head hit the pavement. A 
2 cm long wound in his scalp was seen, but soon he was sitting in a pool of blood. 
 
 
Question 39 :A young man, while sucking a piece of lemon, noticed a painful swilling 
below the mandible with a small nodule related to the swilling. Examination revealed 
a stone in the right submandibular duct. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
a. Why does a scalp wound bleed profusely?  
b. How can you stop the bleeding if you are away from the hospital?  
c. Name arteries supplying the scalp.   
d. Which is the dangerous layer of the scalp? Why is it dangerous? 
Answer 
a. A scalp wound bleed profusely 
Because - The CT septa is attached to the wall of the blood vessels  - The rich vascularity of the scalp. 
b. Bleeding can be stopped by compressing the wound. 
c. Arteries supplying the scalp - Supratrochlear artery. - Supraorbital artery. - Superficial temporal artery. - Posterior auricular artery. - Occipital artery. 
d. The dangerous layer of the scalpis the "loose CT" layer as its emissary veins can 
spread infections from the scalp to the cranial cavity. 
 
a. Where does the duct open in the mouth? 
b. Which nerve is intimately related to the duct?

Question 40 :A 20-year-old student was playing baseball when the ball hit him on 
the side of the head. He immediately fell to the ground unconscious, but after about 
30 seconds he felt well and decided to sit and watch the match. An hour later, he felt 
so sleepy then he became unconscious. He was taken to the hospital. A skull X-ray 
showed a fracture in the region of the pterion. 
a. The duct opens bya narrow orifice on the summit of sublingual papilla at the side 
of frenulum of the tongue. 
b. The nerve related to the duct the lingual nerve hooks around it from the lateral 
to the medial side. 
c. The nerve supply of the submandibular gland is submandibular ganglion 
which convey to the gland: -sensory: from lingual nerve. -sympathetic: from plexus around facial artery. -parasympathetic: from chorda tympani. 
d. Structures related to the lateral surface of the superficial part of the gland. -Mandible. -Insertion of the medial pterygoid. -facial artery. 
 
a. Define the pterion. 
b. Why fractures in this region are extremely dangerous? 
Answer 
a. The pterion it's the thinnest part of the skull and liable to fracture( the meeting of 4 
bones –temporal – parietal – sphenoid – frontal ) 
b. Fractures in this region are dangerous as it may injure  the middle meningeal 
artery which, cause  extradural hemorrhage and cerebral compression.

Question 41 :During surgical removing of a tumor in the infratemporal fossa, an 
intense hemorrhage occurred. The surgeon clamped the main source of arterial 
supply to the area. 
Question 42 :A patient opened his mouth widely while yawing, after which he 
couldn't close his mouth. 
a. Which artery did the surgeon clamp to stop the hemorrhage? 
b. Name the main nerve located in the fossa and its branches. 
c. This patient complained of loss of taste, sensation from anterior part of the tongue 
after the operation. Can you account for this? Name the nucleus that receives taste 
sensation. 
Answer 
a. The artery clamped to stop thehemorrhageis the maxillary artery. 
b. The main nerve located in the fossais the mandibular nerve. 
Branches:  - From the trunk: nervous spinosus, nerve to medial pterygoid, tensor palate and 
tensor tympani. - From anterior division: buccal nerve, nerve to lateral pterygoid, nerve to 
masseter and nerve to temporalis. - From the posterior division:auriculotemporal nerve, lingual nerve and inferior 
alveolar nerve. (ALI) 
c. Loss of taste sensation due to affection of chorda tympani which joins the lingual 
nerve. -The nucleus that receives taste sensation is the nucleus solitaries. 
 
 
a. Name the joint affected and its type. 
b. List ligament of the joint which ligament is important right functionally?  
c. Mention the nerve supply of the joint.  
Answer 
a. The joint affected isT.M.J (tempromandibular joint)  
Type: synovial, bi-condylar  
b. Ligaments of the joint:  
1. Tempro-mandibular ligament “the important right functionally” 
2. stylo-mandibular ligament  
3. Spheno-mandibular ligament 
c. Nerve supply: Auriculotemporal& masseteric nerves.

Question 43 :A patient developed a benign swelling of the parotid gland (superficial

Question 44 :A patient presented with a red, swollen and painful right eye. The 
movements of the right eye were painful and the pupil of that eye was fixed and 
dilated. CT scan showed thrombosis of the cavernous sinus. 
 
a. What is the most important structure that would the doctor take care of?  
b. Mention the distribution of its upper two branches 
c. Mention the cranial nerve carrying parasympathetic supply to the gland and the 
ganglion of relay  
Answer 
 
a. The most important structure is facial nerve because it is the most superficial 
structure in the gland. 
b. distribution of upper two branches of facial is: 
1. Temporal to frontal belly of occiptofrontalis m. &orbiculrisocculi. 
2. Zygomatic to orbicularis occuli m. 
c. Cranial n. carrying parasympathetic is glossopharyngeal (IX) &ganglion of relay 
is otic ganglia. 
 
a. Define the venous sinus and its function. 
b. Describe the site and contents of the cavernous sinus. 
c. Define the dangerous area of the face. Why this area is dangerous? 
d. Name the veins terminate in the cavernous sinus. 
Answer 
a. The venous sinus: - It's a large venous space lying in middle cranial fossa on either side of body of 
sphenoid bone, having 4 walls & 2 ends. It's called "cavernous" because of its 
spongy nature (formed of 2 layers of dura matter ) - It drains the orbit, brain, meninges and CSF 
b. The cavernous sinus:  
Site: in the middle cranial fossa, on each side of the hypophyseal fossa. 
Contents:  
Structures in the lateral wall of the sinus from above downwards: 
I- Oculomotor nerve. 
II- Trochlear nerve. 
III- Ophthalmic nerve. 
IV- maxillary nerve.

Question 45 :A young inexperienced doctor opened a parotid abscess by making a 
vertical incision, the patient became unable to raise the eyebrow on the operated 
side. - Structures passing through the sinus: ICA with its sympathetic plexus & the 
abducent nerve. 
c. The dangerous area of the face:  
It is a triangular area of facial skin including upper lip, nose and medial angle of the 
eye. If this area is infected the infection would spread from: 
_facial vein to the cavernous sinus by sup ophthalmic vein 
_ptrygoid plexus to the cavernous by Emissary vein 
 causing its thrombosis. This affects the cranial nerves III, IV and VI. 
d. The veins terminate in the cavernous sinus: - From the orbit:  
I- superior ophthalmic vein. 
II- inferior ophthalmic vein. 
III- central retinal vein. - From the brain:  
I-superficial middle cerebral vein. 
II- Inferior cerebral veins from the temporal lobe. - From the meninges:  
I- sphenoparietal sinus. 
III- frontal trunk of the middle meningeal vein.  
 
a. Which nerve was injured? Specifically, mention the branch that was cut. 
b. What could the doctor do to avoid the lesion? 
c. What are the structures present within the substance of the parotid gland?  
Mention how they enter and leave the gland. 
d. Mention the surface anatomy of the parotid duct. 
Answer 
a. The nerve injured: Temporal branch of facial n.  
b. The lesion could be avoided by making transverse incision & parallel to terminal 
branches of facial n.  
c. The structures present within the sunbstance of parotid: 
Facial n. (most superficial): enters through posteromedial surface & divides the 
gland to superficial & deep parts forming pes anserinus plexus & then divides to 5 
terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular & cervical.

Retromandibular v.: formed inside the gland by union of maxillary & superficial 
temporal v. then divides into anterior & posterior divisions that leave the gland 
through its apex  
ECA (most deep): enters through posteromedial surface of the gland & divides at 
the level of neck of mandible into 2 terminal branches, maxillary & superficial 
temporal arteries 
Deep parotid L.N.: embedded within its substance 
d. The surface anatomy parotid duct: 
It lies 1 finger breadth below the zygomatic arch, it corresponds to middle 1/3 of a 
line drawn from the tragus of ear to a point midway between ala of nose & upper lip

Question 1:A 30 year-old woman complained of a swelling in the anterior part of 
her neck, nervousness and loss of weight. The doctor examined her and found an 
enlarged thyroid gland which moves up and down with swallowing. He suggested 
that a subtotal thyroidectomy (parietal removal of thyroid gland) had to be 
performed. 
 
 
a. Why do swellings of thyroid gland move up and down with swallowing? 
b. What important structures could be injured on operations of thyroid gland? 
c. Enumerate the main vessels supplying the thyroid gland. 
d. Give the course and distribution of glossopharyngeal nerve. 
 
Answer  
 
a. The swelling move up & down by swallowing because thyroid gland is 
surrounded by the pretracheal fascia which attaches the gland to trachea and larynx. 
b. Imporant structures could be injured: 
Internal jugular vein. 
Left brachiocephalic vein.  
External laryngeal nerve.  
Recurrent laryngeal nerve.  
c. Main vessels supplying thyroid: 
Superior thyroid arteries from ECA. 
Inferior thyroid arteries from 1st part of subclavian artery.  
In 3%: Thyroid ima artery from arch of aorta.  
2 superior & 2 middle thyroid veins which drain into IJV.  
2 inferior thyroid veins which drain into left brachiocephalic vein. 
d. Course: 
 The nerve emerges from the skull through the jugular foramen. 
 Then it passes between the IJV & ICA, then between the ICA & ECA, then on the 
lateral surface of Stylopharyngeus muscle then it enters the pharynx between the 
superior & middle constrictors.  
Distribution 
 Lingual branch: to posterior 1
3
 of tongue and circumvallate papillae.  
 Tonsillar branch: to palatine tonsils. 
 Carotid sinus and carotid body branches.

a. Which artery's pulse did he feel? 
b. From which aortic arch did this artery develop? 
c. At witch level in the neck does it divide into its terminal branches?

Question 4:A 42-year-old woman came to the hospital with a swilling in the front of 
the neck. The swelling extended till the thyroid cartilage. It moved up and down with 
swallowing. This case was diagnosed as a thyroid swilling. Thyroidectomy was 
performed and two months later the patient returned to her doctor complaining of 
changes of her voice and frequently occurring cramps. 
 
a. Why does the swilling move up and down with swallowing? 
b. Explain the thyroid swilling can't extend up beyond oblique line of thyroid cartilage? 
c. Explain the changes in voice and the muscle cramps that this patient had following 
Thyroidectomy 
d. List two anomalies related to the development of the thyroid gland. 
Answer 
a. The swilling move up and down with swallowing because the swilling is invested 
by pretracheal layer of the deep fascia. 
b. Thyroid swilling can't extend up beyond oblique lineof thyroid cartilage: Due 
to attachment of infrahyoid (sternothyroid)  muscles. 
c. The changes in voice and the muscle cramps  
Due to injury of external laryngeal nerve (supplies cricothyroid muscle) during 
ligation of superior thyroid artery. Injury of recurrent laryngeal nerve which 
supplies other laryngeal muscles during ligation of inferior thyroid artery. Muscle 
cramps occur due to removal of the parathyroid glands during Thyroidectomy. 
d. Anomalies related to the development of the thyroidgland. 
1. Agenesis of the gland. 
2. Incomplete descent; the gland may be found at any point the base of the tongue 
and the trachea. 
3. Thyroglossal cyst.

a. What is your diagnosis?

Answer 
 
a. Diagnosis:The case suffers from syringomyelia. 
b. Pain and temperature fibers are only involved:

will affect them only.  
c. The most common site : is in cervical and upper thoracic segments of spinal cord.

Question 1: Discuss the mechanism and properties of synaptic transmission. 
 Synaptic structure: - Synaptic knobs: terminal end of pre synaptic neuron contain: chemical vesicles, mitochondria, 
voltage gated Ca channels, protein molecules on inner surface (releasing factors) - Synaptic cleft: potential space between synaptic knob & synaptic gutter =30-50 nm  - Synaptic gutter: part of post synaptic membrane contain specific receptor, protein or enzymes for 
destruction of neurotransmitter, ligand gated Na channels, voltage gated channels 
 Mechanism: 
1. AP reach knob: opening voltage Ca channels ca influx →forming ca synaptotagmin complex           
poring, fusion and exocytosis  
2. Release of Chemical transmitter &cross cleft to post synaptic membrane 
3. Combine with specific receptor  
4. Change permeability for one or more ions: change RMP to become more or less negative  
5. Removal of transmitter by active reuptake, degradation or passive diffusion  
 Properties 
1. Forward direction (from pre to post synaptic ) 
2. Synaptic delay (0.5 msec)                                       potentiation 
3. Synaptic fatigue                          long term             Depression  
4. Synaptic plasticity                      short term             Enhancement 
                                                                                          Depression  
 
 
Question 2: List four properties of synaptic transmission & explain two of them. 
 
The properties of synaptic transmission: 
a. Forward Conduction (Unidirectional): 
From synaptic knobs to the postsynaptic neurons only. 
b. Synaptic Delay (0.5 m sec): 
It's the time between the arrival of the impulse to synaptic knob & the excitation of postsynaptic 
neuron. 
c. Fatigue of Synaptic Transmission: 
It's  rate of discharge in postsynaptic neurons due to rapid repetitive stimulation, caused by: 
a.  Chemical transmitter in presynaptic terminals.  
b. Down regulation of postsynaptic receptors. 
& its importance is to prevent over excitation in CNS 
d. Synaptic Potentiation (Plasticity):  
It's the ability to change the function of synapse according to demand. 
So, Synaptic transmission can be  or  
for short periods (Short term):  Potentiation & Inhibition 
Or long periods (Long term): Facilitation & Depression

Question 6: Define the generator potential (Receptor potential ) G.P , describe its ionic 
bases & its characteristic 
 
 Def. A state of partial depolarization of the receptor membrane occurring when the receptor is 
stimulated. 
 The ionic bases:  
1. The stimulus energy causes non-specific opening of Na+ channels (their number is directly 
proportionate to the stimulus intensity), this causes Na+ entry leading to partial depolarization. 
2. The G.P spreads passively with deceased intensity to adjacent parts of the sensory n. if 
unmyelinated & to 1st Ranvier node if myelinated 
3. If depolarization reaches threshold, A.P is generated without any effect on G.P 
N.B.  In Some receptors (e.g. photoreceptors), the electromagnetic waves cause closure of Na+ channels 
(hyperpolarization) 
 
 The characteristics: - Doesn't obey “all or none” law - Can be summated - Can initiate repeated A.P - Not blocked by local anesthetics - Longer than A.P (it's time from 5-10 msec. while A.P 2msec) - NO absolute refractory period - Can be graded (first amplitude increases rapidly then slowly to reach maximum) - Spreads passively - It's magnitude increases by increasing the stimulus intensity 
 
  
4. Decrease sensitivity of node of Ranvier 
5. Gradual inactivation of Na channels

Question7:state the general principles of coding sensory information in the nervous 
system? 
1. Modality of sensation  
a. Muller’s law: each receptor gives one type of sensation irrespective of the method of 
stimulation 
b. Labeled line principle: there is specific pathway for each sensation which transmits it to 
specific area in cortex. 
2. Locality “Law of projection" 
Each area in the body is represented in particular area in C.C so when impulse reaches this area 
the cortex project it to its original site. 
(Phantom limb phenomena) 
3. Intensity 
any change in stimulus intensity causes a change in 
a. Number of receptors  
b. Frequency of action potential 
 Weber Fechner law :The frequency of discharge from receptors is directly 
proportional to the logarithm of intensity of applied stimuli . 
c. state of cortical centers (stimulated or inhibited)
