Question 11: Give an account on pathway of deep sensation 
AB fibers medially ( centeral processes of dorsal root ganglion cells (pseudounipolar) 
whose peripheral processes carry sensations from deep receptors in muscles, tendons 
& joints. Runs upwards in the ipsilateral dorsal column and ascend to relay in Gracile & 
Cuneate of medulla  
(Gracile tract carries sensation from lower part of the body and lies medial in dorsal 
column , Cuneate tract carries sensation from upper part and lies lateral )  
Their central processes pass to the spinal cord through the dorsal root. 
N.B.  - They send collateral branches as they ascend that end on the dorsal horn of spinal cord 
which form the septo-marginal tract from gracile & comma-shaped tract from cuneate - Some cervical fibers end on the accessory cuneate nucleus (posterior to cuneate 
nucleus), its axons (cuneo-cerebellar fibers) pass to the cerebellum.

Question 14: Describe referred pain and give 2 examples. Explain the theories of 
referred pain. 
Question 15:Define referred pain and explain its mechanisms. - It is the pain felt away from its original site. It is most frequent in visceral pain and deep somatic 
pain . The pain in one of the visceral organs& referred to an area on the body surface.  - Examples: 
a. Cardiac pain: is referred to the back of the neck, left shoulder & left arm.  
b. Renal pain: is felt as a back pain that radiates to the inguinal region & testicles. 
c. Gastric pain: is felt between umbilicus & xiphoid process.  
d. Gall bladder pain: is referred to epigastrium & tip of the right scapula. 
e. Appendicular pain: is felt around the umbilicus.  
f. Teeth pain: is referred to other teeth. E.g. upper teeth is referred to lower.  - Theories of referred pain: 
1. Convergence projection theory: 
Afferent pain fibers from the diseased viscera converge on the same cells in SGR which receives pain 
impulses from a particular skin area supplied by the same dorsal nerve roots.  
The cells of SGR discharge the impulses along the lateral spinothalamic tract to the sensory area on the 
cortex which is accustomed to receive pain sensation from the skin,  therefore pain impulses from the 
viscera is projected to the skin area. 
2. Facilitation theory: (Subliminal fringe) 
The incoming impulses from the visceral structures lower the threshold of the spinothalamic neurons 
receiving afferent from somatic areas,  so that minor activity in the pain pathway from the somatic 
areas which would normally die out in the spinal cord will pass on to the brain.

Question 2: Indicate the function of stretch reflex. Describe how it is measured 
1- Skeletal muscle tone : 
Def : it's a static starch reflex where it's a state of continuous partial sub tetanic alternating contraction 
of skeletal muscle  
Causes  : a- length of muscle is shorter than the distance from origin to insertion  
B- effect of gravity . " muscle tone in antigravity muscle is higher "  
Functions : 1- antigravity to maintain body postural  
2- Heat production thus regulating body temp. 
3- Help venous & lymphatic drainage  
4- Keep viscera in position 
2- servo assistant function : 
During voluntary contractions  - Supraspinal facilitatory impulses activate both ( α) & (γ) neurons                 contraction if both 
extrafusal  & peripheral ends of nuclear fibers                  excitation of α motor neurons reflexly to 
potentiation of muscle contraction    - Important :  a- allow muscle contraction with minimal nervous energy i.e. energy saving 
B- compensate for muscle weakness or fatigue  
C – maintain constant position of body parts despite  application of different weights " load reflex "  
3- damping function " signal averaging function "  : - weak impulses : - SR               contraction of agonist muscle ( servo-assist) - Strong impulses : - SR               contraction of antagonist muscle  
So all contraction will be average normal strength & oscillation in movement will be prevented [ smooth 
movements ]  
Question 4: List the properties of stretch reflex. Mention the function of gamma (γ)

1. It is a spinal deep reflex (its receptor are deep in the muscle). 
Physiology Questions and Answers  2017 
 
17 
 
2. It is a monosynaptic reflex. 
3. It has short reflex time. 
4. It has no recruitment or after discharge. 
5. It shows reciprocal innervation. 
6. Its activity is controlled by higher centers changing the activity of gamma neuron. 
7. It is inhibited by:  
a. Negative stretch reflex. 
b. Stimulation of antagonist muscle. 
c. Inverse stretch reflex.    
8. It is a semi quantitative reflex. - Function of gamma motor neurons: 
gamma motor neurons innervate the intrafusal fibers .  
1- reflex muscle contraction by stimulating peripheral parts of intrafusal fibers 
2- stimulation of γ-fibers  increase response  of muscle spindle to stretch  
3- prevent unloading & keep the muscle sensitive to starch even during contraction of the extra-fusal 
fibers

Question 9: Explain the significance of gamma motor neurons in the maintenance of

Question 13:Describe the control of body movements. 
 Motor cortex receives various kinds of information from various lobes of the brain like the 
frontal&temporal lobes about motivation & memories. 
 Informationabout surrounding environment & position on space is generated through 
somatosensory, proprioceptive& visual sensory inputs to the posterior parietal cortex. 
 Generation of Idea occurs in prefrontal cortex which receives sensory Information from 
various cortices. 
Physiology Questions and Answers  2017 
 
21 
 
 Role of motivation & memories takes place either rewarding or stopping the desire in limbic 
system. 
 A plan or program is made In BG, cerebellum, premotor cortex&supplementary motor 
areas to determine how the actions will be carried out & decides which muscles will 
contract to give the required movement. 
 Premotor cortex& supplementary motor areassend the plan to primary motor cortex. 
 At the same time, premotor cortexsends Impulses through anterior corticospinal tract to 
adjust the body posture to be suitable for the movement &supplementary cortexadjusts 
posture of hands converting the plan of action into an actual movement. 
 Cortical Input to BG forms a loop as signals are discharged from BG back to SMA, premotor 
area & primary motor area. This helps to initiate movement, to select & trigger well
coordinated voluntary movements. 
 Cerebellum receives Information about the original plan of the Intended movement from 
cortical association area (cerebrocerebellum) &proprioceptive Information from muscles 
& joints (spinocerebellum) then it sends signals back to the motor cortex. These signals 
modify the motor commands to correct any error between actual muscle performance & the 
original plan.

Question 18:Define spinal shock, describe the initial and long-term changes in spinal 
reflexes that follow transection of the spinal cord. 
Def. Complete loss of all reflexes below the level of the lesion, lasts from 2 - 5 weeks in human 
Initial changes in spinal reflexes:  - Flaccid paralysis with loss if all reflexes - Loss of autonomic function e.g. defecation, micturition , erection reflexes and vascular tone. - Loss of all sensations below the level of transaction ( permanent) 
Long  term changes : - In case of giving the patient good care to survive the shock phase  : - Spasticity (hypertonia)  at first in flexor and later on in extensor  - Exaggerated flexion withdrawal reflex  - Return of infantile reflexes which were suppressed by corticospinal tracts e.g. grasp and +ve  
Babinski  - Loss of superficial reflexes ( need intact corticospinal tract ) e.g. abdominal and cremastric  - Automatic bladder : 150 > evacuation occurs - Abnormal reflexes appear as mass reflex appears

Question 23: List the physiological divisions of cerebellum and mention function of each

1. Vestibulocerebellum or archicerebellum consists of folliculonodular lobe and part of the vermis  - Function: concerned with equilibrium   
2. Spinocerebellum or paleocerebellum consists of intermediate zones of cerebellar hemispheres  - Function: coordination  
3. Cerebrocerebellum or neocerebellum consists of lateral zones of cerebellar hemispheres  - Function: Planning and sequencing, prediction and timing  
equilibrium

Question 25: Discuss the different functions of Neocerebellum related to its connections. 
By its connection with B.G, premotor and sensory cortex: it can plan the next movement during 
occurrence of the present movement (smooth progression of movement).  
As it receives various sensory impulses from spinal cord: it can compute changes in rate, time and 
direction of the movement (adjustment of movement to reach a certain goal at a certain time). 
 
Question 27:Differentiate between clinical spasticity and rigidity. 
Spasticity Rigidity 
Hypertonia occurs in UMNL  
(Lesion in corticospinal tracts mostly due to 
hemorrhage or thrombosis In Internal capsule). 
Hypertonia occurs in Parkinsonism 
(Lesion in substantia nigra & loss of 
dopaminergic nigrostriatal neurons). 
It is caused by: Increase In the activity of gamma 
motor neurons due to loss of strong supraspinal 
inhibitory effect on stretch reflex mainly from area 6 & 
BG while some facilitatory discharge remain intact 
along both medial reticulospinal & vestibulospinal 
tract. 
It is caused by: abnormal over excitation of 
alpha and gamma motor neurons (mainly 
alpha) as BG which is Inhibitory is affected. 
It occurs more in antigravity muscles (UL is flexed & 
adducted, LL is extended & adducted). 
It occurs in flexors & extensors but more in 
flexors. 
It appears like clasp knife (sudden release after initial 
resistance). 
In mild cases, it is cogwheel rigidity (not 
continuous) but in severe cases, it is lead 
pipe rigidity (steady & continuous). 
Spasticity is associated with hyperreflexia. Rigidity is associated with normoflexia.

Question 1: Summarize functions of the semicircular canals, the utricle & the saccule? 
I) Function of the semicircular canals: 
During rest : equal discharge from SCCs of both sides so no sense of rotation is detected. 
During rotation from left to right in horizontal plane : - at the beginning : the endolymph move to the left so right crista discharge more than 
left         sensation of body rotation from left to right  - Continuation ( with constant speed ) : Endolymph moves in the same direction of body 
rotation so no sense of rotation  - At the end : Endolymph continue to move in the same direction so the left one discharge 
more          false sensation of rotation to the opposite direction (vertigo )  - After stoppage :the endolymph stops        vertigo disappears  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2) Function of utricle &saccule : 
1. Orientation of the head in space 
i. Head in central position: equal impulses from maculae of both ears:  sensation of 
untilting. 
ii. Tilting head to the right: stretch of macula of right ear than left ear: unequal impulses 
iii. Tilting head to the left: stretch of left macula more than left macula: unequal impulses 
 Utricle: Forward & backward tilt. 
 Saccule: Right & left tilt. 
2. Maintain of body posture during linear acceleration 
SCC 
End    vertigo

stoppage:No sense of 
rotation

Start : Sensation of 
rotation to the same 
direction

Question 2:You cannot detect movement during traveling by a plane but you can detect 
the start and end of movement in a car. Can you explain why? 
As the receptors that detect the linear horizontal acceleration which is the macula of utricle depend on

Question 3: Explain the basic mechanism which maintain the upright posture.  
 The upright posture is maintained by postural reflexes which provide stable postural 
background for performance of voluntary movement. 
 Changes in the excitability of motor neurons (through supra-spinal control) and changes in the 
rate of discharge from gamma efferent neurons to muscle spindles result in changes in the 
excitability of the stretch reflex & this leads to variation in 
the tone of different muscles. 
 The basis of postural reflexes is variation in the tone of the 
muscles.

Factors affecting consolidation of memory:  
1. It requires 5-10 min. for minimal consolidation and about 2 hours to be complete.  
2. It is interrupted by deep anesthesia, brain concussion or electro-convulsive therapy.  
3. It is enhanced by rehearsal of the information & normal quiet sleep which consolidates the 
information received by brain. 
4. It is decreased in mentally fatigued persons.

Question 9: List the areas of the brain believed to be involved in the production of 
speech and their function, describe the different types of aphasias produced by damage 
to these areas. - Speech is two types: 
a. Written speech:Centers of written speech are: 
1. Sensory centers for reading:  - Primary visual area: which allows seeing the words WITHOUT understanding their meanings - Visual association area: which give meaning for every single word without understanding the 
idea of the sentence  
2. Wernicke's area: which allows understanding the idea behind the words, determines the 
thoughts to be expressed and select the best words to answer Motor centers for writing back: - Exner's area: has the program of coordinated movements of hand to give certain written words. 
 
b. Spoken speech:Centers of spoken speech are: 
1. Sensory centers for hearing: - Primary auditory area: allow us to hear spoken words WITHOUT understanding their meanings - Auditory association area: allow understanding meaning of every single word separately - Wernicke's area: as in written speech. 
2. Motor centers of spoken speech: - Broca's area: has the program of spoken words by coordinated movement of laryngeal muscles, 
tongue and lip. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Type of aphasia :

Question 10:Outline the process of normal speech & Differentiate between: Aphasia & 
Dysarthria. 
 
Mechanism of Speech 
1. Understanding a written word 
Written word is seen by 1ry visual area → understood by visual association areas → angular gyrus → 
Wernicke’s area for interpretation & formation of thoughts 
2. Understanding a Spoken word 
Spoken word is heard by 1ry auditory area → understood by auditory association area → Wernicke’s 
area for interpretation & formation of thoughts 
3. To Express by written word 
Wernicke’s area → Discharge to hand skill area → BG & cerebellum for formation of coordinated hand 
movements→ 1ry area for hands → hand Ms 
4. To Express by spoken words 
Wernicke’s area → Broca's area → BG & Cerebellum for formation of a program for vocalization → 1ry 
motor area for face → vocalization 
 
 
 
 
 
Note that : 
 Anomic aphasia: isolated lesion in angular gyrus, cannot give name for seen 
picture &word  
 Conductive aphasia: lesion in &around auditory cortex , cannot put parts of 
words  
 Global  Aphasia    
a) Severe brain lesion  
b) Receptive and expressive aphasia                      c) Non-fluent speech

Question 11: Speech is due to coordinate refined movements. Explain the change in 
speech produced by the following lesions: 
i. Lesion of Neocerebellum.  ii. Lesion of Wernicke’s area.  
i. Lesion of Neocerebellum: lack of coordination giving staccato speech (Dysarthria: abnormality 
of speech due to defect in act of articulation)  
ii. Lesion of Wernicke’s: CauseWernicke’s aphasia 
Patient cannot understand the idea conveyed by the spoken or written words (patient is unable to 
grasp the meaning of the words) and cannot form thoughts so “he speaks excessively but 
neologism”.

Question 12:It is dangerous to swim or dive in water for patient with defective 
labyrinthine function can you explain why? 
Because labyrinth especially macula plays an important role in detection of head position during diving 
under deep water when vision and proprioceptive impulses are not functioning well 
(As in deep water the light source is weak and the more we dive the more the pressure increase)  
 
Question 13: List the functions of the limbic system. 
1. Olfaction: limbic system is responsible for perception & discriminationof olfactory sensation& 
there is relationship bet. Sex and smell  
2. Control of feeding: has a role in regulation of appetite and the lesion in amygdaloid nuclei lead to 
amniophagia (eating all kinds of food) (Hyperphagia) 
3. Control of autonomic response: limbic stimulation produce of autonomic effects which are parts 
of response to emotions  
4. Maternal and sexual behavior  
5. Control of emotions: both limbic system and hypothalamus are concerned with emotion 
genesis(feeling and moods)  
 Fear : caused by stimulation of amygdloid &PVN of hypothalamus . It is abolished by 
destruction of amygdala 
 Rage :It is violent anger to minor stimuli . it is caused by stimulation of Rage area 
(amygdale&lateralhypothalamus ) & by destruction of ventromedial nucleus of hypothalamus  
6. Relation to memory: hippocampus is the site of encoding of short term memory and its 
consolidation & bilateral lesion of hippocampus leads to anterograde amnesia  
7. Motivation: has to centers that control the motivation (reward system in lateral and ventromedial 
nucleus and punishment centers found in periventricular nucleus). 
8. Learning : operant  conditioning  
Papez circuit : - Excitatory ,involved in emotions - Reverberating circuits and long after discharge

## CNS Biochemistry
**Question 1**  
Which one of the following LDH isoenzymes is expressed in neurons?  
A. LDH1  
B. LDH2  
C. LDH3  
D. LDH4  
E. LDH5  

**Correct Answer: A. LDH1**  
*Explanation: “In neurons, this lactate can be used as an energy substrate following its conversion to pyruvate by LDH1 (mainly expressed in neurons).”*

---

**Question 2**  
Neurons uptake glucose from the circulation through which of the following?  
A. Glut 1  
B. Glut 2  
C. Glut 3  
D. Glut 4  
E. Glut 5  

**Correct Answer: C. Glut 3**  
*Explanation: The file states: “Neurons can also take up glucose via the neuronal GLUT3.”*

---

**Question 3**  
Complete: …………. neuronal activity (e.g., sleep and anesthesia) → …………. brain glycogen levels, while …………. neuronal activity → …………. brain glycogen levels.  

**Correct Answer: Decreased ; increased ; increased ; decreased**  
*Explanation: The file states: “Decreased neuronal activity e.g., sleep and anesthesia → increased brain glycogen levels, while increased neuronal activity → decreased brain glycogen levels.”*

---

**Question 4**  
Chemicals in the brain that pass messages among neurons are called:  
A. Glia  
B. Hormones  
C. Neurochemicals  
D. Neurotransmitters  

**Correct Answer: D. Neurotransmitters**  
*Explanation: Direct definition from the slide.*

---

**Question 5**  
Neurotransmitters that increase brain activity are classified as:  
A. Inhibitory  
B. Excitatory  
C. Activity  
D. Disinhibitory  

**Correct Answer: B. Excitatory**  
*Explanation: Excitatory neurotransmitters increase brain activity.*

---

**Question 6**  
Which of the following results from decreased Gamma Amino Butyric Acid (GABA) synthesis?  
A. Depression  
B. Nausea  
C. Headache  
D. Convulsions  
E. Vomiting  

**Correct Answer: D. Convulsions**  
*Explanation: The file states: “GABA deficiency is related to epilepsy and seizure.”*

---

**Question 7**  
Which of the following enzymes is stimulated by cortisol in epinephrine synthesis?  
A. Dopamine hydroxylase  
B. N-methyl transferase  
C. Dopa decarboxylase  
D. Tyrosine hydroxylase  
E. N-acetyl transferase  

**Correct Answer: B. N-methyl transferase**  
*Explanation: Cortisol induces phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which converts norepinephrine to epinephrine.*

---

**Question 8**  
Match the following (more than one answer possible):  
1) Serotonin  
2) Dopamine  
3) Epinephrine  
A) Monoamine oxidase (MAO)  
B) Catechol-O-Methyl Transferase (COMT)  
C) 5-hydroxyindolacetic acid (5-HIAA)  
D) Homovanillic acid (HVA)  
E) Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)  

**Correct Answers: 1→A,C ; 2→A,B,D ; 3→A,B,E**  
*Explanation: Serotonin is catabolized by MAO to 5-HIAA; dopamine and epinephrine are catabolized by MAO and COMT; dopamine gives HVA; epinephrine gives VMA.*

---

**Question 9**  
In carcinoid syndrome, the argentaffin cells of the GIT overproduce which of the following?  
A. Serotonin  
B. Tyrosine  
C. Histamine  
D. Nicotinic acid  
E. Tryptamine  

**Correct Answer: A. Serotonin**  
*Explanation: The file states: “Carcinoid tumor → increased production of serotonin.”*

---

**Question 10**  
Histamine is formed from histidine by which of the following chemical reactions?  
A. Hydroxylation  
B. Decarboxylation  
C. Transamination  
D. Deamination  
E. Dehydrogenation  

**Correct Answer: B. Decarboxylation**  
*Explanation: Histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine.*

---

**Question 11**  
Which of the following releases free ammonia?  
A. Synthesis of purines  
B. Synthesis of monoamines  
C. Synthesis of aminosugars  
D. Catabolism of amino acids  
E. Synthesis of pyrimidines  

**Correct Answer: D. Catabolism of amino acids**  
*Explanation: Deamination of amino acids releases ammonia.*

---

**Question 12**  
Which of the following is/are allosteric activator(s) of glutamate dehydrogenase?  
A. GTP  
B. ADP and GDP  
C. ATP  
D. NADH+H  

**Correct Answer: B. ADP and GDP**  
*Explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and GDP (energy-poor signals).*

**Question 13**  
Which one of the following enzymes catalyzes this reaction? (Carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline)  
A. Ornithine transcarbamoylase  
B. Argininosuccinate synthetase  
C. Arginase  
D. Argininosuccinate lyase  
E. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I  

**Correct Answer: A. Ornithine transcarbamoylase**  
*Explanation: This is the second enzyme of the urea cycle.*

**Question 14**  
Which of the following compounds is a link between urea cycle and citric acid cycle?  
A. Ornithine  
B. Citrate  
C. Fumarate  
D. Urea  
E. Succinate  

**Correct Answer: C. Fumarate**  
*Explanation: Fumarate is produced in the urea cycle (by argininosuccinate lyase) and enters the TCA cycle.*

**Question 15**

**Question 16**

**Question 17**  
Thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP) is required for oxidative decarboxylation of which of the followings?

**Correct Answer: D. α-keto acids**

**Question 21**

## CNS Pathology (from “CNS pathology Q 22.pdf”)

**Question 22**  
Spread of suppurative lung disease to the brain is usually due to:  
a) Lymphatic spread  
b) Retrograde hematogenous spread (paravertebral vessels)  
c) Direct spread  
d) Through normal body passages  

**Correct Answer: b) Retrograde hematogenous spread (paravertebral vessels)**  
*Explanation: Lung infections often reach the brain via Batson’s plexus (retrograde venous spread).*

---

**Question 23**  
A previously healthy 31-year-old woman experiences extensive subarachnoid hemorrhage at the base of the brain. She is afebrile. The CSF protein is slightly increased, but the glucose is normal. Most likely diagnosis:  
a) Acute bacterial meningitis  
b) Ruptured berry aneurysm  
c) Cerebellopontine angle tumor  
d) Pilocytic astrocytoma  
e) Meningioma  

**Correct Answer: b) Ruptured berry aneurysm**  
*Explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage at the base without fever suggests ruptured berry aneurysm (circle of Willis).*

---

**Question 24**  
A 58-year-old hypertensive patient presents with sudden onset of hemiplegia, followed by increased intracranial tension. CT shows extensive intracerebral hemorrhage in the region of basal ganglia. Most probable diagnosis:  
a) Ruptured Arteriovenous malformation  
b) Ruptured congenital berry aneurysm  
c) Ruptured multiple microaneurysms (Charcot‑Bouchard microaneurysms)  
d) Thrombotic occlusion of the middle cerebral artery  

**Correct Answer: c) Ruptured multiple microaneurysms (Charcot‑Bouchard microaneurysms)**  
*Explanation: Hypertensive hemorrhage typically involves basal ganglia/thalamus due to microaneurysm rupture.*

---

**Question 25**  
A 68-year-old man with long‑standing dementia dies. Silver stain of cortex reveals intraneuronal inclusions. These inclusions are:  
a) Lewy bodies  
b) Tau proteins  
c) Negri bodies  
d) Schwann bodies  

**Correct Answer: b) Tau proteins**  
*Explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles (tau) in Alzheimer dementia are silver‑positive.*

---

**Question 26**  
A 50-year-old man has a 3 cm left frontal mass with calcification. Microscopically, sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei and clear halo of cytoplasm. Most likely diagnosis:  
a) Thrombosed berry aneurysm  
b) Oligodendroglioma  
c) Meningioma  
d) Schwannoma  
e) Organizing abscess  

**Correct Answer: b) Oligodendroglioma**  
*Explanation: “Fried egg” appearance (clear halo) and calcification are characteristic of oligodendroglioma.*

---

**Question 27**  
A 9-year-old child has a 4 cm homogenous, well‑circumscribed mass within the fourth ventricle. Microscopically shows rosettes & pseudorosettes. Most likely diagnosis:  
a) Astrocytoma  
b) Ependymoma  
c) Meningioma  
d) Metastatic carcinoma  
e) Schwannoma  

**Correct Answer: b) Ependymoma**  
*Explanation: Fourth ventricle tumor with rosettes/pseudorosettes is ependymoma.*

---

**Question 28**  
A 10-year-old girl develops ataxia and hydrocephalus. CT shows a midline cerebellar mass. Most likely diagnosis:  
a) Schwannoma  
b) Meningioma  
c) Neurofibroma  
d) Medulloblastoma  

**Correct Answer: d) Medulloblastoma**  
*Explanation: Midline cerebellar mass in a child = medulloblastoma.*

---

**Question 29**  
A 65-year-old man has new‑onset seizures and headaches. CT reveals a 6 cm left‑sided intracerebral mass. Most likely diagnosis:  
a) Meningioma  
b) Ependymoma  
c) Schwannoma  
d) Glioblastoma multiforme  

**Correct Answer: d) Glioblastoma multiforme**  
*Explanation: Large, aggressive intracerebral mass in older adult = GBM.*

---

**Question 30**  
Biopsy of a ring‑enhancing tumor in left parietal lobe of a 60‑year‑old shows astrocytic tumor with marked cellular atypia, mitotic activity, pseudopalisading necrosis, and microvascular hyperplasia. Diagnosis:  
a) Astrocytoma, grade I  
b) Astrocytoma, grade 2  
c) Anaplastic astrocytoma  
d) Astrocytoma, grade 4 (glioblastoma multiforme)  

**Correct Answer: d) Astrocytoma, grade 4 (glioblastoma multiforme)**  
*Explanation: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation are hallmarks of GBM.*

---

**Question 31**  
A 9-year-old girl with headaches and ataxia; CT shows midline partially cystic cerebellar mass. Microscopy shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with Rosenthal fibers. Diagnosis:  
a) Astrocytoma, grade I  
b) Astrocytoma, grade 2  
c) Anaplastic astrocytoma  
d) Astrocytoma, grade 4  

**Correct Answer: a) Astrocytoma, grade I (Pilocytic astrocytoma)**  
*Explanation: Rosenthal fibers and biphasic pattern = pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I).*

---

**Question 32**  
A 33-year-old male with seizures; MRI shows ill‑defined infiltrative tumor in frontal lobe. Biopsy shows glial tissue with slightly increased cellularity and mild nuclear pleomorphism. No mitoses, necrosis, or vascular proliferation. Diagnosis:  
a) Astrocytoma, grade I  
b) Astrocytoma, grade 2 (diffuse fibrillar)  
c) Anaplastic astrocytoma  
d) Glioblastoma multiforme  

**Correct Answer: b) Astrocytoma, grade 2 (diffuse fibrillar)**  
*Explanation: Low-grade infiltrative astrocytoma without anaplastic features.*

---

**Question 33**  
An 18-year-old male with a well‑circumscribed mass involving the 4th ventricle. Diagnostic microscopic findings include:  
a) Rosenthal fibers  
b) Chicken wire calcifications  
c) Rosettes & pseudorosettes formation  
d) Verocay bodies  

**Correct Answer: c) Rosettes & pseudorosettes formation**  
*Explanation: Ependymoma (4th ventricle) shows ependymal rosettes.*

---

**Question 34**  
A 45-year-old woman with right‑sided hearing loss and tinnitus. CT shows a 2 cm mass at the cerebellum. Diagnostic microscopic findings include:  
a) Rosenthal fibers  
b) Chicken wire calcifications  
c) Rosettes & pseudorosettes  
d) Verocay bodies  

**Correct Answer: d) Verocay bodies**  
*Explanation: Cerebellopontine angle mass (schwannoma) shows Antoni A/B areas with Verocay bodies.*

---

**Question 35**  
An 86-year-old man with progressive disorientation and language impairment. Microscopic findings include:  
a) Rosenthal fibers  
b) Amyloid β proteins  
c) Lewy bodies  
d) Verocay bodies  

**Correct Answer: b) Amyloid β proteins**  
*Explanation: Alzheimer disease shows amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.*

---

**Question 36**  
Oligodendrogliomas (ODs) are not characterized by:  
a) have IDH 1 mutation  
b) have IDH 2 mutation  
c) Activation of the mitogen‑activated protein kinase (MAPK)  
d) Chromosomes 1p/19q codeletion  

**Correct Answer: c) Activation of MAPK**  
*Explanation: Oligodendrogliomas typically have IDH1/2 mutations and 1p/19q codeletion; MAPK activation is more common in pilocytic astrocytoma.*

---

**Question 37**  
Localized Pilocytic Astrocytoma shows all except:  
A. Activation of the MAPK pathway  
B. Activation, alterations of BRAF  
C. Inactivation of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)  
D. Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2  

**Correct Answer: D. Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2**  
*Explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas have BRAF alterations, not IDH mutations.*

**Question 42**

B. Moclobemide  
C. Selegiline

**Correct Answer: A. Phenelzine**  
*Explanation: Non‑selective MAOIs (phenelzine) cause hypertensive crisis with tyramine (old cheese).*

**Question 45**  
Nocturnal enuresis is treated with imipramine but not fluoxetine because:  
A. Imipramine induces insomnia while fluoxetine induces sedation  
B. Imipramine is safer than fluoxetine  
C. Imipramine possesses anticholinergic effects but fluoxetine does not

**Correct Answer: C. Imipramine possesses anticholinergic effects but fluoxetine does not**  
*Explanation: Anticholinergic effect helps enuresis (relaxes bladder).*

**Question 46**  
Indications of antidepressants do not include:  
A. Convulsive disorders  
B. Eating disorders  
C. Chronic neuropathic pain  
D. Obsessive‑compulsive disorders  

**Correct Answer: A. Convulsive disorders**  
*Explanation: Antidepressants can lower seizure threshold; not indicated for convulsive disorders.*

**Question 47**  
The nonselective MAOIs have limited use as antidepressants because of their:  
A. Low efficacy  
B. High toxicity

**Correct Answer: D. Both B & C**  
*Explanation: High toxicity and many interactions (hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome).*

**Question 48**

A. Imipramine

**Question 49**  
Disadvantages of tricyclic antidepressants include:  
A. Narrow safety margin  
B. Frequent side effects  
C. Delayed therapeutic effect  
D. All of the above  

**Correct Answer: D. All of the above**  
*Explanation: TCAs are toxic in overdose, have many side effects, and take weeks to work.*

**Question 50**

**Correct Answer: None are completely safe; but least teratogenic among options? Valproate is highly teratogenic. Typically lamotrigine is preferred. However, from the file, likely the intended answer is none. But the question asks “safe” – perhaps carbamazepine? No. I’ll state: **No option is safe; however, among these, carbamazepine has lower risk than valproate. But standard answer: **A. Carbamazepine** is sometimes used but not safe. Given the options, carbamazepine is the least teratogenic. But careful: The file says “safe” – none are. I’ll go with A.

A. Have shorter t½ than their respective agonists  
B. Given orally  
C. Given in anesthesia to reverse CNS depression of their agonists  
D. Specific respiratory stimulants in benzodiazepine or opioid toxicity  

**Correct Answer: B. Given orally**  
*Explanation: Both are given IV, not orally.*

---

**Question 83**  
Abuse potential of buspirone is low because:  
A. It has a weak anxiolytic effect  
B. It has no recognizable effect on brain neurotransmitters  
C. It has a delayed onset of action  
D. Its marked sedating effect is troublesome  

**Correct Answer: C. It has a delayed onset of action**  
*Explanation: Buspirone lacks immediate rewarding effects, reducing abuse liability.*

---

**Question 84**  
Dentists avoid extraction in infection because of all the following Except:  
A. Fear of spread of infection  
B. Infection decreases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics  
C. Infection reduces crossing of local anesthetics inside nerve cell  
D. Infection increases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics  

**Correct Answer: D. Infection increases extracellular unionized form**  
*Explanation: Infection lowers pH, decreasing unionized form, not increasing.*

---

**Question 85**  
The following is not true concerning ester type local anesthetics:  
A. Shorter acting than amides  
B. Less liable to induce allergy  
C. Less liable to systemic toxicity than amides  
D. Procaine is a member of this group  

**Correct Answer: B. Less liable to induce allergy**  
*Explanation: Esters are more allergenic due to PABA metabolite.*

---

**Question 86**  
The following is not true about local anesthetics:  
A. Adding sodium bicarbonate increases activity  
B. Bupivacaine is short acting  
C. Lidocaine is an amide  
D. Benzocaine is used as a surface anesthetic  

**Correct Answer: B. Bupivacaine is short acting**  
*Explanation: Bupivacaine is long acting.*

---

**Question 87**  
The following is not true about cocaine:  
A. It is a local anesthetic  
B. Acute toxicity may result in convulsions  
C. It is a potent vasodilator  
D. Chronic abuse results in psychosis  

**Correct Answer: C. It is a potent vasodilator**  
*Explanation: Cocaine is a vasoconstrictor.*

---

**Question 88**  
Sumatriptan precautions include all of the following except:  
A. Should not be used for long term  
B. Diabetic patient  
C. Men over 40  
D. Postmenopausal  

**Correct Answer: C. Men over 40**  
*Explanation: Triptans are avoided in men over 40 with cardiac risk, but the exception is “men over 40” is not a precaution per se; typical precautions include cardiovascular disease, not just age.*

---

**Question 89**  
Gangrene may be associated with:  
A. Acetaminophen  
B. Metoclopramide  
C. Opioid  
D. Dihydroergotamine  

**Correct Answer: D. Dihydroergotamine**  
*Explanation: Ergot derivatives cause vasospasm and gangrene.*

---

**Question 90**  
All mentioned drugs useful in prophylaxis of migraine except:  
A. Amitriptyline  
B. Clonidine  
C. Diazepam  
D. Topiramate  

**Correct Answer: C. Diazepam**  
*Explanation: Diazepam is not a migraine prophylactic.*

---

**Question 91**  
All mentioned drugs useful in treatment of migraine except:  
A. Nifedipine  
B. Ergotamine  
C. Benzodiazepine  
D. Morphine  

**Correct Answer: A. Nifedipine**  
*Explanation: Nifedipine is not used for acute migraine.*

---

**Question 92**  
Mild infrequent migraine attack is managed by:  
A. Triptan  
B. Ergot  
C. Diazepam  
D. Ibuprofen  

**Correct Answer: D. Ibuprofen**  
*Explanation: NSAIDs are first‑line for mild migraine.*

---

**Question 93**  
Resistant migraine attack is managed by:  
A. Metoclopramide  
B. Dihydroergotamine  
C. Diazepam  
D. Sumatriptan  

**Correct Answer: B. Dihydroergotamine**  
*Explanation: DHE is used for refractory migraine.*

---

**Question 94**  
One of the following pairs of drugs used in treatment of migraine could be used intranasally:  
A. Sumatriptan and diazepam  
B. Metoclopramide and morphine  
C. Ergotamine and triptan  
D. Triptan and dihydroergotamine  

**Correct Answer: D. Triptan and dihydroergotamine**  
*Explanation: Both sumatriptan and DHE have intranasal formulations.*

**Question 95**  
One of the following drugs could be used sublingually in treatment of migraine attacks:  
A. Ergotamine  
B. Triptan  
C. Topiramate  
D. Acetaminophen  

**Correct Answer: A. Ergotamine**  
*Explanation: Ergotamine is available sublingually.*

---

**Question 96**  
Sumatriptan should not be combined within 24 hours with the following drug:  
A. Naproxen  
B. Morphine  
C. Ergotamine  
D. Atropine  

**Correct Answer: C. Ergotamine**  
*Explanation: Additive vasoconstriction.*

## Parasitology (from “parasitology.pdf”)

**Question 97**  
What is the most common parasitic infection of the CNS?

b) Sparganosis  
c) Cerebral malaria  
d) Neurocysticercosis  
e) Amoebic brain abscess  

**Correct Answer: d) Neurocysticercosis**  
*Explanation: The file states it is the most common parasitic CNS infection.*

**Question 98**  
The most common presenting problem associated with neurocysticercosis is:  
a) Nausea and vomiting  
b) Decreased level of consciousness  
c) New onset seizures  
d) Blurred vision  
e) Facial palsy  

**Correct Answer: c) New onset seizures**  
*Explanation: The file lists seizures as the most common presentation.*

**Question 99**  
20-year-old immigrant from China with headache, confusion, seizures, multiple subcutaneous nodules, and eating raw frog meat. Suspect:  
a) Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE)  
b) Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM)  
c) Sleeping sickness  
d) Cerebral malaria  
e) Sparganosis  

**Correct Answer: e) Sparganosis**  
*Explanation: The file associates raw frog meat with sparganosis.*

---

**Question 100**  
A 23-year-old woman, former pig farmer from Angola, with left-sided weakness and seizures. MRI shows parietal cysts. Diagnosis:  
a) Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis  
b) Cerebral malaria  
c) Neurocysticercosis  
d) Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis  
e) Sleeping sickness  

**Correct Answer: c) Neurocysticercosis**  
*Explanation: History of pig farming and cystic lesions suggest neurocysticercosis.*

**Question 101**  
Which mode of transmission accounts for neurocysticercosis?  
a) Drinking water containing cyclops infected with procercoid larva  
b) Swimming water contaminated with Naegleria fowleri trophozoites  
c) Swallowing Taenia solium eggs in contaminated water or food  
d) Inhaling Acanthamoeba cyst or trophozoite through nasal passages  
e) Using frog tissues as poultices  

**Correct Answer: c) Swallowing Taenia solium eggs**  
*Explanation: The file states: “The patient ingested eggs of Taenia solium in food or drink contaminated by stools.”*

---

**Question 102**  
A 17-year-old male with palpebral edema, conjunctival congestion, and a nodular mass removed from the eye. Most probable diagnosis:  
a) Acanthamoeba keratitis  
b) Toxoplasmosis  
c) Naegleria fowleri infection  
d) Sparganosis  
e) Cysticercosis  

**Correct Answer: d) Sparganosis**  
*Explanation: Subcutaneous/ocular nodule from frog/cyclops exposure – sparganosis.*

**Question 103**  
A previously healthy 12-year-old boy with fever, headache, altered taste/smell, confusion after swimming in a freshwater lake. CSF shows PMN leukocytosis and motile cells. Death. Most likely diagnosis:  
a) Bacterial meningitis  
b) Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis  
c) Neurocysticercosis  
d) Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis  
e) Sparganosis  

**Correct Answer: d) Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis**  
*Explanation: The file describes Naegleria fowleri from warm freshwater, rapid course, altered taste/smell.*

**Question 104**  
Which parasite causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis?  
a) Naegleria fowleri  
b) Entamoeba histolytica

**Question 105**

**Question 106**

**Question 107**

**Question 108**  
As regards Acanthamoeba encephalitis:

**Question 109**  
A baby born with hydrocephalus (image). Which infection?

**Question 1**  
Concerning the lateral ventricle, choose one correct answer:  
a. Its anterior horn lies in the parietal lobe.  
b. Its posterior horn lies in the temporal lobe.  
c. It is the cavity of the cerebral hemisphere.  
d. Has no choroid plexus.  

**Correct Answer: c. It is the cavity of the cerebral hemisphere.**  
*Explanation: The lateral ventricles are the cavities of the cerebral hemispheres.*

---

**Question 2**  
The cisterna magna of subarachnoid space is a name given to the:  
a. interpeduncular cistern.  
b. cistern of the corpus callosum.  
c. cistern of the lateral fissure.  
d. cerebello‑medullary cistern.  

**Correct Answer: d. cerebello‑medullary cistern.**  
*Explanation: The cisterna magna is the cerebellomedullary cistern.*

---

**Question 3**  
One of the following, does not belong to the long association fibers:  
a. fornix.  
b. superior longitudinal bundle.  
c. uncinate fasciculus.  
d. inferior longitudinal bundle.  

**Correct Answer: a. fornix.**  
*Explanation: The fornix is a projection fiber (part of the limbic system), not a long association fiber.*

---

**Question 4**  
The paracentral lobule contains motor and sensory areas for one of the following parts:  
a. head and neck.  
b. trunk.  
c. upper limb.  
d. lower limb.  

**Correct Answer: d. lower limb.**  
*Explanation: The paracentral lobule contains the leg and foot area of the primary motor and sensory cortices.*

---

**Question 5**  
One of the following muscles is not inserted into the mandible:  
a. temporalis.  
b. buccinator.  
c. masseter.  
d. medial pterygoid.  

**Correct Answer: b. buccinator.**  
*Explanation: The buccinator inserts into the orbicularis oris and the pterygomandibular raphe, not into the mandible.*

---

**Question 6**  
Regarding the parotid duct, the following statements are correct, except:  
a. it courses across masseter below transverse facial artery.  
b. it opens into vestibule of mouth opposite upper second molar tooth.  
c. it can be palpated against the contracted masseter muscle.  
d. it pierces masseter muscle to reach the vestibule of mouth.  

**Correct Answer: d. it pierces masseter muscle to reach the vestibule of mouth.**  
*Explanation: The parotid duct pierces the buccinator, not the masseter.*

**Question 7**  
The following are branches of the mandibular nerve or its divisions, except:  
a. nerve to the medial pterygoid from the trunk.  
b. superior alveolar nerve from its anterior division.  
c. inferior alveolar nerve from its posterior division.  
d. auriculo‑temporal nerve from its posterior division.  

**Correct Answer: b. superior alveolar nerve from its anterior division.**  
*Explanation: The superior alveolar nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve, not the mandibular.*

---

**Question 8**  
The following nerves are embedded in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus except:  
a. oculomotor.  
b. trochlear.  
c. ophthalmic division of the trigeminal.  
d. mandibular division of the trigeminal.  

**Correct Answer: d. mandibular division of the trigeminal.**  
*Explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) does not pass through the cavernous sinus; it exits via foramen ovale.*

---

**Question 9**  
A patient noticed on tongue protrusion it deviates to the left. Possibly this is due to damage of:  
a. left lingual nerve.  
b. left chorda tympani nerve.  
c. left vagus nerve.  
d. left hypoglossal nerve.  

**Correct Answer: d. left hypoglossal nerve.**  
*Explanation: The genioglossus (protrudes tongue) is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; deviation toward the side of the lesion.*

---

**Question 10**  
The sensory supply of the mucous membrane of the larynx below the level of the vocal cords is:  
a. recurrent laryngeal nerve.  
b. superior laryngeal nerve.  
c. external laryngeal nerve.  
d. internal laryngeal nerve.  

**Correct Answer: a. recurrent laryngeal nerve.**  
*Explanation: Below the vocal folds, sensation is from the recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus).*

---

**Question 11**  
The only muscle of the soft palate that is not supplied by the vagus nerve is the:  
a. palatoglossus.  
b. palatopharyngeus.  
c. tensor palate.  
d. levator palate.  

**Correct Answer: c. tensor palate.**  
*Explanation: The tensor veli palatini is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3), not the vagus.*

**Question 12**  
Which of the following muscles can retract the mandible?  
a. platysma.  
b. buccinator.  
c. temporalis.  
d. masseter.  

**Correct Answer: c. temporalis.**  
*Explanation: The posterior fibers of the temporalis retract the mandible.*

**Question 13**  
One of the followings is a feature of the mandible of old age:  
a. The mandible consists of two halves.  
b. The mental foramen lies near the upper margin of the mandible.  
c. The ramus of the mandible is nearly vertical.  
d. The mandibular canal lies near the lower border of the mandible.  

**Correct Answer: c. The ramus of the mandible is nearly vertical.**  
*Explanation: In old age, after tooth loss, the ramus becomes more vertical and the angle increases.*

**Question 14**  
The maxillary nerve leaves the cranial cavity by passing through:  
a. Foramen ovale  
b. Sphenopalatine foramen  
c. Foramen spinosum

**Correct Answer: d. Foramen rotundum.**  
*Explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.*

**Question 15**  
Regarding the arterial supply of the face, one of the following arteries is a branch of the ophthalmic artery:  
a. Dorsal nasal

**Correct Answer: a. Dorsal nasal.**

**Question 16**  
The insertion of which of the following muscles of mastication is close to the wisdom tooth?  
a. Masseter  
b. Temporalis  
c. Lateral pterygoid

**Correct Answer: b. Temporalis.**

**Question 18**  
The Parasympathetic root of sphenopalatine ganglion is:  
a. Lesser superficial petrosal nerve  
b. Chorda tympani nerve  
c. Deep petrosal nerve  
d. Greater superficial petrosal nerve  

**Correct Answer: d. Greater superficial petrosal nerve.**

**Question 19**  
The insertion of which of the following muscles prevents an upward enlargement of a thyroid tumor?  
a. Sternohyoid  
b. Omohyoid  
c. Sternothyroid

**Question 20**  
The 1st cervical spinal nerve communicates with the:

**Question 35**

**Question 36**  
The parasympathetic nucleus supplying the lacrimal gland is:  
A. Superior salivary

**Question 37**

**Question 39**  
What is the muscle responsible for flexion of the head to the same side and rotation of the face to the opposite side?  
A. Trapezius  
B. Sternomastoid

**Question 40**  
A 35‑year‑old man came to the outpatient clinic complaining of dripping of saliva and accumulation of the food in the vestibule of the mouth cavity. Which muscle was most probably affected?  
A. Temporalis  
B. Masseter  
C. Buccinator  
D. Lateral pterygoid  

**Correct Answer: C. Buccinator.**  
*Explanation: The buccinator keeps the vestibule clear; its paralysis causes food accumulation in the cheek.*

**Question 41**  
A 55‑year‑old man is admitted to the hospital with severe scalp lacerations, which were sutured. After three days the wound is inflamed, swollen, and painful. Which of the following layers of the scalp is the dangerous area?  
A. Skin  
B. Connective tissue  
C. Aponeurosis of occipitofrontalis  
D. Loose areolar tissue  

**Correct Answer: D. Loose areolar tissue.**  
*Explanation: Infection in the loose areolar tissue (dangerous area) can spread to the cranial cavity via emissary veins.*

**Question 42**  
The muscle which rotates the eyeball downwards and laterally is:  
A. Superior rectus  
B. Inferior rectus  
C. Superior oblique  
D. Lateral rectus  

**Correct Answer: C. Superior oblique.**  
*Explanation: The superior oblique primarily intorts and depresses, but also abducts (down and out).*

**Question 43**  
A 38‑year‑old man was admitted to the hospital for a partial thyroidectomy. After the operation, the patient could not abduct the true vocal cords due to a nerve injury. Which of the following muscles was most likely affected?  
A. Posterior cricoarytenoid  
B. Lateral cricoarytenoid  
C. Thyroarytenoid  
D. Cricothyroid  

**Correct Answer: A. Posterior cricoarytenoid.**  
*Explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal cords; supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.*

**Question 44**  
The parotid duct opens into the vestibule of the mouth opposite:  
A. The upper 2nd premolar tooth.  
B. The upper 1st molar tooth.  
C. The upper 2nd molar tooth.  
D. The upper 3rd molar tooth  

**Correct Answer: C. The upper 2nd molar tooth.**  
*Explanation: The parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar.*

---

**Question 45**  
The lesser palatine nerve originates from:  
A. Maxillary nerve  
B. Greater palatine nerve  
C. Otic ganglion  
D. Sphenopalatine ganglion  

**Correct Answer: D. Sphenopalatine ganglion.**  
*Explanation: The lesser palatine nerve is a branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion (sphenopalatine ganglion).*

---

**Question 46**  
The only tributary of the subclavian vein is:  
A. IJV  
B. EJV  
C. Brachiocephalic  
D. Anterior jugular  

**Correct Answer: B. EJV.**  
*Explanation: The external jugular vein is a tributary of the subclavian vein.*

---

**Question 47**  
The anterior boundary of tonsillar fossa is:  
A. Palatoglossal fold  
B. Palatopharyngeal fold  
C. Soft palate  
D. Dorsum of the tongue  

**Correct Answer: A. Palatoglossal fold.**  
*Explanation: The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar) forms the anterior boundary of the tonsillar fossa.*

---

**Question 48**  
In case of right corticobulbar tract injury above the level of the motor nucleus of facial nerve, which side of the face is affected?  
A. Upper ½ right side.  
B. Lower ½ right side.  
C. Upper ½ left side.  
D. Lower ½ left side.  

**Correct Answer: D. Lower ½ left side.**  
*Explanation: UMN lesion of right corticobulbar tract → contralateral lower face weakness (left lower face).*

---

**Question 49**  
Which of the following structures has an extrapyramidal function?  
A. Amygdaloid nucleus  
B. Claustrum  
C. Corpus striatum  
D. Fornix  

**Correct Answer: C. Corpus striatum.**  
*Explanation: The corpus striatum (caudate + putamen) is part of the basal ganglia (extrapyramidal system).*

---

**Question 50**  
The following are projection fibers of the cerebral hemisphere:  
A. Corticobulbar  
B. Cingulum  
C. Arcuate  
D. Uncinate  

**Correct Answer: A. Corticobulbar.**  
*Explanation: Corticobulbar fibers are projection fibers (cortex to brainstem).*

---

**Question 51**  
A 69‑year‑old woman was brought to the ER with inability to speak. She was diagnosed that she had motor aphasia. Which lobe of the brain is affected?  
A. Frontal  
B. Parietal  
C. Temporal  
D. Occipital  

**Correct Answer: A. Frontal.**  
*Explanation: Broca’s area (motor speech) is in the inferior frontal gyrus.*

---

**Question 52**  
The part of the cerebellum concerned with planning and programming movement is:  
A. Spinocerebellar  
B. Vestibulocerebellum  
C. Archicerebellum  
D. Neocerebellum  

**Correct Answer: D. Neocerebellum.**  
*Explanation: The neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum) is involved in planning and coordination of voluntary movements.*

---

**Question 53**  
A patient came to ER presenting with headache; fever; nausea; stiffness of the neck. He was diagnosed as meningitis. What is the name of the procedure by which a special needle is inserted into the subarachnoid space to get sample of CSF to confirm the diagnosis?  
A. Conus medullaris  
B. Lumbar cistern  
C. Lumbar puncture  
D. Filum terminale  

**Correct Answer: C. Lumbar puncture.**  
*Explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed to obtain CSF from the subarachnoid space.*

---

**Question 54**  
The skin over buccinator is supplied by the following nerve:  
a) Ophthalmic  
b) Mandibular  
c) Maxillary  
d) Facial  

**Correct Answer: b) Mandibular.**  
*Explanation: The buccal branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) supplies skin over the buccinator.*

---

**Question 55**  
The parasympathetic supply of the parotid gland is from the following nerve:  
a) Lesser petrosal  
b) Deep petrosal  
c) Greater petrosal  
d) External petrosal  

**Correct Answer: a) Lesser petrosal.**  
*Explanation: The lesser petrosal nerve (from the tympanic plexus) carries preganglionic parasympathetics to the otic ganglion for the parotid gland.*

---

**Question 56**  
Which of the following lymph nodes drains directly the tip of the tongue?  
a) Jugulo‑digastric  
b) Jugulo‑omohyoid  
c) Submental  
d) Submandibular  

**Correct Answer: c) Submental.**  
*Explanation: The tip of the tongue drains to the submental lymph nodes.*

---

**Question 57**  
The only infrahyoid muscle which is not supplied by ansa cervicalis is:  
a) Sternohyoid  
b) Thyrohyoid  
c) Omohyoid  
d) Sternothyroid  

**Correct Answer: b) Thyrohyoid.**  
*Explanation: Thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 via the hypoglossal nerve, not by ansa cervicalis.*

---

**Question 58**  
The rootlets of the vagus nerve are emerging between:  
a) Pyramid and olive.  
b) Pyramid and pons.  
c) Olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.  
d) Gracile and cuneate tubercles.  

**Correct Answer: c) Olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.**  
*Explanation: Vagus rootlets emerge from the medulla in the post‑olivary sulcus (between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle).*

---

**Question 59**  
The part of the cerebellum concerned with balance is:  
a) Paleocerebellum  
b) Neocerebellum  
c) Flocculonodular  
d) Lateral zone area  

**Correct Answer: c) Flocculonodular.**  
*Explanation: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) is concerned with balance and eye movements.*

---

**Question 60**  
Deep inguinal ring is a gap in:  
a) Fascia transversalis  
b) External spermatic fascia  
c) External oblique aponeurosis  
d) Cremasteric muscle  

**Correct Answer: a) Fascia transversalis.**  
*Explanation: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia.*

---

**Question 61**  
The short gastric arteries originate from:  
a) Hepatic  
b) Coeliac  
c) Gastroduodenal  
d) Splenic  

**Correct Answer: d) Splenic.**  
*Explanation: Short gastric arteries are branches of the splenic artery.*

---

**Question 62**  
The bare area of the liver is enclosed by which of the following ligaments:  
a) ligamentum teres  
b) Coronary ligament  
c) Ligamentum venosum  
d) Falciform ligament  

**Correct Answer: b) Coronary ligament.**  
*Explanation: The bare area of the liver is bounded by the two layers of the coronary ligament.*

---

**Question 63**  
Which of the following nerves emerges from the medial aspect of psoas major muscle?  
a) Obturator  
b) Iliohypogastric  
c) Ilioinguinal  
d) Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh  

**Correct Answer: a) Obturator.**  
*Explanation: The obturator nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas major.*

---

**Question 64**  
The following single branch of abdominal aorta arises at the level of L3:  
a) Coeliac  
b) Superior mesenteric  
c) Inferior mesenteric  
d) Median sacral  

**Correct Answer: d) Median sacral.**  
*Explanation: The median sacral artery arises from the aorta just above its bifurcation (L4 level usually, but among options it is the most caudal).*

---

**Question 65**  
The lateral umbilical fold is raised by:  
a) Obliterated umbilical artery  
b) Obliterated urachus  
c) Deep circumflex iliac artery  
d) Inferior epigastric artery  

**Correct Answer: d) Inferior epigastric artery.**  
*Explanation: The lateral umbilical fold contains the inferior epigastric vessels.*

---

**Question 66**  
A 68 year‑old man with forward tilting of the trunk and short steps, rigidity and trembling. Diagnosis: Parkinson’s disease. Which area of the midbrain is suspected to be affected?  
a. Crus cerebri  
b. Substantia nigra  
c. Tegmentum  
d. Tectum  

**Correct Answer: b. Substantia nigra.**  
*Explanation: Parkinson’s disease involves degeneration of the substantia nigra pars compacta (dopaminergic neurons).*

---

**Question 67**  
A 64‑year‑old man unable to produce speech but understands and can write words. What area is affected?  
a. Broca's area  
b. Premotor area  
c. Wernicke's area  
d. Supplementary motor area  

**Correct Answer: a. Broca's area.**  
*Explanation: Broca’s aphasia (non‑fluent) affects speech production with preserved comprehension.*

---

**Question 68**  
A 45‑year‑old male with absent cremasteric reflex. Which nerve is responsible for the efferent limb?  
a) Ilioinguinal  
b) Iliohypogastric  
c) Genitofemoral  
d) Pudendal  

**Correct Answer: c) Genitofemoral.**  
*Explanation: The cremasteric reflex efferent limb is via the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.*

---

**Question 69**  
A 70‑year‑old man with 90% blockage at the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery. Which artery would provide collateral supply to the descending colon?  
a) Left gastroepiploic  
b) Middle colic artery  
c) Sigmoid artery  
d) Superior rectal artery  

**Correct Answer: b) Middle colic artery.**  
*Explanation: The middle colic artery (from superior mesenteric) can collateralize with the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric).*

---

**Question 70**  
A 55‑year‑old man with a perforating ulcer in the posterior wall of the stomach. Where would peritonitis most likely develop initially?  
a) Omental bursa  
b) Greater sac  
c) Morison's pouch  
d) Right subhepatic space  

**Correct Answer: a) Omental bursa.**  
*Explanation: Posterior gastric ulcer perforates into the lesser sac (omental bursa).*

Chapter 1
?
1. What are neurodegenerative diseases?
y Disorders characterized by the cellular 
degeneration of subsets of neurons that 
are typically related by function, rather than 
physical location in the brain.
Neurodegenerative
7. 
Pathology
What is the protein responsible for the 
creation of Aß in Alzheimer’s Disease?
y Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP)
8. What is the major genetic risk factor for 
Alzheimer’s Disease?
2. How are neurodegenerative diseases classified?
y They can be classified based on:
Clinical presentation
Type of protein
Pathological processes
Genetic abnormalities.
3. What is dementia?
y The development of memory impairment 
and other cognitive deficits severe enough 
to decrease the affected person’s capacity 
to function at the previous level despite a 
normal level of consciousness.
4. What is the most common cause of 
dementia in the elderly population?
y Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)
5. What is the crucial event in the 
pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)?
y The accumulation of Beta Amyloid Peptide 
(Aß) in the brain over time.
6. What is the role of Amyloid Precursor 
Protein (APP) in Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)?
y APP is sequentially cleaved by enzymes to 
generate Aß. 
y Mutations in APP or in enzymes responsible 
for its degradation can lead to familial AD.
y Apolipoprotein E variant e4 (ApoE4)
9. What are the microscopic features of 
Alzheimer’s Disease?
y Neuronal loss & Gliosis
y Extracellular neuritic plaques
y Intracellular Neurofibrillary tangles
y Cerebral amyloid angiopathy 
10. What is the common coexisting 
neuropathology seen with Alzheimer’s 
Disease?
y Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy
11. What is the clinical feature that can assist 
in distinguishing Frontotemporal lobe 
degeneration from Alzheimer’s Disease?
y Temporal deterioration of language and 
frontal lobes degeneration and atrophy
12. What are the causes of Parkinsonism?
y Parkinson’s disease, Viral encephalitis, 
Vascular (post-stroke), Environmental Toxin, 
Drug-Induced
13. What gene mutations cause autosomal 
dominant Parkinson’s Disease?
y Point mutations and duplications of the 
gene encoding α-synuclein

14. What are the clinical features of 
Frontotemporal lobe degeneration (FTLD)?
 yTemporal deterioration of language and 
frontal lobe degeneration and atrophy. 
 yThese symptoms precede memory 
disturbances.

 yUp to 40% of FTLD cases show autosomal

encoding for microtubule-associated 
protein tau.

 yMovement disorder progression
 yAn increased risk of suicide
 yEarly cognitive symptoms that may progress

 yYes, Huntington Chorea is an autosomal

 yParkinson’s disease itself (85%), 
 yViral encephalitis
 yVascular factors (post-stroke)
 yEnvironmental toxins
 yDrug-induced factors (e.g., antipsychotic

Sphingolipids related disorders
?
1. What is Multiple Sclerosis?
y An autoimmune demyelinating disorder 
characterized by distinct episodes of 
neurologic deficits.
2. True or False: Multiple Sclerosis is more 
common in men than women.
y False
3. What is the main pathology of Multiple 
Sclerosis?
y Autoimmune disease caused by a loss of 
tolerance to myelin antigens.
4. Which cells are involved in the 
pathogenesis of Multiple Sclerosis?
y CD4+ T cells
y CD8+ T cells
y B cells.
5. What are the gross characteristics of 
Multiple Sclerosis lesions?
y Multiple, well-circumscribed
y Gray-tan plaques near the ventricles and in 
various areas of the CNS.
6. What is the microscopic appearance of 
active Multiple Sclerosis plaques?
y Evidence of ongoing myelin breakdown 
with abundant macrophages containing 
myelin debris.
7. 
What is the clinical course of Multiple 
Sclerosis?
y Relapsing and remitting episodes of 
neurologic impairment with gradual 
accumulation of deficits over time.
Pathology
8. What imaging studies are mandatory for 
Multiple Sclerosis diagnosis?
y MRI brain
9. True or False: Oligoclonal bands are 
usually identified in the CSF of patients 
with Multiple Sclerosis.
y True
10. What are the main symptoms of Multiple 
Sclerosis?
y Fatigue, visual impairment, cognitive 
impairment, weakness, spasms, pain, and 
bowel and urinary dysfunction.
11. What is the primary lipid of myelin?
y The primary lipid of myelin is a glycolipid 
called ‘’galactocerebroside’’.
12. What are demyelinating disorders?
y Demyelinating disorders are diseases of the 
nervous system in which the myelin sheath 
of neurons is damaged, impairing the 
conduction of signals in the affected nerves.
13. What is Krabbe disease?
y Krabbe disease is an autosomal recessive 
disorder characterized by a deficiency of 
Galactosyl ceramidase, resulting in the 
accumulation of unmetabolized lipids, 
leading to demyelination and severe 
progressive degeneration of motor skills.
14. What are primary diseases of myelin?
y Primary diseases of myelin refer to diseases 
within the CNS where axons are tightly 
ensheathed by myelin, and myelin is not formed 
properly or has abnormal turnover kinetics.

 yEndogenous: endorphins - enkephalins -

8. How do opioids work?
 yOpioids (directly or through release of 
opio-peptides) activate opioid receptors 
(Mu, kappa & delta) present in the CNS and 
periphery, producing morphine-like effects.

 yAfferent pain-conducting fibers (peripheral

 ySpinal cord (spinal analgesia)
 yBrain stem, thalamus & cerebral cortex

 y Limbic system (euphoria & emotional

by opioids?
 yEuphoria is due to increased dopamine in 
the nucleus accumbens, which is formed in 
the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
11. What is the cellular mechanism of opioid 
action?
 yActivation of opioid receptors inhibits 
neuronal activity through: 
 inhibition of Ca2+ entry 
 stimulation of K+ outflux, leading to 
neuronal inhibition.

 yAnalgesia, Sedation, Euphoria, Vasodilation,

Drug Therapy of Parkinson’s Disease
?
1. What is the cause of iatrogenic Parkinson’s 
disease?
y Long-term use of D2 antagonists that 
cross the blood-brain barrier such as 
antipsychotics 
2. What is the aim of drug therapy in 
Parkinson’s disease?
y To restore balance between dopamine and 
acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia
3. What is L-Dopa?
y L-Dopa is a dopamine precursor that can 
cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
4. How is L-Dopa converted to dopamine?
y L-Dopa is decarboxylated by the central 
dopa decarboxylase enzyme to dopamine 
(DA) in the dopaminergic neurons.
5. What is the purpose of carbidopa in L-Dopa 
therapy?
y Carbidopa, a peripheral decarboxylase 
enzyme inhibitor, is given with L-Dopa 
to prevent its conversion to dopamine 
peripherally.
6. What causes fluctuations in response of 
L-dopa?
y Short half-life 
y fluctuation in L-dopa level
7. 
How can on-off effect be managed?
y Add Entacapone 
y or Use Apomorphine (SC)
8. What is end-of-dose akinesia?
y Gradual loss of the useful effect (wearing 
off) before the time of the next dose
9. How can end-of-dose akinesia be managed?
y Add Selegiline 
y Use dopamine agonists

 yShorten sleep latency 
 y Increase stage 2 NREM sleep 
 yDecrease stage 3 & 4 NREM sleep 
 yDecrease REM sleep

 y Intermediate acting: Alprazolam, Lorazepam

 yRapid onset 
 yLess tolerance & dependence 
 yLess adverse effects on cognitive function,

 yREM sleep suppression

 yDelayed onset (2 weeks)
 yNot effective in insomnia or panic attacks
8. What are the general guidelines for

 yDrug therapy is indicated only in severe

acute insomnia 
 yStart with a small dose for a short time to 
avoid abuse and dependence 
 yTerminate slowly to avoid withdrawal

 yAdjust dose in hepatic dysfunction

 yBinds to the BZD1 receptor subtype 
(involved in sedation & hypnosis) facilitating 
the inhibitory effects of GABA

4. How does the rate of firing affect the 
effectiveness of local anesthetics?
y Blockade of Na+ channels by LA is use
dependent, making it is more effective in 
rapid-firing nerves (sensory nerves) than 
slow firing nerves (motor nerves).
5. Which nerve fibers are more sensitive to 
local anesthetics?
y Small nerve fibers conducting pain, 
temperature, and autonomic activity are 
more sensitive to LA than large fibers 
conducting pressure and motor impulses.
6. What is the mechanism of action of local 
anesthetics?
y They block Na+ channels in nerve 
membranes from inside, preventing the 
generation and propagation of action 
potentials.
Local Anesthesia

Pharmacology

y Vasoconstrictors are added to prolong the 
duration of action and reduce systemic 
adverse effects and bleeding tendency

anesthetics?
y Plasma protein binding
y lipid solubility
y pKa of the drug
y addition of vasoconstrictors
y extracellular and intracellular pH.

General Anesthesia 
8. How do general anesthetics inhibit 
neuronal activity?
y They facilitate inhibitory effects of GABA at 
GABA receptors 
y Inhibit excitatory effects of glutamate at 
NMDA receptors.
9. What is MAC (Minimal Alveolar 
Concentration)?
y The minimal concentration of anesthetic gas 
that produces immobility in 50% of patients 
when exposed to a painful stimulus.
3. What are the two main types of inhalation 
anesthetics used for maintenance?
y Gas: Nitrous oxide (N2
O) 
y Volatile liquids (halogenated drugs such as 
Halothane, Flurane).

y Barbiturates (Thiopental Na+) 
y Non-barbiturates (Propofol, Ketamine, 
opioid analgesics, and BZDs).
5. What are general anesthetics used for?
y Inducing reversible loss of consciousness, 
analgesia, amnesia, and skeletal muscle 
relaxation.
6. What is the purpose of balanced anesthesia?
y To achieve all requirements for general 
anesthesia and minimize adverse effects of 
individual drugs.
7. 
List the components of balanced anesthesia.
y Preanesthetic medication 
y IV anesthetics plus succinylcholine 
y Inhalation anesthetics and NMBs (if needed) 
during operation

11. What is dissociative anesthesia?
y A hypnotic state with dissociation, 
amnesia, and analgesia, where patients are 
irresponsive to commands. It is induced by

12. What is conscious sedation?
y A state of amnesia, sedation, and analgesia 
without complete loss of consciousness. 
Patients can respond to commands. It is 
induced by Propofol alone or midazolam +

13. What is deep sedation?
y A state of unconsciousness that is

Chapter 6
Drug therapy of depression 
?
1. What is the mechanism of action of 
antidepressants?
Pharmacology
5. What are the drug interactions with 
tricyclic antidepressants?
y Increase brain biogenic amines 
(norepinephrine and serotonin) within 12 
hours, leading to downregulation of brain β 
and 5-HT2
 receptors (delayed for 2-4 weeks)
y increase brain-derived neurotrophic factor 
essential for survival and function of neurons
2. What is the mechanism of action of MAO 
inhibitors?
y Inhibit metabolism of biogenic amines 
inside cytoplasm of nerve endings, resulting 
in increased stores available for release by 
exocytosis
3. What is the mechanism of action of amine 
pump inhibitors?
y Inhibit reuptake of biogenic amines into 
neurons, resulting in their accumulation in 
the synaptic cleft and enhancing their effect 
at post-synaptic receptors
4. What are the different classes of amine 
pump inhibitor?
y Tricyclics (TCA)
y selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI)
y serotonin norepinephrine reuptake 
inhibitors (SNRI)
y dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake 
inhibitors (NDRI)
y Alcohol and anesthetics (sedation)
y hypotensive drugs (potentiate postural 
hypotensive effects of TCAs)
y sympathomimetics (TCAs inhibit uptake of 
biogenic amines)
y MAOIs (may induce acute serotonin syndrome)
y SSRIs (inhibits metabolism of TCA, leading 
to increased TCA toxicity)
6. What is the treatment for TCA toxicity?
y NaHCO3
y Diazepam
7. 
Is hemodialysis recommended for TCA 
toxicity treatment?
y No
8. What is the mechanism of action of TCAs?
y They block the reuptake of NE and 5-HT, as 
well as autonomic receptors (H1, M, a).
9. What are the adverse effects of MAOIs?
y Postural hypotension and atropine-like 
adverse effects 
y Insomnia, shift to mania, and weight gain 
y Serious food and drug interactions
10. What are the precautions with MAOIs?
y Warn patients about serious food (rich in 
tyramine) and drug interactions 
y Avoid using TCAs or SSRIs within 2 weeks of 
stopping MAOIs (washing out period) 
y Avoid MAOIs in the elderly due to their 
postural hypotension effect and atropine
like actions

8. What are the clinical manifestations of 
Tetanus?
y Glucose and maltose fermentation
y gelatin liquefaction
y H2S production.
2. How can the presence of toxin be detected 
in botulism?
y In patient blood or food remnants using 
PCR or ELISA.
3. What is the treatment for infections 
affecting muscle tone causing flaccid 
paralysis ?
y Trivalent antitoxin (types A, B, and E) 
y Respiratory support.
4. What is Tetanus?
y A bacterial infection caused by Clostridium 
tetani that produces a toxin causing painful 
muscle contractions.
5. What is the etiology of Tetanus? And what 
are its morphological features?
y Clostridium tetani
y Gram +ve bacilli, Anaerobic, spore forming 
& motile.
6. What are the virulence factors of 
Clostridium tetani?
y Exotoxin production ‘Tetanospasmin’, no invasion.
7. 
How does Tetanospasmin cause muscle 
contractions?
y Tetanospasmin binds to ganglioside 
receptor inhibiting release of inhibitory 
neurotransmitters such as GABA and glycine
y Causing continuous excitation of motor 
neurons.
y Lockjaw or trismus
y Exaggerated reflexes
y Respiratory failure leading to death.
9. How is Tetanus diagnosed?
y Strictly clinical
y Lab diagnosis is only for epidemiological 
purposes. Gram +ve spore forming bacilli 
‘Drum stick’ seen under microscopy.
10. What is the prevention for Tetanus?
y Tetanus toxoid vaccination:
DTap for children 
TdaP as a booster dose for adolescents.
11. What is the treatment for Tetanus?
y General measures to maintain airway and 
place patient in a dark quiet area
y Administration of antitoxin (Tetanus 
immunoglobulin)
y Antibiotics such as Metronidazole or 
Penicillin G.
12. What is Botulism?
y Food poisoning caused by ingestion 
of Botulinum toxin preformed in food 
contaminated with Clostridium botulinum.
13. What is the etiology of Botulism? And 
what are its morphological features?
y Clostridium botulinum
y Gram +ve bacilli, Anaerobic, spore forming 
& motile.

16. What causes prion diseases?
y The disease is caused by a misfolded form 
of a normal prion protein
y Thereby altering the function of the protein, 
and leading to death of neurons.
1 7. Where does prion diseases primarily affect?
y The disease is confined to the CNS where 
death of neurons causes vacuolation and 
spongiform changes in the brain.
18. What are the clinical presentations of prion

y Gradual onset, slowly progressive dementia,

y Severe disease resulting in coma and death.
19. How can prion diseases be diagnosed?
y Brain biopsy shows spongiform changes. 
y No serologic tests are available, and Prions 
cannot be grown in culture.
20. What is the prevention and treatment for

y Infected animals should be slaughtered,

y No available treatment or vaccine is present.

27. Explain convergence-projection theory. 
y The afferent pain fibers from skin and 
diseased viscera converge on the same cell 
of SGR and activate the same cortical neuron. 
Whatever the source of pain the cortex will 
project the pain to the skin because it is the 
most common source of pain.
28.   Explain the convergence-facilitation theory. 
y Afferent fibers of skin and viscera converge 
on SGR. 2nd order neuron of the skin 
pathway is facilitated by visceral afferents. 
So, pain is felt in the skin due to activation of 
its pathway from SGR to cortex.

27. Define spinal shock
y Complete loss of all reflexes below the level 
of the lesion.
28. Mention cause of spinal shock 
y Sudden withdrawal of the facilitatory 
corticospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal 
impulses. This result in decrease excitability of 
spinal motor neurons, and loss of their response 
to stimulation by afferents in reflex pathway.

y The development of denervation 
hypersensitivity by the remaining spinal 
neurons, and so they can now respond to 
afferent stimulation. 
y Another possibility is the increase of 
collaterals from existing neurons, with the 
formation of more excitatory endings on 
interneuron’s and motor neurons.

3. What are the subdivision of motor neurons

y Analeptic drugs

10. What is the character of theta (ε) brain wave?
y Primary (localized) evoked potentials: 
characterized by a positive wave followed 
by a negative wave. 
y Secondary (diffuse) evoked potentials: 
characterized by a large positive wave due to 
the activation of non-specific thalamic nuclei.

activity in a conscious person.

anaesthetized person

y Mapping of brain 
y Diagnosis of disease

cannot be aroused
5. What is sleep?
y Physiological and spontaneous 
unconsciousness from which a person can 
be aroused by stimuli
6. What are the functions of sleep?
y Restoration of physiological & biochemical 
processes (Cognition, metabolic, thermal, 
caloric & immune processes) 
y Helps learning & memory 
y Neural plasticity (maturation)
7. 
What are the stages and EEG 
characteristics of very light sleep?
y Theta waves
8. What are the stages and EEG 
characteristics of light sleep?
y Theta waves + sleep spindles (Large α: 12
14 Hz) & K complexes (Large & slow)
y Delta (3-3.5 Hz)
10. What are the stages and EEG 
characteristics of deep sleep?
y Low frequency Delta (0.5-1.5 Hz)
11. What are the characteristics of Non-Rapid 
Eye Movement (Non-REM) sleep?
y Slow wave sleep with absence of dreams 
and penile erection
12. What are the EEG characteristics of Rapid 
Eye Movement (REM) sleep?
y Rapid, irregular, low voltage, desynchronized 
β waves with presence of dreams and penile 
erection
13. What happens to sleep after the first cycle?
y Sleep lightens
y non-REM time decreases
y stages 3 and 4 decrease
y REM time increases
14. What are the three theories of sleep?
y Passive theory
y Metabolic theory
y Active theory
15. What is the passive theory of sleep?
y Fatigue and decreased activity of Reticular 
Activating System (RAS) lead to a decrease 
in positive feedback of cortical excitation
16. What is the metabolic theory of sleep?
y Prolonged wakefulness leads to the 
accumulation of Sleep Inducing Substances 
(SIS) in the cerebrospinal fluid or brain stem, 
resulting in inhibition of RAS

y The process where a noxious stimulus leads

stimulus occurs with it 
Physiology
36. What is the mechanism of sensitization?
y Presynaptic facilitation
y Release of serotonin by the neuron that 
transmits the noxious Stimulus, increases 
adenyl cyclase enzyme, which increases 
cAMP in the Presynaptic neuron of the 
habituated synapse, block of K+ Channels 
leads to depolarization and release of the 
Transmitter leads to prolonged augmented 
response.
37. What neurotransmitter is released in the 
process of sensitization?
y Serotonin
38. What is the value of sensitization?
y It’s the basis of Short-Term Memory (STM) 
and Long-Term Memory (LTM)
39. What is classical conditioning?
y Pairing of an unconditioned stimulus 
that naturally produces a response with a 
conditioned neutral stimulus that doesn’t 
produce a response.
40. What is operant conditioning?
y Teaching a person to perform tasks to 
obtain a reward or avoid punishment

3. Describe the microscopic structure of free 
nerve endings.
y The afferent nerve fibers arise from the 
subepidermal plexus of nerves then lose 
their myelin and neurolemmal sheath. The 
naked nerve fibers penetrate the epidermis, 
run between the epidermal cells and 
terminate by small swellings or knobs upon 
the surface of cells. In cornea, they reach to 
the superficial layers.
4. Describe the microscopic structure of 
peritrichial nerve endings.
y The afferent nerve fibers arise from the 
subepidermal plexus of nerves then lose their 
sheath and form a basket like arborization 
around the connective sheath of the hair 
follicle, just below its sebaceous gland.
5. Describe the microscopic structure of 
Merckle’s cell.
y L.M.: each cell has lobulated nucleus and 
cytoplasmic secretory granules close to the 
disc.
y E.M.: the Merkel’s cells have cytoplasmic 
projections that extend between the 
keratinocytes, to which they are joined by 
desmosomes.
y The widely distributed in the epidermis 
of the skin, cornea, mucous membrane of 
visceral organs, serous membrane, muscle, 
deep fascia. They are more numerous in the 
skin.
