AN91. [*] Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the chorda tympani relay in the:
A. Otic ganglion
B. Pterygopalatine ganglion
C. Submandibular ganglion
D. Ciliary ganglion
E. Geniculate ganglion
Answer: C — Chorda tympani → submandibular ganglion (to submandibular/sublingual glands).

AN92. [*] The lateral (temporomandibular) ligament of the TMJ chiefly prevents:
A. Posterior dislocation of the mandible
B. Anterior dislocation
C. Lateral deviation
D. Excessive depression of the mandible at rest
E. Protrusion
Answer: A — It resists posterior displacement of the condyle.

AN93. [*] Stimulation of the amygdaloid nucleus is chiefly associated with:
A. Fine motor coordination
B. Conscious proprioception and discriminative touch
C. Thermoregulation
D. Visual processing
E. Emotional responses such as fear and rage
Answer: E — The amygdala mediates emotional/affective responses.

AN94. [*] The periventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus is linked with the sensation of:
A. Pleasure and reward sensation
B. Aversion / punishment
C. Thirst
D. Hunger
E. Thermoregulation
Answer: B — Periventricular/medial zones → punishment-aversion responses.

AN95. [*] The fornix connects the hippocampus with the:
A. Amygdala
B. Caudate nucleus
C. Red nucleus
D. Pineal gland
E. Mammillary body
Answer: E — Hippocampus → fornix → mammillary body (Papez circuit).

AN96. [*] The forceps major (occipital forceps) is an example of a:
A. Association fiber
B. Projection fiber
C. Internal arcuate fiber
D. Commissural fiber
E. Climbing fiber
Answer: D — It is a commissural bundle of the splenium of the corpus callosum.

AN97. [*] The cingulum is an example of a fiber connecting different areas of the:
A. Two hemispheres (commissural fiber)
B. Same hemisphere (association fiber)
C. Cortex to spinal cord (projection fiber)
D. Cerebellum to cortex
E. Thalamus to cortex
Answer: B — The cingulum is an association tract.

AN98. [*] The Edinger–Westphal nucleus is best described as a:
A. General visceral efferent (parasympathetic) nucleus
B. General somatic efferent nucleus
C. Special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) cell column
D. General somatic afferent nucleus
E. Special somatic afferent nucleus
Answer: A — It is the GVE (parasympathetic) nucleus at the midbrain.

AN99. [*] The lateral aperture (foramen of Luschka) opens into the subarachnoid space at the:
A. Cisterna magna
B. Cerebellopontine angle
C. Interpeduncular cistern
D. Quadrigeminal cistern
E. Lumbar cistern
Answer: B — Luschka opens at the cerebellopontine angle.

AN100. [*] The nerve of the pterygoid canal is formed by union of the:
A. Greater petrosal and deep petrosal nerves
B. Lesser and greater petrosal nerves
C. Deep petrosal and chorda tympani
D. Greater petrosal nerve and the chorda tympani
E. Lesser petrosal and deep petrosal
Answer: A — Greater petrosal (parasympathetic) + deep petrosal (sympathetic).

AN101. [*] The paleospinothalamic (slow pain) tract terminates mainly in the:
A. Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
B. Lateral geniculate body
C. Medial geniculate body
D. Anterior nucleus
E. Intralaminar/reticular thalamic nuclei
Answer: E — It ends diffusely in intralaminar nuclei and reticular formation.

AN102. [*] The pons contains the nuclei of which cranial nerves?
A. III and IV
B. IX, X, XI and XII together
C. I and II
D. XI only
E. V, VI, VII and VIII
Answer: E — Trigeminal, abducent, facial and vestibulocochlear nuclei lie in the pons.

AN103. [*] The non-specific thalamic nuclei are the:
A. Intralaminar nuclei
B. Ventral posterolateral nucleus
C. Lateral geniculate body
D. Medial geniculate body
E. Anterior nucleus
Answer: A — Intralaminar (and midline) nuclei are non-specific.

AN104. [*] The "spinal lemniscus" is another name for the:
A. Medial lemniscus
B. Lateral lemniscus
C. Spinothalamic tract
D. Trigeminal lemniscus
E. Dorsal column
Answer: C — The spinal lemniscus = anterolateral (spinothalamic) system.

AN105. [*] In the adult the spinal cord usually ends at the level of:
A. L1–L2
B. T12 vertebra
C. L3
D. S2
E. L5
Answer: A — Conus medullaris ends at L1–L2 in adults (about L3 in newborns).

AN106. [*] A characteristic feature of the first cervical (C1) spinal nerve is that it:
A. Is purely sensory
B. Has the largest dorsal root ganglion
C. Supplies the diaphragm alone
D. Carries parasympathetic fibers
E. Often lacks a dorsal (sensory) root
Answer: E — C1 frequently has no dorsal root, so it is essentially motor.

AN107. [*] The genioglossus is supplied predominantly by:
A. Contralateral corticobulbar fibers only
B. Ipsilateral corticobulbar (corticonuclear) fibers
C. Bilateral equal innervation
D. The facial nucleus
E. The trigeminal motor nucleus
Answer: A — Hence tongue deviates to the weak side in a UMN lesion.

AN108. [*] The great cerebral vein (of Galen) lies within the:
A. Cisterna magna
B. Interpeduncular cistern between the cerebral peduncles
C. Lumbar cistern
D. Pontine cistern
E. Cisterna ambiens (quadrigeminal cistern)
Answer: E — It runs in the quadrigeminal/ambient cistern.

AN109. [*] White rami communicantes (preganglionic sympathetic) are found only at which vertebral levels (e.g., T5)?
A. C1–C8
B. All spinal levels
C. T1–L2
D. S2–S4
E. L3–S1
Answer: C — White rami are limited to thoracolumbar (T1–L2) segments.

AN110. [*] The two enlargements of the spinal cord (cervical and lumbosacral) correspond to innervation of the:
A. Trunk muscles
B. Diaphragm
C. Face
D. Limbs
E. Perineum
Answer: D — They reflect the large neuron pools for the limbs.

========================================
SECTION 2 — PHYSIOLOGY
========================================

PH1. [***] A patient with an upper motor neuron lesion develops spastic hypertonia. This is mainly due to:
A. Unopposed pontine reticulospinal drive
B. Loss of muscle spindle sensitivity
C. Degeneration of the alpha motor neurons
D. Acute cerebellar hemisphere damage
E. Peripheral nerve demyelination
Answer: A — Loss of cortical inhibition leaves the facilitatory pontine reticular system unopposed.

PH2. [***] Awareness of the position of the body and limbs in space is a function of cortical areas:
A. 3, 1 and 2 (postcentral gyrus)
B. 41 and 42
C. 17
D. 44 and 45
E. 5 and 7 (posterior parietal)
Answer: E — The posterior parietal association cortex (areas 5,7) handles spatial body sense.

PH3. [***] Crude touch with two-point tactile discrimination is detected mainly by:
A. Pacinian corpuscles
B. Free nerve endings
C. Merkel discs
D. Meissner corpuscles
E. Ruffini endings
Answer: D — Meissner corpuscles mediate fine discriminative touch.

PH4. [**] Fibers projecting from the cerebral cortex to the corpus striatum are:
A. GABAergic
B. Dopaminergic
C. Cholinergic (muscarinic) fibers
D. Serotonergic
E. Glutamatergic (excitatory)
Answer: E — Corticostriatal fibers use glutamate.

PH5. [**] By the gate-control theory, rubbing a painful area relieves pain by:
A. Releasing histamine locally
B. Blocking alpha motor neurons
C. Directly exciting C fibers
D. Increasing substance P release
E. Stimulating large Aβ fibers
Answer: E — Large-fiber input closes the spinal "gate" to pain.

PH6. [**] Gamma motor neurons synapse with:
A. Extrafusal muscle fibers
B. Golgi tendon organs
C. Pacinian corpuscles
D. Intrafusal muscle fibers
E. Renshaw cells
Answer: D — They set muscle-spindle sensitivity.

PH7. [**] Hypotonia is a characteristic result of a lesion of the:
A. Cerebellum
B. Internal capsule
C. Premotor cortex
D. Basal ganglia
E. Red nucleus
Answer: A — Cerebellar disease reduces muscle tone.

PH8. [**] Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection) syndrome produces:
A. Bilateral loss of all sensory modalities below the level of the lesion
B. Ipsilateral proprioceptive loss + contralateral pain/temp loss
C. Contralateral proprioceptive loss only
D. Ipsilateral pain and temperature loss only
E. Complete loss of movement with fully intact sensation
Answer: B — Dorsal columns are ipsilateral; spinothalamic is crossed.

PH9. [**] The resting tremor of Parkinson disease arises from abnormal oscillation between the:
A. Cerebellar nuclei and the contralateral red nucleus
B. Thalamus and the sensory cortex
C. Globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus
D. Motor cortex and anterior horn cells
E. Caudate and putamen
Answer: C — Basal-ganglia loop oscillation (GPi–STN) underlies the static tremor.

PH10. [**] The dissociated sensory loss of syringomyelia is:
A. Loss of fine touch with fully preserved pain sensation
B. Complete sensory loss
C. Loss of proprioception only
D. Loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch
E. Loss of motor power only
Answer: D — Central cavity interrupts crossing spinothalamic fibers.

PH11. [**] Which is a rapidly adapting touch receptor?
A. Merkel disc
B. Ruffini ending
C. Meissner corpuscle
D. Free nerve ending (nociceptor)
E. Muscle spindle
Answer: C — Meissner (and Pacinian) corpuscles are rapidly adapting.

PH12. [**] In spinal cord hemisection, dorsal-column sensation is lost:
A. Contralateral and below the lesion
B. Bilaterally at the lesion level
C. Ipsilateral and below the lesion
D. Contralateral at the lesion only
E. Ipsilateral above the lesion
Answer: C — The uncrossed dorsal column is lost on the same side.

PH13. [**] Basic factual knowledge ("knowing that") is stored as:
A. Episodic memory
B. Semantic memory
C. Procedural memory
D. Working memory
E. Sensory memory
Answer: B — Semantic memory holds general facts.

PH14. [**] Sleepwalking and sleep-talking typically occur during:
A. REM sleep
B. Stage 1 only
C. Quiet wakefulness with eyes closed
D. Non-REM (slow-wave) sleep
E. Paradoxical sleep
Answer: D — They are NREM parasomnias.

PH15. [**] The electroencephalogram (EEG) records the:
A. Spontaneous electrical activity of the cortex
B. Action potentials of individual single neurons
C. Skeletal muscle activity
D. Cerebral blood flow
E. Cardiac electrical activity
Answer: A — It reflects summed cortical postsynaptic potentials.

PH16. [*] Fast (first) pain is characterized by being:
A. Long-lasting and burning
B. Poorly localized, diffuse and aching
C. Carried only by C fibers
D. Sharp, short, and well localized
E. Mediated mainly by substance P
Answer: D — Fast pain travels in Aδ fibers.

PH17. [*] A painful stimulus to one foot causes extension of the opposite leg. This is the:
A. Stretch reflex
B. Golgi tendon reflex
C. Ipsilateral withdrawal reflex
D. Crossed extensor reflex
E. Babinski reflex
Answer: D — The crossed extensor reflex supports the body weight.

PH18. [*] The damping function that prevents overshoot of movement is a role of the:
A. Vestibulocerebellum
B. Basal ganglia
C. Primary motor cortex
D. Spinocerebellum
E. Thalamus
Answer: D — The spinocerebellum smooths ongoing movement.

PH19. [*] Resting muscle tone is maintained mainly through the:
A. Golgi tendon organ inhibitory reflex
B. Pacinian corpuscle
C. Free nerve endings
D. Renshaw cells
E. Muscle spindle stretch reflex
Answer: E — Spindle afferents drive the tonic stretch reflex.

PH20. [*] The nucleus raphe magnus contributes to analgesia by releasing:
A. Dopamine
B. Acetylcholine
C. Glutamate
D. Histamine
E. Serotonin
Answer: E — Serotonergic fibers descend to inhibit dorsal-horn pain transmission.

PH21. [*] Loss of motor learning follows damage to which cerebellar input?
A. Mossy fibers
B. Climbing fibers
C. Basket cells
D. Golgi cells
E. Parallel fibers
Answer: B — Climbing fibers (from the inferior olive) mediate motor learning.

PH22. [*] Thermal nociceptors for heat pain are activated above about:
A. 20 °C
B. 45 °C
C. 30 °C
D. 37 °C
E. 10 °C
Answer: B — Tissue-damaging heat (>45 °C) excites nociceptors.

PH23. [*] Consolidation of new long-term memory depends on the:
A. Cerebellum
B. Basal ganglia of the forebrain
C. Limbic system (hippocampus)
D. Occipital cortex
E. Medulla
Answer: C — Hippocampal circuits consolidate declarative memory.

PH24. [*] The categorical (dominant) hemisphere is specialized for:
A. Three-dimensional spatial perception
B. Musical and artistic appreciation
C. Recognition of faces
D. Language and sequential analysis
E. Emotional prosody of speech
Answer: D — The dominant hemisphere handles language and detail.

PH25. [*] Sudden, maintained dorsiflexion of the foot eliciting rhythmic oscillation is called:
A. Babinski sign
B. Ankle clonus
C. Fasciculation
D. Intention tremor
E. Chorea
Answer: B — Clonus reflects hyperactive stretch reflexes (UMN lesion).

PH26. [*] A substance that directly stimulates pain receptors is:
A. Insulin (a peptide hormone)
B. Albumin
C. Bradykinin (a kinin)
D. Glucose
E. Cortisol
Answer: C — Kinins are potent algesic chemicals.

PH27. [*] Flaccid dysarthria is characterized by:
A. Strained, strangled, effortful speech
B. Scanning, sing-song speech
C. Normal articulation
D. Weak, breathy, nasal speech
E. Explosive loud speech
Answer: D — LMN weakness gives a breathy, hypernasal voice.

PH28. [*] Stereognosis (object recognition by touch) depends on the:
A. Lateral spinothalamic tract
B. Anterior spinothalamic tract of the cord
C. Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway
D. Posterior spinocerebellar tract
E. Corticospinal tract
Answer: C — Fine discriminative touch/proprioception travels in the dorsal columns.

PH29. [*] A "gloves and stockings" pattern of sensory loss is typical of:
A. Spinal cord hemisection
B. Syringomyelia
C. Thalamic lesion
D. Cortical lesion
E. Peripheral neuritis
Answer: E — Length-dependent polyneuropathy affects the extremities first.

PH30. [*] Dopamine acting on D1 receptors:
A. Inhibits the direct striatal output pathway entirely
B. Excites the indirect pathway
C. Excites the direct pathway of the basal ganglia
D. Has no effect on movement
E. Destroys the substantia nigra
Answer: C — D1 stimulation facilitates the movement-promoting direct pathway.

PH31. [**] Ankle clonus is associated with an increase in:
A. Gamma motor neuron discharge
B. Golgi tendon organ activity
C. Renshaw cell inhibition
D. Alpha motor neuron inhibition
E. Descending serotonergic tone
Answer: A — Increased gamma drive heightens the stretch reflex.

PH32. [**] Crude, poorly localized sensation reaches conscious perception at the level of the:
A. Primary somatosensory cortex
B. Spinal cord
C. Thalamus
D. Cerebellum
E. Midbrain
Answer: C — The thalamus gives crude awareness; the cortex localizes it.

PH33. [**] The medial motor system (e.g., vestibulospinal, reticulospinal) mainly controls:
A. Fine independent movements of the fingers
B. Eye movements
C. Axial and proximal (postural) muscles
D. Facial expression
E. Tongue movement
Answer: C — Medial pathways control posture/axial muscles; lateral control distal limbs.

PH34. [**] Secondary hyperalgesia refers to increased pain sensitivity:
A. Only at the very center of the injury site
B. In a phantom limb
C. During general anesthesia
D. Confined to deep viscera
E. In the normal skin surrounding an injury
Answer: E — Central sensitization spreads to undamaged surrounding skin.

PH35. [**] The tenderness of sunburned skin (primary hyperalgesia) is due to:
A. Loss of pain receptors
B. Sensitization of nociceptors by released tissue products
C. Increased motor tone
D. Reduced blood flow
E. Demyelination of the peripheral sensory nerves in the area
Answer: B — Prostaglandins/kinins lower the nociceptor threshold.

PH36. [**] The cerebellum coordinates movement on the:
A. The opposite (contralateral) side only
B. Both sides equally
C. Lower limb only
D. Same (ipsilateral) side of the body
E. Trunk only
Answer: D — Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion.

PH37. [**] Spastic paralysis typically follows:
A. A cortical (upper motor neuron) infarction
B. A peripheral nerve injury
C. A muscle disease
D. Anterior horn cell loss
E. A transmission block at the neuromuscular junction
Answer: A — UMN lesions cause spastic (not flaccid) paralysis.

PH38. [**] GABA produces inhibition by increasing membrane permeability to:
A. Chloride
B. Sodium
C. Calcium
D. Potassium only
E. Magnesium
Answer: A — GABA-A opens chloride channels, hyperpolarizing the cell.

PH39. [**] Headache from extracranial muscles and vessels is best classified as:
A. Referred (deep) pain
B. Phantom pain
C. Neuropathic (nerve) pain
D. Central pain
E. Causalgia
Answer: A — It is poorly localized deep/referred pain.

PH40. [*] Stimulation-produced analgesia from the periaqueductal grey is mediated by:
A. Enkephalin (endogenous opioid)
B. Histamine
C. The excitatory amino acid glutamate
D. Substance P
E. Adrenaline
Answer: A — The PAG uses enkephalinergic links in the descending analgesic system.

PH41. [*] The stretch (myotatic) reflex is:
A. Polysynaptic
B. Purely autonomic
C. Monosynaptic
D. Dependent on the cortex
E. Mediated by C fibers
Answer: C — Ia afferent synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron.

PH42. [*] The analgesic effect of acupuncture is best explained by:
A. Direct destruction of the peripheral nerve
B. The gate-control / endorphin mechanism
C. Vasoconstriction
D. Muscle paralysis
E. Cortical ablation
Answer: B — It activates large fibers and endogenous opioids.

PH43. [*] Deep (visceral) pain is characteristically:
A. Sharp and precise
B. Fast-conducting
C. Poorly localized
D. Carried by Aβ fibers
E. Absent at rest
Answer: C — Visceral pain is diffuse and poorly localized.

PH44. [*] The sensory loss of syringomyelia classically has a:
A. Cape / jacket-like distribution
B. Glove-and-stocking pattern
C. Hemisection pattern
D. A dermatomal band confined to one limb
E. Saddle distribution
Answer: A — The expanding central cavity causes a shawl/cape pattern.

PH45. [*] The putamen circuit of the basal ganglia is concerned with:
A. Relaying conscious sensation to the cerebral cortex
B. Hearing
C. Thermoregulation
D. Vision
E. Execution of learned (skilled) movement patterns
Answer: E — It helps store and run over-learned motor programs.

PH46. [*] Pain from the gallbladder is commonly referred to the:
A. Tip of the right scapula / shoulder
B. Left arm
C. Umbilicus
D. The left iliac fossa and lower abdomen
E. Knee
Answer: A — Phrenic/segmental convergence refers it to the right shoulder region.

PH47. [*] An intention (kinetic) tremor that worsens toward a target indicates a lesion of the:
A. Basal ganglia
B. Posterior column
C. Peripheral nerve
D. Neuromuscular junction
E. Cerebellum
Answer: E — Cerebellar disease produces a terminal/intention tremor.

PH48. [*] Classic migraine begins with a phase of:
A. Diffuse cerebral vasodilation
B. Cerebral vasoconstriction
C. Hemorrhage
D. Raised CSF pressure
E. Muscle spasm
Answer: B — An initial vasoconstrictive (aura) phase precedes vasodilation.

PH49. [*] During REM sleep, growth hormone secretion is:
A. Sharply increased
B. Unchanged
C. Maximal
D. Completely abolished and permanent
E. Decreased (it peaks in deep NREM)
Answer: E — GH surges in slow-wave sleep, not REM.

PH50. [*] Delta waves on the EEG indicate:
A. Alert wakefulness
B. Deep (slow-wave) sleep
C. REM sleep
D. Mental arithmetic
E. Eyes-closed relaxation
Answer: B — High-amplitude delta waves mark stage 3–4 sleep.

PH51. [*] Explicit (declarative) memory is characterized by:
A. Automatic performance of motor skills
B. Reflex conditioning
C. Habituation
D. Sensitization
E. Conscious recall of facts and events
Answer: E — Declarative memory is consciously retrievable.

PH52. [*] Habituation is the process of learning to:
A. Strengthen a reflex
B. Form long-term memory
C. Ignore a repeated unimportant stimulus
D. Progressively increase pain sensitivity
E. Coordinate movement
Answer: C — The response wanes to a harmless repeated stimulus.

PH53. [*] The neurotransmitter of the brain's reward ("pleasure") pathway is:
A. GABA
B. Glycine
C. Dopamine
D. Acetylcholine
E. Histamine
Answer: C — Mesolimbic dopamine mediates reward.

PH54. [*] A lesion of cortical area 4 produces:
A. Loss of hearing
B. Contralateral paralysis with loss of fine movement
C. Loss of vision
D. A resting tremor
E. Contralateral sensory neglect of the opposite half of space
Answer: B — The primary motor cortex controls contralateral skilled movement.

PH55. [*] Loss of vibration sense in the right leg suggests injury to the:
A. Right cuneate fasciculus
B. Left gracile fasciculus
C. Right gracile fasciculus
D. Right spinothalamic tract
E. Left corticospinal tract
Answer: C — Lower-limb dorsal-column fibers run in the (ipsilateral) gracile tract.

PH56. [*] The flexor (withdrawal) reflex is initiated by stimulation of:
A. Free nerve endings (nociceptors)
B. Muscle spindles
C. Golgi tendon organs in the tendon
D. Pacinian corpuscles
E. Merkel discs
Answer: A — Nociceptive afferents drive the protective withdrawal reflex.

PH57. [*] In an upper motor neuron lesion the superficial abdominal reflexes are:
A. Exaggerated
B. Lost
C. Normal
D. Replaced by clonus
E. Unchanged
Answer: B — Superficial reflexes disappear with corticospinal damage.

PH58. [*] Excessive muscle tension activates the Golgi tendon organ, which:
A. Inhibits the alpha motor neuron (autogenic inhibition)
B. Directly excites the alpha motor neuron supplying the muscle
C. Excites gamma neurons
D. Has no effect
E. Stimulates the muscle spindle
Answer: A — Ib afferents inhibit the homonymous motor neuron.

PH59. [*] A to-and-fro oscillating movement of a limb reflects loss of:
A. Cerebellar damping of movement
B. Spinal reflexes
C. Muscle spindles
D. Pain sensation
E. Normal vestibular balance function
Answer: A — Without cerebellar damping, movements overshoot and oscillate.

PH60. [*] Planning of complex, bilateral, sequential hand movements is a function of the:
A. Primary motor cortex (area 4)
B. Postcentral gyrus
C. Occipital cortex
D. Supplementary motor area
E. Cerebellar vermis
Answer: D — The SMA programs complex bimanual sequences.

========================================
SECTION 3 — BIOCHEMISTRY
========================================

BC1. [**] The rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis is:
A. Tyrosine hydroxylase
B. Dopa decarboxylase
C. Dopamine β-hydroxylase
D. Phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase
E. Monoamine oxidase
Answer: A — Tyrosine hydroxylase is the committed, rate-limiting step.

BC2. [**] Dopamine is synthesized from the amino acid:
A. Tryptophan
B. Tyrosine
C. Histidine
D. Glutamate
E. Arginine
Answer: B — Tyrosine → DOPA → dopamine.

BC3. [**] Serotonin (5-HT) is synthesized from:
A. Tryptophan
B. Tyrosine
C. Glycine
D. Histidine
E. Phenylalanine
Answer: A — Tryptophan → 5-HTP → serotonin.

BC4. [*] GABA is formed from glutamate by the enzyme:
A. Glutamate decarboxylase
B. Monoamine oxidase
C. GABA transaminase
D. Glutamine synthetase enzyme
E. Glutaminase
Answer: A — Glutamate decarboxylase (a PLP/B6 enzyme) makes GABA.

BC5. [*] The principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS is:
A. GABA
B. Glycine
C. Dopamine
D. Glutamate
E. Acetylcholine
Answer: D — Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter.

BC6. [*] The chief inhibitory neurotransmitter of the spinal cord is:
A. Glycine
B. Glutamate
C. Dopamine
D. Substance P
E. Aspartate
Answer: A — Glycine mediates spinal inhibition (e.g., Renshaw cells).

BC7. [*] Acetylcholine is synthesized from choline and acetyl-CoA by:
A. Acetylcholinesterase
B. Pseudocholinesterase
C. Choline acetyltransferase
D. Choline kinase
E. Carnitine acetyltransferase
Answer: C — Choline acetyltransferase forms ACh.

BC8. [*] Acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft is rapidly hydrolyzed by:
A. Monoamine oxidase
B. Acetylcholinesterase
C. Catechol-O-methyltransferase
D. Choline acetyltransferase
E. Diamine oxidase
Answer: B — AChE terminates cholinergic transmission.

BC9. [**] Phenylketonuria is caused by deficiency of:
A. Tyrosinase
B. Homogentisate oxidase enzyme
C. Tyrosine hydroxylase
D. Phenylalanine hydroxylase
E. Dopa decarboxylase
Answer: D — Lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase raises phenylalanine, harming the brain.

BC10. [*] Tay–Sachs disease results from deficiency of:
A. Glucocerebrosidase
B. Sphingomyelinase
C. Arylsulfatase A
D. Hexosaminidase A
E. α-Galactosidase A
Answer: D — Hexosaminidase A deficiency → GM2 ganglioside accumulation.

BC11. [*] In the fed state the obligatory energy substrate of the brain is:
A. Free fatty acids
B. Glucose
C. Ketone bodies
D. Lactate
E. Amino acids
Answer: B — The brain normally depends on glucose.

BC12. [*] During prolonged starvation the brain increasingly uses:
A. Glucose exclusively
B. Fatty acids
C. Ketone bodies
D. Glycogen
E. Protein
Answer: C — Ketone bodies spare glucose during fasting.

BC13. [*] Glucose crosses the blood–brain barrier mainly via:
A. GLUT1 carrier
B. Simple diffusion
C. SGLT1 active transport
D. Endocytosis
E. GLUT4 (insulin-dependent)
Answer: A — GLUT1 mediates insulin-independent transport into the brain.

BC14. [*] Norepinephrine is formed from dopamine by:
A. Tyrosine hydroxylase enzyme
B. Dopa decarboxylase
C. Dopamine β-hydroxylase
D. COMT
E. Monoamine oxidase
Answer: C — Dopamine β-hydroxylase hydroxylates the side chain.

BC15. [*] Conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine (by PNMT) requires a methyl group donated by:
A. Folate
B. S-adenosylmethionine
C. Biotin
D. Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
E. Pyridoxal phosphate
Answer: B — SAM is the methyl donor for PNMT.

BC16. [*] Catecholamines are inactivated by which two enzymes?
A. AChE and BChE
B. GAD and GABA-T
C. ALT and AST
D. MAO and COMT
E. Lipase and esterase
Answer: D — Monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase.

BC17. [*] The principal urinary metabolite of catecholamines is:
A. 5-HIAA
B. Homovanillic acid (HVA) in urine
C. Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
D. Uric acid
E. Creatinine
Answer: C — VMA is measured to assess catecholamine turnover.

BC18. [*] The major metabolite of dopamine is:
A. Homovanillic acid (HVA)
B. VMA
C. 5-HIAA
D. Normetanephrine in plasma
E. Uric acid
Answer: A — HVA reflects dopamine breakdown.

BC19. [*] The major metabolite of serotonin is:
A. 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
B. VMA
C. Homovanillic acid, a dopamine metabolite
D. Metanephrine
E. Uric acid
Answer: A — 5-HIAA is the urinary marker of serotonin.

BC20. [*] The cofactor required by tyrosine and phenylalanine hydroxylases is:
A. Thiamine pyrophosphate (B1)
B. Pyridoxal phosphate
C. Biotin
D. FAD
E. Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
Answer: E — BH4 is the essential cofactor for aromatic hydroxylases.

BC21. [*] Histamine is synthesized by decarboxylation of:
A. Tyrosine
B. Tryptophan
C. Glutamate
D. Arginine
E. Histidine
Answer: E — Histidine decarboxylase forms histamine.

BC22. [*] Nitric oxide, a gaseous neurotransmitter, is synthesized from:
A. Citrulline
B. Arginine
C. Ornithine
D. Glutamine
E. Aspartate
Answer: B — Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine to NO + citrulline.

BC23. [*] The resting membrane potential of neurons is maintained mainly by the:
A. Calcium pump
B. Chloride channel
C. Na+/K+ ATPase
D. Proton pump
E. GLUT1 carrier
Answer: C — The sodium–potassium pump sets the ionic gradients.

BC24. [*] Release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic terminal is triggered by influx of:
A. Calcium
B. Sodium
C. Potassium
D. Chloride
E. Magnesium
Answer: A — Ca2+ entry triggers vesicle fusion.

BC25. [*] Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity injures neurons mainly through:
A. Excess Ca2+ entry via NMDA receptors
B. Potassium efflux
C. Chloride influx
D. Reduced mitochondrial ATP synthesis only
E. Sodium pump activation
Answer: A — NMDA-receptor Ca2+ overload kills neurons.

BC26. [*] Ammonia is detoxified in the brain mainly by forming:
A. Urea
B. Uric acid
C. Glutamine
D. Creatinine
E. Alanine
Answer: C — Glutamine synthetase (in astrocytes) traps ammonia as glutamine.

BC27. [*] Myelin is especially rich in:
A. Nucleic acids
B. Glycogen
C. Cerebrosides (galactolipids)
D. Water
E. Water-soluble cytoplasmic protein
Answer: C — Myelin has a very high lipid content, notably cerebrosides.

BC28. [*] Niemann–Pick disease is due to deficiency of:
A. Hexosaminidase A
B. Glucocerebrosidase
C. Arylsulfatase A
D. Sphingomyelinase
E. α-Galactosidase A
Answer: D — Sphingomyelinase deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulation.

BC29. [*] Gaucher disease results from deficiency of:
A. Sphingomyelinase
B. Hexosaminidase A
C. Arylsulfatase A
D. Glucocerebrosidase
E. Galactocerebrosidase
Answer: D — Glucocerebrosidase deficiency → glucocerebroside accumulation.

BC30. [*] Metachromatic leukodystrophy is caused by deficiency of:
A. Arylsulfatase A
B. Hexosaminidase A
C. Glucocerebrosidase
D. Sphingomyelinase
E. α-Galactosidase A
Answer: A — Arylsulfatase A deficiency → sulfatide accumulation/demyelination.

BC31. [*] Krabbe disease is due to deficiency of:
A. Sphingomyelinase
B. Hexosaminidase A
C. Glucocerebrosidase (acid β-glucosidase) enzyme
D. Galactocerebrosidase (galactosylceramidase)
E. Arylsulfatase A
Answer: D — Galactocerebrosidase deficiency damages myelin.

BC32. [*] Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of:
A. Phenylalanine hydroxylase
B. Homogentisate oxidase
C. Branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase
D. Cystathionine synthase
E. The enzyme fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase
Answer: C — Block in branched-chain amino acid catabolism.

BC33. [*] Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in the CNS classically causes:
A. Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome
B. Pellagra
C. Subacute combined degeneration
D. Beriberi rash
E. Scurvy
Answer: A — Wernicke encephalopathy/Korsakoff psychosis.

BC34. [*] Vitamin B12 deficiency damages the cord by producing:
A. Subacute combined degeneration
B. Pellagra
C. Wernicke–Korsakoff encephalopathy
D. Tabes dorsalis
E. Syringomyelia
Answer: A — Demyelination of dorsal and lateral columns.

BC35. [*] Dementia of pellagra results from deficiency of:
A. Thiamine
B. Niacin
C. Folate
D. Vitamin B12
E. Vitamin C
Answer: B — Niacin (B3) deficiency causes the 3 D's (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).

BC36. [*] Glutamate decarboxylase requires which cofactor?
A. Thiamine pyrophosphate (B1)
B. Biotin
C. FAD
D. Pyridoxal phosphate (B6)
E. Tetrahydrofolate
Answer: D — PLP is essential; B6 deficiency lowers GABA and causes seizures.

BC37. [*] The universal methyl-group donor in neurotransmitter metabolism is:
A. ATP
B. NADPH
C. S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)
D. Acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA)
E. Biotin
Answer: C — SAM donates methyl groups (e.g., for COMT, PNMT).

BC38. [*] A common intracellular second messenger for neurotransmitter receptors is:
A. Glucose
B. Cyclic AMP
C. Glutathione
D. Pyruvate
E. Lactate
Answer: B — cAMP relays signals from many G-protein-coupled receptors.

BC39. [*] In the glutamate–glutamine cycle, glutamine is supplied to neurons by:
A. Astrocytes
B. Microglia
C. Oligodendrocytes
D. Endothelium
E. Ependyma
Answer: A — Astrocytes recycle glutamate to glutamine for neurons.

BC40. [*] A rapidly mobilizable high-energy phosphate store in neurons is:
A. Glycogen
B. Stored triglyceride fat
C. ATP synthase
D. Creatine phosphate
E. Pyruvate
Answer: D — Creatine phosphate buffers ATP levels.

BC41. [*] Glycine is synthesized mainly from:
A. Tyrosine
B. Histidine
C. Serine
D. Tryptophan
E. Arginine
Answer: C — Serine hydroxymethyltransferase converts serine to glycine.

BC42. [*] Adrenoleukodystrophy is characterized by accumulation of:
A. Phytanic acid
B. Sphingomyelin
C. GM2 ganglioside within neurons
D. Very long chain fatty acids
E. Sulfatides
Answer: D — A peroxisomal defect raises VLCFA, demyelinating the CNS.

BC43. [*] Refsum disease is caused by accumulation of:
A. Phytanic acid
B. VLCFA
C. GM2 ganglioside
D. Glucocerebroside
E. Homogentisic acid
Answer: A — Defective α-oxidation accumulates phytanic acid.

BC44. [*] Gangliosides are most concentrated in the:
A. White matter
B. Grey matter (neuronal membranes)
C. Myelin sheath
D. Membranes of peripheral nerve axons
E. Choroid plexus
Answer: B — Gangliosides are enriched in neuronal (grey-matter) membranes.

BC45. [*] The GABA-A receptor is a:
A. Ligand-gated chloride channel
B. G-protein-coupled receptor
C. Tyrosine kinase receptor
D. Voltage-gated sodium ion channel
E. Cytoplasmic receptor
Answer: A — It is an ionotropic Cl− channel.

BC46. [*] Fabry disease is due to deficiency of:
A. Hexosaminidase A
B. Sphingomyelinase
C. Arylsulfatase A
D. α-Galactosidase A
E. Glucocerebrosidase
Answer: D — α-Galactosidase A deficiency accumulates ceramide trihexoside.

BC47. [*] Dopamine acting at D1 receptors raises intracellular:
A. Intracellular calcium via the IP3 pathway
B. Chloride
C. Cyclic AMP (Gs/adenylyl cyclase)
D. cGMP
E. Potassium efflux
Answer: C — D1 receptors couple to Gs and increase cAMP.

BC48. [*] Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency can cause convulsions because it impairs synthesis of:
A. Glutamate
B. Acetylcholine
C. GABA
D. Glycine
E. Dopamine only
Answer: C — PLP is required by GAD to make the inhibitory transmitter GABA.

BC49. [*] A large fraction of the brain's ATP is consumed by the:
A. Calcium pump
B. Protein synthesis machinery
C. Glycogen synthase
D. Urea cycle
E. Sodium–potassium pump
Answer: E — Maintaining ionic gradients (Na+/K+ ATPase) is the major energy cost.

BC50. [*] The major inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain is:
A. GABA
B. Glutamate
C. Aspartate
D. Acetylcholine
E. Substance P
Answer: A — GABA is the principal inhibitory transmitter in the brain.

========================================
SECTION 4 — HISTOLOGY
========================================

HI1. [**] In the central nervous system, myelin is formed by:
A. Schwann cells
B. Oligodendrocytes
C. Microglia
D. Astrocytes
E. Ependymal lining cells
Answer: B — One oligodendrocyte myelinates several CNS axons.

HI2. [**] In peripheral nerves, myelin is formed by:
A. Oligodendrocytes
B. Astrocytes
C. Microglia
D. Satellite cells
E. Schwann cells
Answer: E — Each Schwann cell forms one internode.

HI3. [**] Nissl bodies of the neuron correspond ultrastructurally to:
A. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
B. Mitochondria
C. Golgi apparatus
D. Lysosomes
E. Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Answer: E — Nissl substance is stacked rough ER and ribosomes.

HI4. [**] The phagocytic (immune) cells of the CNS are the:
A. Astrocytes
B. Microglia
C. Oligodendrocytes
D. Ependymal cells
E. Schwann cells
Answer: B — Microglia are the resident macrophages of the brain.

HI5. [*] The blood–brain barrier is reinforced by the foot processes of:
A. Astrocytes
B. Microglia
C. Oligodendrocytes
D. Ependymal cells
E. Schwann cells
Answer: A — Astrocytic end-feet surround capillaries.

HI6. [*] Flask-shaped Purkinje cells are found in the:
A. The cerebral cortex
B. Spinal cord
C. Cerebellar cortex
D. Retina
E. Hippocampus
Answer: C — They lie in a single layer of the cerebellar cortex.

HI7. [*] Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted by the:
A. Arachnoid villi
B. Choroid plexus
C. Pia mater
D. Dura mater
E. Subarachnoid space
Answer: B — The choroid plexus is modified ependyma over capillaries.

HI8. [*] The ventricles and central canal are lined by:
A. Astrocytes
B. Oligodendrocytes
C. Microglia
D. Endothelium
E. Ependymal cells
Answer: E — Ependymal epithelium lines the ventricular system.

HI9. [*] The neurons of the dorsal root ganglion are:
A. Multipolar neurons
B. Pseudounipolar
C. Bipolar
D. Anaxonic
E. Pyramidal
Answer: B — Sensory ganglion cells are pseudounipolar.

HI10. [*] The giant pyramidal (Betz) cells are located in which layer of the motor cortex?
A. Layer I
B. Layer II
C. Layer III
D. Layer VI
E. Layer V
Answer: E — Betz cells occupy the internal pyramidal layer (V).

HI11. [*] The cerebellar cortex consists of how many layers?
A. Two
B. Three
C. Four layers
D. Five
E. Six
Answer: B — Molecular, Purkinje and granular layers.

HI12. [*] The neocortex (cerebral cortex) typically has:
A. Three layers
B. Six layers
C. Four layers
D. Five layers
E. Seven layers
Answer: B — Six histological layers.

HI13. [*] The immunohistochemical marker of astrocytes is:
A. GFAP
B. Neurofilament
C. Myelin basic protein
D. CD68
E. Synaptophysin
Answer: A — Glial fibrillary acidic protein marks astrocytes.

HI14. [*] Unlike other neuroglia, microglia are derived from:
A. Neuroectoderm of neural tube
B. Endoderm
C. Neural crest
D. Mesoderm (monocyte lineage)
E. Notochord
Answer: D — Microglia arise from blood monocytes/mesoderm.

HI15. [*] The most numerous neuroglial cells in the CNS are the:
A. Astrocytes
B. Microglia
C. Ependymal cells
D. Oligodendrocytes
E. Schwann cells
Answer: A — Astrocytes are the most abundant glia.

HI16. [*] The small cells that surround neuronal cell bodies in a ganglion are:
A. Microglia
B. Astrocytes
C. Ependymal cells
D. Oligodendrocytes
E. Satellite cells
Answer: E — Satellite (capsule) cells support ganglion neurons.

HI17. [*] Which region of the neuron lacks Nissl substance?
A. Soma
B. The dendritic processes
C. Nucleus
D. Axon hillock and axon
E. Perikaryon
Answer: D — The axon hillock and axon are Nissl-free.

HI18. [*] Dispersal of Nissl substance after axonal injury is called:
A. Apoptotic cell death
B. Necrosis
C. Gliosis
D. Chromatolysis
E. Atrophy
Answer: D — Central chromatolysis follows axotomy.

HI19. [*] After a nerve is cut, degeneration of the axon distal to the injury is termed:
A. Retrograde degeneration
B. Wallerian degeneration
C. Chromatolysis
D. Demyelination
E. Apoptosis
Answer: B — Wallerian (anterograde) degeneration occurs distally.

HI20. [*] Saltatory conduction depends on the gaps in myelin called:
A. Internodes
B. Nodes of Ranvier
C. Schmidt–Lanterman clefts
D. Synaptic clefts
E. Axon hillocks
Answer: B — Impulses jump between nodes of Ranvier.

HI21. [*] The dark pigment within neurons of the substantia nigra is:
A. Lipofuscin
B. Hemosiderin
C. Neuromelanin
D. Bilirubin
E. Melanin of skin type
Answer: C — Dopaminergic nigral neurons contain neuromelanin.

HI22. [*] A single oligodendrocyte differs from a Schwann cell in that it:
A. Myelinates several axons
B. Myelinates only one internode
C. Cannot form myelin
D. Lies in the PNS
E. Phagocytoses debris
Answer: A — One oligodendrocyte myelinates many CNS axons.

HI23. [*] The smallest and most numerous neurons of the cerebellar cortex are the:
A. Granule cells
B. Purkinje cells
C. Basket cells
D. Golgi cells
E. Stellate cells
Answer: A — Granule cells pack the granular layer.

HI24. [*] The delicate innermost meningeal layer that closely invests the brain is the:
A. Pia mater
B. Dura mater
C. Arachnoid mater
D. Periosteum
E. Epineurium
Answer: A — The pia adheres to the brain surface.

HI25. [*] The connective-tissue sheath surrounding a bundle (fascicle) of nerve fibers is the:
A. Endoneurium
B. Epineurium
C. Periosteum
D. Perimysium
E. Perineurium
Answer: E — Perineurium ensheathes each fascicle.

HI26. [*] The fine connective tissue surrounding an individual nerve fiber is the:
A. Endoneurium
B. Perineurium
C. Epineurium
D. Mesoneurium
E. Periosteum
Answer: A — Endoneurium surrounds single axons.

HI27. [*] The outer sheath enclosing the whole peripheral nerve is the:
A. Endoneurium
B. Perineurium
C. Pia mater
D. Perimysium
E. Epineurium
Answer: E — Epineurium binds the fascicles together.

HI28. [*] The lamellated (onion-like) receptor for deep pressure/vibration is the:
A. Meissner corpuscle
B. Pacinian corpuscle
C. Merkel disc
D. Ruffini ending
E. Free nerve ending
Answer: B — The Pacinian corpuscle has concentric lamellae.

HI29. [*] Meissner corpuscles for fine touch are located in the:
A. Subcutaneous fat
B. Dermal papillae
C. Deep dermis
D. Periosteum
E. Epidermal basal layer
Answer: B — They lie in the dermal papillae of glabrous skin.

HI30. [*] The synapse between a motor nerve and skeletal muscle is the:
A. Motor end plate (neuromuscular junction)
B. Nodes of Ranvier
C. Synaptic glomerulus of the olfactory bulb
D. Chemical ganglion
E. Electrical synapse
Answer: A — The NMJ/motor end plate transmits to muscle.

HI31. [*] The yellow-brown "wear-and-tear" pigment that accumulates in aging neurons is:
A. Neuromelanin
B. Hemosiderin
C. Lipofuscin
D. Bilirubin
E. Melanin
Answer: C — Lipofuscin is a residual-body (age) pigment.

HI32. [*] The specialized glia whose fibers guide neurons in the cerebellum are:
A. Microglia
B. Tanycytes
C. Schwann cells
D. Bergmann glia
E. Satellite cells
Answer: D — Bergmann glia lie in the Purkinje cell layer.

HI33. [*] Fibrous astrocytes predominate in:
A. White matter
B. Grey matter
C. Ganglia
D. Choroid plexus
E. Peripheral nerve
Answer: A — Protoplasmic astrocytes are in grey matter, fibrous in white.

HI34. [*] Specialized ependymal cells lining the third ventricle floor are:
A. Satellite cells
B. Bergmann glia
C. Microglia
D. Oligodendrocytes
E. Tanycytes
Answer: E — Tanycytes contact CSF and capillaries.

HI35. [*] The most common morphological type of neuron is the:
A. Multipolar
B. Bipolar
C. Pseudounipolar
D. Anaxonic
E. Unipolar
Answer: A — Most CNS neurons (e.g., motor neurons) are multipolar.

HI36. [*] Neurotransmitter molecules are stored in the presynaptic terminal within:
A. Terminal mitochondria
B. Nissl bodies
C. Lysosomes
D. Microtubules
E. Synaptic vesicles
Answer: E — Synaptic vesicles release transmitter by exocytosis.

HI37. [*] The optic nerve is myelinated by oligodendrocytes because it is:
A. A peripheral nerve outside the CNS
B. Purely autonomic
C. Devoid of myelin
D. Part of the central nervous system
E. A cranial ganglion
Answer: D — The optic nerve is a CNS tract, not a true peripheral nerve.

HI38. [*] Following CNS injury, the glial scar is formed mainly by:
A. Microglia
B. Oligodendrocytes
C. Astrocytes
D. Ependymal cells
E. Schwann cells
Answer: C — Reactive astrocytes (astrogliosis) form the scar.

========================================
SECTION 5 — PHARMACOLOGY
========================================

PM1. [**] Levodopa rather than dopamine is used in Parkinson disease because levodopa:
A. Is more potent
B. Has no side effects
C. Acts directly on serotonin receptors
D. Crosses the blood–brain barrier
E. Is an enzyme inhibitor
Answer: D — Dopamine cannot cross the BBB, but its precursor L-DOPA can.

PM2. [**] Carbidopa is combined with levodopa because it:
A. Crosses into the brain
B. Blocks central dopamine receptors directly
C. Is itself converted to dopamine
D. Stimulates the vomiting center
E. Inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase
Answer: E — It reduces peripheral conversion, increasing brain delivery.

PM3. [*] Selegiline aids Parkinson disease by inhibiting:
A. COMT
B. DOPA decarboxylase
C. Tyrosine hydroxylase
D. Monoamine oxidase B
E. Acetylcholinesterase
Answer: D — MAO-B inhibition slows dopamine breakdown.

PM4. [*] Entacapone prolongs levodopa action by inhibiting:
A. MAO-B
B. DOPA decarboxylase
C. Catechol-O-methyltransferase
D. Acetylcholinesterase
E. Dopamine β-hydroxylase enzyme
Answer: C — COMT inhibition reduces levodopa metabolism.

PM5. [*] The Parkinsonian tremor responds to anticholinergic drugs such as:
A. Benztropine
B. Neostigmine
C. Pilocarpine
D. Bethanechol
E. Physostigmine
Answer: A — Central antimuscarinics relieve tremor and rigidity.

PM6. [*] Bromocriptine acts in Parkinson disease as a:
A. Dopamine antagonist
B. MAO inhibitor
C. Cholinergic agonist
D. A voltage-gated sodium-channel blocker
E. Dopamine (D2) receptor agonist
Answer: E — It directly stimulates dopamine receptors.

PM7. [**] Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A function by increasing the:
A. Duration of each chloride channel opening
B. Sodium influx
C. Calcium release
D. Potassium efflux
E. Frequency of chloride channel opening
Answer: E — They raise the frequency of Cl− channel opening.

PM8. [*] Barbiturates potentiate GABA-A by increasing the:
A. Frequency of chloride channel opening
B. Sodium conductance
C. Calcium influx
D. Duration of chloride channel opening
E. Receptor number
Answer: D — They prolong each channel opening.

PM9. [**] Phenytoin controls seizures mainly by blocking:
A. Voltage-gated calcium channels
B. Potassium channels
C. GABA receptors
D. Voltage-gated sodium channels
E. NMDA receptors
Answer: D — It stabilizes inactivated Na+ channels.

PM10. [*] The drug of first choice for trigeminal neuralgia is:
A. Morphine sulfate
B. Carbamazepine
C. Aspirin
D. Diazepam
E. Levodopa
Answer: B — Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia.

PM11. [*] Ethosuximide controls absence seizures by blocking:
A. Sodium channels
B. GABA transaminase enzyme
C. T-type calcium channels
D. NMDA receptors
E. Potassium channels
Answer: C — It blocks thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels.

PM12. [*] A broad-spectrum antiepileptic effective in many seizure types is:
A. Oral ethosuximide
B. Vigabatrin
C. Bromocriptine
D. Atropine
E. Sodium valproate
Answer: E — Valproate works in generalized and partial seizures.

PM13. [*] The first-line drug for terminating status epilepticus is an intravenous:
A. Continuous intravenous barbiturate infusion
B. Benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam)
C. Phenytoin load only
D. Opioid
E. Antipsychotic
Answer: B — IV benzodiazepines abort status epilepticus.

PM14. [*] Local anesthetics such as lidocaine act by blocking:
A. Sodium channels
B. Potassium channels
C. Calcium channels
D. GABA receptors
E. Acetylcholinesterase
Answer: A — They block voltage-gated Na+ channels in axons.

PM15. [**] The analgesic action of morphine is mediated mainly by:
A. GABA-A receptors
B. NMDA receptors
C. Beta-adrenergic receptors
D. Nicotinic receptors
E. Mu opioid receptors
Answer: E — μ-receptor agonism produces analgesia.

PM16. [*] The specific antidote for opioid overdose is:
A. Flumazenil
B. Atropine
C. Naloxone
D. Physostigmine
E. Protamine
Answer: C — Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist.

PM17. [*] Fluoxetine relieves depression by:
A. Blocking dopamine D2 receptors
B. Inhibiting monoamine oxidase
C. Blocking sodium channels
D. Inhibiting serotonin reuptake
E. Releasing acetylcholine
Answer: D — SSRIs block presynaptic serotonin reuptake.

PM18. [*] Tricyclic antidepressants act mainly by:
A. Inhibiting MAO
B. Selectively blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the brain
C. Opening chloride channels
D. Inhibiting noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake
E. Blocking calcium channels
Answer: D — They inhibit reuptake of NE and 5-HT.

PM19. [*] The drug of choice for long-term control of bipolar disorder is:
A. Lithium
B. Levodopa
C. Phenytoin
D. Atropine
E. Morphine
Answer: A — Lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder.

PM20. [**] Typical antipsychotics produce extrapyramidal side effects because they block:
A. Dopamine D2 receptors
B. Muscarinic cholinergic receptors
C. Serotonin receptors
D. GABA receptors
E. Histamine receptors
Answer: A — Nigrostriatal D2 blockade causes Parkinsonism/dystonia.

PM21. [*] Long-term haloperidol use may cause involuntary orofacial movements known as:
A. A pill-rolling resting tremor
B. Chorea minor
C. Myoclonus
D. Hemiballismus
E. Tardive dyskinesia
Answer: E — Tardive dyskinesia follows chronic D2 blockade.

PM22. [*] The atypical antipsychotic that requires white-cell monitoring (agranulocytosis) is:
A. Haloperidol
B. Chlorpromazine
C. Fluphenazine
D. Sulpiride
E. Clozapine
Answer: E — Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis.

PM23. [*] Symptomatic treatment of Alzheimer disease uses inhibitors of:
A. Monoamine oxidase type B at the synapse
B. COMT
C. Acetylcholinesterase (e.g., donepezil)
D. Sodium channels
E. Dopamine reuptake
Answer: C — Cholinesterase inhibitors raise synaptic ACh.

PM24. [*] Memantine, used in Alzheimer disease, is a:
A. NMDA receptor antagonist
B. Cholinesterase inhibitor
C. Dopamine agonist
D. GABA agonist
E. Sodium-channel blocker
Answer: A — It blocks excitotoxic NMDA-receptor activity.

PM25. [*] Sumatriptan aborts migraine by acting as a:
A. Dopamine antagonist
B. Beta-receptor agonist
C. Calcium-channel blocker
D. Histamine agonist
E. 5-HT1 receptor agonist
Answer: E — 5-HT1B/1D agonism causes cranial vasoconstriction.

PM26. [*] Essential (familial) tremor is best treated with:
A. Oral levodopa
B. Atropine
C. Morphine
D. Propranolol
E. Phenytoin
Answer: D — The beta-blocker propranolol reduces essential tremor.

PM27. [*] Baclofen relieves spasticity by acting as an agonist at:
A. GABA-A receptors
B. NMDA receptors
C. Nicotinic receptors
D. GABA-B receptors
E. Opioid receptors
Answer: D — GABA-B agonism reduces spinal excitatory transmission.

PM28. [*] Botulinum toxin produces flaccid paralysis by:
A. Competitively blocking postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
B. Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase
C. Blocking acetylcholine release at the nerve terminal
D. Depleting dopamine
E. Blocking sodium channels
Answer: C — It prevents ACh exocytosis at the neuromuscular junction.

PM29. [*] Atropine differs from glycopyrrolate in that it:
A. Acts instead as a direct muscarinic receptor agonist
B. Crosses the blood–brain barrier (central effects)
C. Blocks nicotinic receptors
D. Stimulates sweating
E. Causes bradycardia
Answer: B — As a tertiary amine it has central antimuscarinic effects.

PM30. [*] Strychnine causes convulsions by antagonizing:
A. GABA receptors
B. Dopamine receptors
C. Nicotinic receptors
D. NMDA receptors
E. Glycine receptors
Answer: E — Loss of glycine inhibition produces tonic spasms.

PM31. [*] Tetanus toxin produces spastic paralysis by blocking release of:
A. Acetylcholine only
B. Glycine and GABA
C. Dopamine
D. Noradrenaline
E. Histamine
Answer: B — It prevents inhibitory transmitter release from Renshaw cells.

PM32. [*] Neostigmine improves myasthenia gravis by:
A. Irreversibly blocking acetylcholine receptors
B. Releasing dopamine
C. Blocking sodium channels
D. Reversibly inhibiting acetylcholinesterase
E. Stimulating GABA receptors
Answer: D — It raises ACh at the neuromuscular junction.

PM33. [*] Amphetamine produces central stimulation chiefly by:
A. Releasing catecholamines from terminals
B. Blocking presynaptic dopamine receptors
C. Inhibiting MAO only
D. Activating GABA receptors
E. Blocking sodium channels
Answer: A — It promotes release of dopamine and noradrenaline.

PM34. [*] Cocaine produces its central effects mainly by:
A. Releasing acetylcholine
B. Directly activating opioid receptors
C. Inhibiting COMT
D. Opening chloride channels
E. Blocking catecholamine reuptake
Answer: E — It blocks reuptake of dopamine/noradrenaline.

PM35. [*] The CNS-stimulant action of caffeine is due to antagonism of:
A. Dopamine receptors
B. GABA receptors
C. Histamine receptors
D. Opioid receptors
E. Adenosine receptors
Answer: E — Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors.

PM36. [*] The only drug shown to prolong survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is:
A. Riluzole
B. Levodopa
C. Donepezil
D. Baclofen
E. Phenytoin
Answer: A — Riluzole reduces glutamate excitotoxicity.

PM37. [*] Chorea of Huntington disease can be reduced by tetrabenazine, which:
A. Blocks postsynaptic dopamine receptors directly
B. Stimulates dopamine release
C. Inhibits acetylcholinesterase
D. Depletes dopamine by inhibiting VMAT2
E. Blocks GABA receptors
Answer: D — VMAT2 inhibition depletes presynaptic dopamine.

PM38. [*] Gabapentin and pregabalin relieve neuropathic pain by acting on:
A. The α2δ subunit of calcium channels
B. Sodium channels
C. Presynaptic mu opioid receptors centrally
D. NMDA receptors
E. GABA-A receptors
Answer: A — They reduce excitatory transmitter release.

PM39. [*] Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia by acting on the:
A. The presynaptic neuromuscular junction terminal
B. Sodium channel
C. GABA receptor
D. Motor cortex
E. Ryanodine receptor (sarcoplasmic Ca2+ release)
Answer: E — It blocks Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

PM40. [*] A characteristic chronic adverse effect of phenytoin is:
A. Pulmonary interstitial fibrosis
B. Cataract
C. Gingival hyperplasia
D. Deafness
E. Renal stones
Answer: C — Gum hypertrophy (with nystagmus, ataxia) is classic.

PM41. [*] The drug commonly given rectally to abort a prolonged febrile seizure in a child is:
A. Phenytoin
B. Morphine
C. Diazepam
D. Levodopa
E. Atropine
Answer: C — Rectal diazepam quickly terminates seizures.

PM42. [*] Vigabatrin raises brain GABA by inhibiting:
A. Glutamate decarboxylase
B. COMT
C. Acetylcholinesterase
D. GABA transaminase
E. Monoamine oxidase
Answer: D — GABA-T inhibition increases GABA levels.

PM43. [*] After several years of levodopa therapy, a common problem is:
A. Complete cure of the underlying disease
B. Permanent paralysis
C. Deafness
D. Blindness
E. Dyskinesias and "on–off" fluctuations
Answer: E — Motor fluctuations and dyskinesia develop with chronic use.

PM44. [*] Amantadine is useful in Parkinson disease because it:
A. Blocks dopamine receptors
B. Inhibits acetylcholinesterase
C. Blocks GABA receptors
D. Inhibits MAO-A
E. Enhances dopamine release
Answer: E — It promotes dopamine release (and blocks NMDA receptors).

PM45. [*] Excessive daytime sleepiness of narcolepsy is treated with:
A. Diazepam
B. Morphine
C. Atropine
D. Modafinil
E. Phenobarbital
Answer: D — Modafinil is a wake-promoting agent.

PM46. [*] The stimulant used to treat attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is:
A. Diazepam tablets
B. Methylphenidate
C. Haloperidol
D. Baclofen
E. Levodopa
Answer: B — Methylphenidate increases synaptic dopamine/noradrenaline.

PM47. [*] A patient on a monoamine oxidase inhibitor who eats aged cheese may develop:
A. Hypoglycemia
B. Acute flaccid paralysis
C. Diarrhea
D. A hypertensive crisis
E. Deafness
Answer: D — The tyramine reaction causes a hypertensive crisis.

PM48. [*] High fever, rigidity, and autonomic instability after antipsychotics suggest:
A. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
B. Tardive dyskinesia
C. Serotonin syndrome
D. Anesthetic malignant hyperthermia
E. Status epilepticus
Answer: A — NMS is a life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists.

PM49. [*] Ergotamine relieves migraine mainly through:
A. Dopamine blockade
B. Sodium-channel blockade centrally
C. GABA agonism
D. Opioid agonism
E. Cranial vasoconstriction
Answer: E — It constricts dilated cranial vessels.

PM50. [*] Triptans are contraindicated in patients with:
A. Hay fever
B. Eczema
C. Ischemic heart disease
D. Mild iron-deficiency anemia
E. Myopia
Answer: C — Coronary vasoconstriction makes them unsafe in IHD.

PM51. [*] Physostigmine differs from neostigmine in that it:
A. Is a quaternary amine
B. Does not inhibit cholinesterase
C. Is an antimuscarinic
D. Blocks nicotinic receptors
E. Crosses the blood–brain barrier
Answer: E — As a tertiary amine it enters the CNS.

PM52. [*] Pramipexole is used in Parkinson disease as a:
A. A selective MAO-B inhibitor
B. Anticholinergic
C. COMT inhibitor
D. Dopamine receptor agonist
E. NMDA antagonist
Answer: D — It is a non-ergot D2/D3 agonist.

PM53. [*] Diazepam relaxes skeletal muscle (spasticity) by enhancing inhibition mediated by:
A. Glycine
B. Dopamine
C. Acetylcholine
D. Glutamate
E. GABA
Answer: E — It potentiates GABA-A-mediated inhibition in the cord.

PM54. [*] Flumazenil is used to reverse the effects of:
A. Opioids
B. Barbiturates
C. Benzodiazepines
D. Local anesthetics
E. Antipsychotics
Answer: C — It is a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist.

SECTION 6 — PATHOLOGY
========================================

PA1. [*] Rupture of a berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis causes:
A. Subarachnoid hemorrhage
B. Extradural hemorrhage
C. Subdural hemorrhage
D. Intraventricular hemorrhage only
E. Epidural empyema
Answer: A — Berry aneurysms bleed into the subarachnoid space.

PA2. [*] An epidural (extradural) hematoma with a lucid interval is due to rupture of the:
A. Middle meningeal artery
B. Bridging veins
C. Internal carotid artery
D. Great cerebral vein
E. Basilar artery
Answer: A — Often with a temporal bone fracture.

PA3. [*] A subdural hematoma results from tearing of the:
A. Middle meningeal artery
B. Bridging (cortical) veins
C. Cerebral arteries
D. Anterior choroidal artery
E. Vertebral artery
Answer: B — Venous bleeding between dura and arachnoid.

PA4. [*] The plaques of multiple sclerosis represent:
A. Extracellular amyloid deposits
B. Neuronal tumors
C. Old hemorrhage
D. Calcification
E. Demyelination of white matter
Answer: E — Perivenular demyelinating plaques, often periventricular.

PA5. [*] The commonest malignant primary brain tumor in adults is:
A. Glioblastoma multiforme
B. Meningioma
C. Schwannoma
D. Medulloblastoma
E. Craniopharyngioma (sellar)
Answer: A — GBM is the most frequent malignant glioma.

PA6. [*] A benign tumor arising from arachnoid cap cells is the:
A. Glioblastoma
B. Meningioma
C. Astrocytoma
D. Ependymoma
E. Oligodendroglioma
Answer: B — Meningiomas show psammoma bodies and whorls.

PA7. [*] The commonest malignant brain tumor of childhood, arising in the cerebellum, is:
A. Meningioma
B. Glioblastoma
C. Medulloblastoma
D. Schwannoma
E. Pituitary adenoma
Answer: C — Medulloblastoma is a posterior-fossa tumor of children.

PA8. [*] Parkinson disease is characterized pathologically by:
A. Amyloid plaques
B. Caudate atrophy
C. Loss of substantia nigra neurons with Lewy bodies
D. Demyelinating plaques
E. Hemorrhagic necrosis of the mammillary bodies bilaterally
Answer: C — Depigmentation of the nigra with α-synuclein Lewy bodies.

PA9. [*] The histological hallmarks of Alzheimer disease are:
A. Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles
B. Lewy bodies
C. Negri bodies
D. Spongiform vacuolation of the cerebral cortex
E. Demyelination
Answer: A — Senile (amyloid) plaques plus tau tangles.

PA10. [*] Marked atrophy of the caudate nucleus is typical of:
A. Parkinson disease
B. Alzheimer disease
C. Multiple sclerosis
D. Wernicke encephalopathy
E. Huntington disease
Answer: E — Striatal (caudate) degeneration; CAG-repeat disorder.

PA11. [*] Hemorrhagic lesions of the mammillary bodies are characteristic of:
A. Wernicke encephalopathy
B. Huntington disease (chorea)
C. Multiple sclerosis
D. Tabes dorsalis
E. Rabies
Answer: A — Thiamine deficiency damages the mammillary bodies.

PA12. [*] Degeneration of the dorsal columns in neurosyphilis is called:
A. Tabes dorsalis
B. Syringomyelia
C. Subacute combined degeneration
D. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
E. Multiple sclerosis
Answer: A — Tabes dorsalis affects dorsal columns and roots.

PA13. [*] Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis involves degeneration of the:
A. The dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts only
B. Cerebellum
C. Basal ganglia
D. Optic nerve
E. Anterior horn cells and corticospinal tracts
Answer: E — Combined upper and lower motor neuron loss.

PA14. [*] A reliable sign of chronically raised intracranial pressure is:
A. Miosis
B. Papilledema
C. Hypotension
D. Hypothermia
E. Diarrhea
Answer: B — Optic disc swelling reflects raised ICP.

PA15. [*] The earliest microscopic marker of irreversible neuronal ischemia is the:
A. Lewy body
B. Negri body
C. Neurofibrillary tangle formation
D. Psammoma body
E. Red (eosinophilic) neuron
Answer: E — "Red neurons" appear within hours of ischemia.

PA16. [*] Hydrocephalus due to obstruction within the ventricular system is termed:
A. Communicating (non-obstructive) hydrocephalus
B. Hydrocephalus ex vacuo
C. Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus
D. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
E. Pseudotumor cerebri
Answer: C — A block (e.g., aqueduct) prevents CSF outflow.

PA17. [*] Glioblastoma multiforme characteristically shows:
A. Psammoma bodies
B. Rosenthal fibers with eosinophilic granular bodies
C. Necrosis with pseudopalisading of tumor cells
D. Negri bodies
E. Amyloid plaques
Answer: C — Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation.

PA18. [*] Neurofibrillary tangles are composed of:
A. Extracellular beta-amyloid peptide
B. Hyperphosphorylated tau protein
C. Alpha-synuclein
D. Prion protein
E. Ubiquitin alone
Answer: B — Paired helical filaments of tau.

SECTION 7 — MICROBIOLOGY

MI1. [*] The commonest causes of neonatal bacterial meningitis are:
A. Neisseria meningitidis
B. Group B streptococcus and E. coli
C. Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacilli
D. Cryptococcus neoformans
E. Herpes simplex virus
Answer: B — Perinatally acquired organisms.

MI2. [*] The leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults is:
A. Haemophilus influenzae
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae
C. Listeria monocytogenes
D. E. coli
E. Staphylococcus epidermidis
Answer: B — Pneumococcus is the commonest adult cause.

MI3. [*] Epidemic meningitis with a petechial rash in young adults is caused by:
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. Listeria monocytogenes
C. Cryptococcus neoformans
D. Group B streptococcus
E. Neisseria meningitidis
Answer: E — Meningococcus causes meningococcemia with purpura.

MI4. [*] Meningitis in neonates, the elderly, and the immunocompromised may be caused by the Gram-positive rod:
A. Neisseria meningitidis
B. Listeria monocytogenes
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Haemophilus influenzae
E. E. coli
Answer: B — Listeria affects the extremes of age and immunosuppressed.

MI5. [*] In acute bacterial meningitis the CSF typically shows:
A. Lymphocytes with a normal glucose level
B. Entirely normal findings
C. Eosinophilia
D. Red cells only
E. Neutrophils, low glucose, high protein
Answer: E — Purulent CSF with hypoglycorrhachia.

MI6. [*] In viral (aseptic) meningitis the CSF typically shows:
A. Neutrophils with very low glucose
B. Turbid fluid with high protein
C. Lymphocytes with normal glucose
D. Marked eosinophilia
E. No cells at all
Answer: C — Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose.

MI7. [*] Neisseria meningitidis appears on Gram stain as:
A. Gram-positive cocci in chains
B. Gram-positive rods
C. Gram-negative rods
D. Gram-negative diplococci
E. Acid-fast bacilli
Answer: D — Kidney-shaped Gram-negative diplococci.

MI8. [*] Streptococcus pneumoniae appears as:
A. Gram-negative bean-shaped diplococci in pairs
B. Gram-positive rods
C. Spirochaetes
D. Acid-fast bacilli
E. Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci
Answer: E — Encapsulated Gram-positive diplococci.

MI9. [*] Childhood meningitis from Haemophilus influenzae type b has fallen sharply because of:
A. Antibiotic resistance
B. Improved nutrition alone
C. Antiviral therapy
D. Routine Hib vaccination
E. Better sanitation alone
Answer: D — The conjugate Hib vaccine dramatically reduced cases.

MI10. [*] Negri bodies in neurons are diagnostic of:
A. Poliomyelitis
B. Rabies
C. Herpes encephalitis
D. Measles
E. Tetanus
Answer: B — Cytoplasmic Negri bodies mark rabies.

MI11. [*] Poliovirus produces flaccid paralysis by destroying the:
A. Dorsal root ganglia
B. Corticospinal tract
C. Anterior horn cells
D. Cerebellum
E. Basal ganglia
Answer: C — Lower motor neuron loss causes flaccid paralysis.

MI12. [*] Herpes simplex encephalitis characteristically affects the:
A. Occipital lobe
B. Temporal lobe
C. Cerebellum
D. Spinal cord
E. Brainstem only
Answer: B — Hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobes.

MI13. [*] Tetanus is caused by a neurotoxin produced by:
A. Clostridium tetani
B. Clostridium botulinum
C. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
D. Clostridium perfringens
E. Bacillus cereus
Answer: A — Tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory transmitters.

MI14. [*] Flaccid paralysis after eating contaminated canned food is caused by:
A. Clostridium tetani
B. Clostridium botulinum
C. Staphylococcus aureus
D. Salmonella
E. Shigella
Answer: B — Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release.

MI15. [*] India-ink staining of CSF revealing an encapsulated yeast indicates:
A. Tuberculous meningitis
B. Meningococcal meningitis
C. Viral meningitis
D. Cryptococcal meningitis
E. Listeria meningitis
Answer: D — Cryptococcus neoformans (common in HIV).

MI16. [*] Tuberculous meningitis characteristically involves the:
A. Convexity of the cerebrum
B. Spinal cord only
C. Cerebellum only
D. Ventricles only
E. Base of the brain
Answer: E — Basal exudate with lymphocytic, low-glucose CSF.

MI17. [*] Spongiform change of the cortex without inflammation suggests:
A. Acute bacterial meningitis infection
B. Viral encephalitis
C. Multiple sclerosis
D. Toxoplasmosis
E. Creutzfeldt–Jakob (prion) disease
Answer: E — Prion disease causes spongiform encephalopathy.

MI18. [*] Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a late complication of:
A. Mumps
B. Rubella
C. Polio
D. Measles
E. Rabies
Answer: D — A persistent measles infection of the CNS.

MI19. [*] Guillain–Barré syndrome is often preceded by infection with:
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. E. coli
C. Listeria
D. Campylobacter jejuni
E. Staphylococcus aureus
Answer: D — Molecular mimicry triggers demyelination.

MI20. [*] Neurosyphilis is caused by:
A. Borrelia burgdorferi
B. Leptospira
C. Treponema pallidum
D. Mycobacterium leprae
E. Rickettsia
Answer: C — The spirochaete of syphilis.

MI21. [*] The commonest origin of a brain abscess is:
A. Spread from a contiguous focus, often polymicrobial
B. A single bloodborne viral infection from a distant site
C. A prion
D. A parasite only
E. A fungus only
Answer: A — Otitis, sinusitis or hematogenous spread.

MI22. [*] Cryptococcal and tuberculous meningitis are especially common in:
A. Immunocompromised (e.g., HIV) patients
B. Otherwise healthy young competitive athletes
C. Newborns only
D. Vaccinated children
E. Pregnant women only
Answer: A — Opportunistic CNS infections.

MI23. [*] Arboviruses are an important cause of:
A. Peripheral neuropathy
B. Brain abscess
C. Prion disease
D. Spinal cord compression
E. Viral encephalitis
Answer: E — Mosquito-borne encephalitides.

SECTION 8 — PARASITOLOGY

PR1. [*] Cerebral malaria is caused by:
A. Plasmodium vivax
B. Plasmodium ovale
C. Plasmodium malariae species
D. Plasmodium falciparum
E. Toxoplasma gondii

PR2. [*] Neurocysticercosis is caused by the larvae of:
A. Taenia saginata
B. Taenia solium
C. Echinococcus granulosus
D. Ascaris lumbricoides
E. Trichinella spiralis
Answer: B — Pork tapeworm larvae (cysticerci).

PR3. [*] Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in an AIDS patient are most often due to:
A. Plasmodium falciparum
B. Toxoplasma gondii
C. Naegleria fowleri
D. Trypanosoma brucei
E. Schistosoma
Answer: B — Reactivated cerebral toxoplasmosis.

PR4. [*] Rapidly fatal amebic meningoencephalitis after freshwater swimming is caused by:
A. Acanthamoeba
B. Entamoeba histolytica
C. Toxoplasma gondii
D. Naegleria fowleri
E. Giardia lamblia
Answer: D — Naegleria enters via the nose.

PR5. [*] Granulomatous amebic encephalitis in immunocompromised patients is caused by:
A. Naegleria fowleri
B. Acanthamoeba
C. Plasmodium
D. Taenia solium
E. Echinococcus
Answer: B — Acanthamoeba causes chronic granulomatous encephalitis.

PR6. [*] African sleeping sickness is caused by:
A. Trypanosoma cruzi
B. Leishmania donovani species (kala-azar)
C. Plasmodium
D. Toxoplasma
E. Trypanosoma brucei (tsetse fly)
Answer: E — T. brucei invades the CNS causing somnolence.

PR7. [*] A hydatid cyst of the brain is caused by:
A. Taenia solium
B. Echinococcus granulosus
C. Schistosoma mansoni
D. Ascaris lumbricoides worm
E. Toxocara canis
Answer: B — The dog tapeworm forms hydatid cysts.

PR8. [*] Eosinophilic meningitis is classically caused by:
A. Naegleria
B. Angiostrongylus cantonensis
C. Plasmodium
D. Toxoplasma
E. Trypanosoma species (African)
Answer: B — The rat lungworm causes eosinophilic meningitis.

PR9. [*] CNS reactivation in immunocompromised Latin-American patients occurs with:
A. Naegleria
B. Echinococcus species
C. Trypanosoma cruzi
D. Schistosoma
E. Giardia
Answer: C — Chagas disease can cause meningoencephalitis.

PR10. [*] In endemic regions, the commonest cause of acquired adult-onset epilepsy is:
A. Cerebral malaria infection
B. Toxoplasmosis
C. Hydatid disease
D. Neurocysticercosis
E. Schistosomiasis
Answer: D — Calcified cysticerci are highly epileptogenic.

PR11. [*] Naegleria fowleri reaches the brain by crossing the:
A. Blood–brain barrier from the bloodstream
B. Cribriform plate from the nasal mucosa
C. Choroid plexus
D. Spinal nerve roots
E. Optic nerve
Answer: B — It ascends the olfactory nerves through the cribriform plate.

PR12. [*] Coma in cerebral malaria is due to:
A. A circulating exotoxin released into the bloodstream by the parasite
B. Demyelination
C. Sequestration of infected red cells in cerebral microvessels
D. Aneurysmal hemorrhage
E. An autoimmune attack
Answer: C — Cytoadherence obstructs cerebral microcirculation.

PR13. [*] Spinal cord schistosomiasis (myelopathy) is caused by:
A. Taenia solium larval cysts in the cord
B. Echinococcus
C. Toxoplasma
D. Schistosoma eggs lodging in the cord
E. Plasmodium
Answer: D — Ectopic eggs incite a granulomatous myelopathy.
